Dramatic gannet dive wins Bird Photographer of the Year competition

New Scientist September 21, 2026

This dramatic shot of a northern gannet diving for prey bested 24,000 other images to win the overall prize in the Bird Photographer of the Year 2026 competition.

The photo was taken off Shetland, UK, as the bird hunted for fish to feed its offspring. When gannets spot fish, they turn to fly into the wind, stretch out their wings as brakes, precisely adjust their position and then dive-bomb into the water with wings tucked at speeds of up to 86 kilometres per hour.

They have evolved to handle this dramatic moment, with muscles that lock their vertebrae into position, air sacs in the face and chest to protect from impact, and nostrils that prevent jets of water entering.

Advertisement

“The handsome northern gannets lead a dualistic existence,” said Spiers in an announcement about the win. “In the nest, their newborn is carefully nurtured, and a couple’s bond is reinforced by pointing sharp beaks to the sky as they tenderly stroke their white necks together. In flight, hunting mode takes over, and piercing yellow eyes, fringed with blue circles, scour the sea for prey.”

Spiers had been diving in the chilly, 10°C (50°F) waters of Shetland when he realised the sun was visible from his position under the sea. “Even in summer, sunshine is far from guaranteed in this remote British archipelago, so my creative engine started firing when the sunball was visible from underwater. I envisioned the shot of the gannet diving straight through the middle of it, and dedicated my entire dive to capturing that single frame,” he says. “The gannets were diving all around me, but I refused to be distracted and kept my camera pointed at the sun. After a long wait, a gannet finally dived through in the perfect spot and I met the bird as it careened under the sea. The moment was over in a split second.”

A bronze award in the prize’s portrait category was given to David Stowe, who captured this western parotia (Parotia sefilata), below, dancing in the dark rainforest of West Papua, Indonesia, in a dazzling attempt to attract a female.

Donald Chin photographed this protective tawny frogmouth (Podargus strigoides), shown below, near Perth in Australia. As rain falls in the forest, this fledgling seems to raise a wing to cover its siblings. Chin won a gold award in the “bird behaviour” category of the prize.

The below image by Alex Pansier features hundreds, if not thousands, of guillemots (Uria aalge) in flight over Hornøya, Norway. The repeating shapes have an Escher-like quality. Pansier took a silver award in the “birds in flight” category of the prize.

Luca Eberle from Italy photographed the – unfortunately killed, stuffed and discarded – Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus) shown below in Malta. Authorities inspect taxidermy samples to catch illegal hunting of protected species like this one, causing some collectors to dispose of older specimens. Here, a BirdLife Malta officer is shown finding the stuffed vulture, which had been left by the roadside. Eberle won a bronze award in the “conservation, single image” category for this shot.

Another underwater shot, from Romain Barats, features gentoo penguins (Pygoscelis papua) feeding in Charcot Bay, Antarctica, below. Barats was snorkelling when a raft of gentoo penguins appeared to fish and feed on krill. “These iconic birds are incredibly curious so they went straight to me to evaluate if I could be a threat or not. They spent a while swimming so fast around me,” he said in an announcement about the competition, in which he won a bronze award in the “birds in the environment” category.

Swimmer made of quantum light breaks Newton’s third law

New Scientist September 21, 2026

For most objects, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. But if you are swimming upstream in a river of quantum light, the normal rules don’t apply. Physicists have demonstrated that breaking Isaac Newton’s third law of motion in such a setting can be useful, leading to new ways of controlling quantum light in experiments and devices.

Moving upstream against the current is possible, as some animals and boats do, but at the cost of expending energy. Yi Hu at Nankai University in China and his colleagues wondered whether a passive swimmer that doesn’t do so could still move upstream.

The researchers studied upstream swimming in a quantum system. Because past experiments established precise ways of controlling quantum light, they used it to make both their river and swimmer. They created this quantum light fluid by shooting lasers into a special crystal that was exposed to an electric voltage, which made the photons interact and form a river-like system. The swimmer was another beam of quantum light, but this one was shaped to form a single, solitary wave.

Advertisement

Sperm caught breaking Newton’s third law of motion

The action-reaction principle of Newton’s third law would have the swimmer and the river experience the same type of force – either repulsive or attractive – similar to how gravity leads to mutual attraction between our bodies and Earth. Earth attracts us downwards, and experiences an upwards attraction towards us. In contrast, in the experiment, the swimmer experienced an attractive interaction with the river, but the river experienced a repulsive force on the swimmer. This was a “non-reciprocal” interaction that breaks the action-reaction principle. Its net effect was an upstream force on the swimmer, says Hu.

“For me, the biggest takeaway is that active behaviour does not necessarily require an intrinsically active particle or swimmer,” he says.

Mathias Albert at Côte d’Azur University in France says that upstream motion has previously been achieved in other quantum fluids of light, but it always relied on creating tiny vortices behind the swimmer in the fluid, with the recoil from their creation pushing the swimmer, so the new experiment demonstrates a fundamentally different mechanism for motion.

Subscriber-only newsletter

We already know that non-reciprocal interactions can be crucial for shaping the motion of “active matter” systems where objects consume energy to move, such as bacterial mixtures, flocks of birds or swarms of tiny robots. But the experiments by Hu and his colleagues focused on an object that doesn’t consume energy, yet still benefited from non-reciprocal interactions. Their work could therefore usher in the creation of a new type of active matter in a quantum system.

“This question is very much in the air at the moment, with several groups exploring how the concepts of active matter can be combined with quantum fluids and photonic systems,” says Albert.

Sonoluminescence, in which small bubbles in a liquid produce flashes of light when they collapse, is now known to be a quantum process

He says that, eventually, the ability to control chunks of light so they move in some preferred direction could be useful within devices that use quantum light. Such devices are prevalent in, for example, communications or quantum information processing.

Hu says that the team now wants to construct more complex experiments where they could control the swimmer’s motion more precisely or add several swimmers to the fluid at once.

Physical Review A DOI: 10.1103/lwyj-7m5f

The collapse of the AMOC would be catastrophic. How will we know when it’s coming?

New Scientist September 21, 2026

On a sunny evening in July, a research ship called the Sir David Attenborough was working near the Sorgenfri glacier in south-eastern Greenland when a kilometre-long wall of craggy, bulging ice collapsed into the fjord. The scientists on deck watched in stunned silence as an estimated 18 million tonnes of ice slowly flipped over, sending up vast plumes of spray.

Iceberg calving on this scale was once relatively rare – but it has become commonplace in recent years as Earth warms. And that acceleration could have catastrophic impacts that extend far beyond Greenland. It is weakening a system of ocean currents in the North Atlantic that is vital to societies in Europe and around the world. If the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) were to shut down, the continent would plunge into “ice age” winters with year-round long droughts, and agriculture would become close to impossible.

Yet whether the AMOC really will fail, when that might happen and how quickly – these points all remain highly uncertain. And because of that, the threat remains a distant one in policy-makers’ minds. That is why an £81 million plan is now afoot to build an early warning system that could alert humanity if AMOC is nearing a dangerous tipping point.

Advertisement

Oceans are darkening all over the planet – what’s going on?

Data now being collected by the Attenborough research ship is core to that plan. “We might be committed to centuries of change without knowing it,” said ocean scientist Paul Holland at the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as he prepared to set sail from the port of Harwich, UK, some weeks earlier. “We might be passing these tipping points without realising.”

So how worried should we be about the AMOC collapsing, what will it take to build an early warning system, and will the alarm bells persuade governments to pull back from the point of no return – or at least to prepare for the consequences?

The AMOC is a crucial section of an undulating but well-established conveyor belt of ocean currents that flow around the globe. Traversing the entire belt takes a typical “parcel” (about 1 cubic metre) of water about 1000 years.

Like the rest of this conveyor belt, the AMOC, which circulates between North America and Europe, is driven by temperature and salinity. Around the Gulf of Mexico, the harsh sun heats the ocean and drives evaporation. The resulting warm, salty water flows towards the seas between Greenland and the UK in a part of the AMOC called the Gulf Stream. As the circulation pushes north, the atmosphere cools the salty water, so that it becomes denser and cascades towards the ocean floor like a subsurface waterfall. From there, water flows southward along the seafloor back towards the Americas. To replace the water sinking in the North Atlantic, more warm water must then flow from the Gulf of Mexico, powering the circulation.

Without the AMOC, models predict that sea ice would cover the North Sea down to Norfolk in the UK and Friesland in the Netherlands. London would experience an average winter temperature of 2°C (36°F), with cold snaps of -20°C (-4°F). Similar cold would descend on Amsterdam, Brussels, Dublin and Paris. Oslo would see deep freezes of -48°C (-54°F) or below at least every 10 years.

“The winter is like being in the ice age, and in Scotland, it’s in the ice age for half the year,” says Earth system scientist Tim Lenton at the University of Exeter, UK.

Yet this vital circulation is also the section of the global conveyor belt most likely to slow down, or shut down completely, in the coming decades or centuries due to climate change. This possibility was first suggested in a 1987 paper by geochemist Wallace Broecker at Columbia University in New York. Fluctuations in Earth’s climate aren’t always gradual, he wrote, and human-made “global warming”– a term he popularised – could disrupt the feedbacks fuelling the AMOC.

At the time, evidence was mounting that AMOC had shut down in the past because of natural changes in the planet’s temperature. About 12,900 years ago, as the last glacial period was ending, the northern hemisphere suddenly slipped back into near-glacial conditions for 1300 years – a period called the Younger Dryas, after an Arctic flower that spread through Europe then. Shortly after Broecker’s paper was published, geochemists studying the composition of shells trapped in marine sediments found that the AMOC was sending less surface water to the seafloor during the Younger Dryas.

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

Broecker and others argued that the melting of an ice sheet over North America had injected fresh water into the North Atlantic, diluting the salty water arriving via the Gulf Stream and slowing its cascade towards the seafloor. “We play Russian roulette with the climate,” he wrote at the time.

Today, a similar process may be happening again, only with fresh water from Greenland. “There are 200 fjords around Greenland… pumping out icebergs and gushing out meltwater five times faster than they were 30 years ago,” says marine geophysicist Kelly Hogan, who is part of the BAS mission.

Since 2004, sensors measuring water flow have been anchored across the Atlantic as part of the Rapid Climate Change programme. Although it has found early indications that AMOC is weakening, it will take several further decades of data collection to confirm this. Alongside this monitoring, an analysis of how historical Atlantic surface temperatures have shifted concluded that AMOC has slowed 15 per cent since 1950. And the appearance of a “cold blob” in the North Atlantic – the only part of Earth’s surface that has been cooling over the past 150 years – suggests the AMOC is delivering less warm water to the area than before.

These aren’t good omens. Yet climate models still vary hugely in terms of how soon they predict the AMOC could reach a tipping point, and how soon after that it would shut down. In June, for instance, a study found a 10 to 20 per cent chance the AMOC has already crossed the point of no return, in which case it could collapse as soon as 2060. But other research this year found the AMOC would weaken only gradually or, if humanity emits carbon at a lesser rate, not at all.

The Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a UK government-backed science agency, is building an early warning system to improve these forecasts and update them in almost real time – rather than waiting years, or decades, for studies to come to fruition. To do this, researchers first need to figure out the amount of meltwater from Greenland that is entering the AMOC, what form it is in and how that is altering its flow.

On the Attenborough research ship before the expedition, Holland pulled up a map of results from the UK government’s flagship climate model on a screen. Red pixels south of Greenland indicated where dense, salty water is sinking in the AMOC today. Then Holland switched to a forecast for intense global warming in 2090. The red sinking pixels had almost completely disappeared. “This is a really terrifying prospect. So the question is, is this realistic?” he said.

Roughly half of the fresh water from Greenland comes from the surface of the ice sheet, which is being melted by warming air temperatures. The other half comes from the fjords, where warming ocean waters melt the glaciers from below, and where icebergs calve off, like the enormous ice face that toppled in front of the ship.

The second half is difficult to model. For instance, many fjord glaciers rest on relatively shallow sills of bedrock. If they recede into deeper regions of the fjord, the calving can speed up. “It’s an unstable, self-sustaining process,” says oceanographer Pierre Dutrieux at BAS. “It’s going to retreat like crazy until it finds another sill.”

As a result, the UK’s top climate model may be either under- or overestimating the fresh water coming from Greenland. And because icebergs can float thousands of kilometres before they melt, it may be incorrectly predicting where and when that fresh water hits the AMOC. “We need to measure the entire chain of processes,” said Holland.

To do that, researchers on the ARIA-funded Greenland Ice to Atlantic (or GIANT) mission have a suite of gadgets at their disposal. “GIANT is the James Bond of science projects,” joked Athena Dinar, head of communications at BAS. Boaty McBoatface, an autonomous underwater vehicle shaped like a fat yellow torpedo, will scan the position of icebergs and bergy bits in the fjords; DriX, a red surface robot with a sonar pod underneath it, will map the geometry of ice sheet faces; and small bundles of sensors will, once delivered by a robot, automatically drill themselves into glacier fronts, all to measure how much of the retreat is due to calving versus ice melt. This information will then be fed into ice-sheet models, which will be included in climate models to improve AMOC tipping-point forecasts.

The next phase of the ARIA project will focus on finding a way to give routine updates about these risks. One idea is to build an AI model that can reproduce these forecasts without weeks or months of supercomputing time. The AI would automatically analyse satellite imagery of ice fronts to spot accelerations in glacier loss that could increase the freshwater input to the AMOC. As a side point, regular warnings like these would be valuable to local Inuit who fish and hunt seals and whales in Greenland’s coastal fjords. They would know that an outpouring of meltwater or icebergs was coming that might affect these crucial hunting grounds.

An early warning system would also need to analyse changes in AMOC ocean circulation. Climate scientist Jon Robson at the University of Reading, UK, is on one of several ARIA-funded teams that are focusing on a crucial part of the AMOC called the subpolar gyre, a vast swirl of ocean currents south of Greenland where warm, salty water is cooled by the atmosphere and sinks.

The ice sheet’s melt is expected to slow down the rotation and sinking of that water. Then, a sudden shock could push the weakened AMOC past its tipping point. Because we have never directly observed AMOC collapse – or any climate tipping point – we need to figure out what to look for, says Robson. He and his colleagues are trying to find potential shocks, such as a sudden influx of fresh water from disintegrating Arctic sea ice. “It may be that there is a very definite threshold in the system,” he says. “But it could be that it’s much more blurry.”

Although it is challenging to pin down exactly when the AMOC could shut down, its impacts are more certain. Besides lowering winter temperatures across Europe, AMOC collapse would amplify the North Atlantic storm track, bringing more frequent winter storms and causing wild swings between these cold snaps and warm spells. European summers would be almost as hot as today, thanks largely to continued global warming. But the weather would be drier year-round, especially in southern Europe. Droughts like the one that has helped fuel record wildfires in France and Spain this summer would become more frequent and intense. The cold and especially the dryness would wipe out agriculture in some places. Only 7 per cent of the UK would be arable, down from 32 per cent today.

AMOC collapse would also diminish monsoon rainfall by almost 30 per cent in West Africa and 20 per cent in India. This could undermine food supplies not only in these areas, where most agriculture relies on the annual rains, but also around the world, since India is the biggest producer of rice and the Ivory Coast of cocoa.

“You’re getting a whole-system shock,” says René van Westen at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. “Our global society is built around a strong AMOC.”

Free newsletter

The ARIA team is aiming to have a prototype early warning system ready by 2030. They hope that by giving governments and key industries an evolving forecast of how imminent a tipping point is, it could spur them to invest in adapting to the potential consequences, as well as in trying to avoid collapse altogether.

Discussions about how this would work in practice are only just beginning. Each year, the Met Office, the UK’s weather service, issues a forecast of global temperature and weather trends over the next decade, such as the per cent chance that global warming will exceed 1.5°C. That could be expanded to include the latest probability of AMOC collapse, says Robson. In addition, an early warning system could issue monthly reports of the risks. These could range from a level one, representing no elevated threat, to level three, indicating imminent subpolar gyre collapse, to level five, showing the AMOC tipping point has been crossed, says Lenton.

In July, ARIA met with representatives from the UK and other European governments, as well as from industries like water, insurance and finance, to ask what information they would find useful. One idea is that the system could give a running menu of the options available for adapting to AMOC collapse, such as building reservoirs or desalination plants, and insulating houses. “[We could put] it in terms of, well, in 10 years’ time, those opportunities might be more limited or more expensive,” says Gemma Bale, programme director at ARIA.

An ambitious form of climate modelling aims to pin the blame for disasters – from floods to heatwaves – on specific companies. Is this the tool we need to effectively prosecute the world’s biggest carbon emitters?

Researchers’ biggest fear isn’t that the ARIA programme will fail to build an early warning system, but that governments and industry will fail to heed the warning. They have been alerting politicians to the dire consequences of climate change, including AMOC collapse, for almost 40 years. Other attempts to warn of risk thresholds, such as the goal to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, have failed.

Even today, in the UK’s relatively mild and stable climate, 13 per cent of households have trouble keeping their homes warm, while the government doesn’t keep grain reserves and no new water reservoirs have been built since 1992.

Van Westen sees little point in building an early warning system. “The risk of reaching the tipping point… is too high to ignore,” he says. “That should be already enough motivation.”

But Hogan argues that the ARIA programme is our best hope of avoiding these catastrophic outcomes before it’s too late. She has a 16-year-old daughter who could live to see the societal upheaval caused by a slowing AMOC.

“I look at her future and think, what’s it going to be like for them?”

SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight

New Scientist September 18, 2026

SpaceX’s reusable rocket, Starship – the tallest and most powerful ever launched – will orbit Earth for the first time within days. And because it will also release working Starlink V3 satellites, it will be the first commercially useful Starship mission.

The company has announced that a launch window will open at 7.15am CDT (1.15pm BST) on 22nd September, during which Starship will launch from the company’s Starbase site in Texas.

The flight – Starship’s 14th – will reach an altitude of 275 kilometres and complete six orbits of Earth over 10 hours, with re-entry and splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean, to the west of Chile.

Advertisement

SpaceX’s 1 million satellites could avoid environmental checks

This will make it by far the longest and most ambitious test flight of Starship to date. All 13 previous Starship test flights have been, at best, sub-orbital.

Starship is made up of two parts: an upper stage, confusingly also called Starship, and a lower stage, called Super Heavy. Currently, SpaceX is testing the latest third generation of each section using a fail-fast, learn-fast strategy more common to Silicon Valley than the conservative world of space exploration.

SpaceX is several years into its development programme for Starship, intended to be a rapidly reusable and extremely powerful launch vehicle that will take over the rollout of the company’s Starlink satellites and be a central part of NASA’s Artemis moon missions.

Free newsletter

The 14th flight will also see 26 Starlink V3 satellites launched for the first time. Thousands of these new devices will join the existing constellation of satellites that provides internet connections around the world. Until now, Starship test flights have launched only dummy test satellites.

Davide Amato at Imperial College London says that an orbital test is indicative of confidence within the company that the rocket will at least survive the journey to orbit and the release of satellites. But he says that re-entry, where the company has faced problems during recent tests, may be another matter.

“In short, they’re making good progress towards introducing Starship as a successful commercial launcher,” says Amato. “Whether Starship will be ‘revolutionary’, as promised by their CEO, will depend on whether they will be able to achieve a high launch cadence and on whether their design is cost-effective.”

SpaceX is about to launch tallest and most powerful rocket in history

Leah-Nani Alconcel at the University of Birmingham, UK, says that the 14th test flight will be a key step for SpaceX. Not only will the release of V3 satellites help the company update its Starlink constellation – the new satellites fly in a lower orbit than existing Starlink satellites and have higher data capacity – but their larger size than previous models will go some way to showing whether Starship is up to the task of launching its proposed Starmind data centre spacecraft, which are substantially larger.

“I don’t think it’s a huge jump in operational complexity for the launch vehicle, but demonstrating the Starlink V3 delivery to orbit is a significant step,” says Alconcel. “It may not be as flashy as the ‘chopstick catch‘ for the vehicle stages, but it would be a big boost to their commercial capabilities to have both the already-established high-cadence Falcon 9 and a proven Starship in their repertoire.”

A rocket launched last year is thought to have smashed into the lunar surface this morning, creating the moon’s newest crater

Three of the satellites due to be released on this flight have been modified to include cameras that can scan Starship’s heat shield whilst in orbit and transmit images to engineers on Earth.

During the 13th test flight, the booster stage made its ascent as planned, but during descent only eight of the 13 engines intended to slow its fall reignited, causing it to make a hard splashdown into the ocean rather than the planned gentle simulated landing on water. Neither the booster nor upper stage will attempt to make a controlled landing on the 14th flight.

Only two Starship flights have taken place so far in 2026, with flight 14 due to be the third. The upcoming flight will also be the second since SpaceX’s flotation on the stock market, which made controversial founder Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire. The number of flights has fallen far beyond bold estimates made in previous years; SpaceX officials hoped to launch as many as 25 Starship test flights last year. In reality, only five test flights occurred that year.

SpaceX didn’t respond to a request for an interview, but the company says on its website that “there have been several modifications to hardware and software to address issues seen on the previous flight”.

Physicists are scrambling to make sense of possible dark matter signal

New Scientist September 18, 2026

We may have finally spotted a dark matter particle – but figuring out exactly what kind of particle it was is a daunting task. Even as researchers race to confirm they really did detect an unknown particle, physicists around the world have already started working out what sort of dark matter particle it might have been.

The potential particle in question was found at the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector in South Dakota and announced on 1 September. The detector uses a huge tank of liquid xenon to look for signatures of dark matter particles smashing into the nuclei of xenon atoms, which are expected to produce a burst of light in response to any collision that would then be picked up by the arrays of cameras surrounding the tank.

The LZ group recorded only a single burst of light, and there is about a 1-in-200 chance that the signal was a fluke event rather than evidence that dark matter was there – but nevertheless it is tantalising.

Advertisement

Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics

What makes the signal even more intriguing is that it was at a higher energy than would be expected if the particle were a standard weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP, the simplest proposed type of dark matter. “It’s an anomalous event,” says Henning Flaecher at the University of Bristol in the UK, part of the LZ group. “It’s not what you would expect from the most general dark matter models.” The fact that this high-energy event was spotted, with no accompanying lower-energy collisions, makes it exceedingly unlikely that this particle, if it exists, is a “vanilla” WIMP, he says.

In the weeks since the announcement, theorists have released scores of papers digging into the data, searching for answers. “The large number of papers is less a statement that theorists believe the event is a [true] dark matter discovery and more a reflection of the fact that, if it persists, its energy already tells us quite a lot about types of physical processes that could produce it,” says Juri Smirnov at the University of Liverpool in the UK.

Many of those papers debate the possibility that the particle could be what is called a higgsino, a type of non-“vanilla” WIMP. It arises from a theoretical framework called supersymmetry, in which every known particle is proposed to have a “superpartner”, with some similar properties but different spin. In supersymmetry, the higgsino would be the superpartner of the Higgs boson.

Subscriber-only newsletter

A higgsino is the simplest WIMP explanation still available to explain the LZ signal, according to JiJi Fan at Brown University in Rhode Island. “It gives rise to a wealth of signals that could be searched for at different experimental frontiers.” Plus, a higgsino detection event is predicted to be unaccompanied by a host of lower-energy collisions, matching the signal detected by the LZ group.

However, the higgsino has its problems. The most basic model of that sort of particle that could explain the LZ detection seems to be ruled out by constraints from other experiments. This doesn’t mean the particle couldn’t have been a higgsino, but it does suggest the higgsino in question would need to have had a much higher mass than expected.

Many other models have been proposed to explain the detection, though. Among them are several models of dark matter particles originating in extra dimensions. While this may seem an unnecessarily complicated line of enquiry, these models were already being studied to solve other problems in particle physics, says Lisa Randall at Harvard University, a co-author of one such paper. “In some sense, the data looks like it’s calling out for something like this: it avoids the pre-existing constraints and fits quite naturally.”

Particle collisions are inherently quantum, but much of that character is lost when we turn them into classical data. Sarah Alam Malik explores whether preserving more of it could help us spot signs of dark matter and other new physics

An extra-dimensional dark matter candidate could both fit the LZ detection and explain why the fundamental particles have the masses they do, a long-standing puzzle, she says. Other models propose a whole dark matter sector, with multiple types of dark particles.

Right now, there is no way to tell which, if any, of these models might be correct. “I don’t think the data currently justify saying one of these is ‘the’ explanation,” says Smirnov. Some of them do come with additional predictions, though, which will be particularly useful when trying to pick through so many ideas, he says.

As the LZ team and other teams at detectors around the world continue to analyse their data, looking for additional events to confirm that the dark matter particle was real, all of these ideas could help them know exactly what it is they are looking for. “Anomalies could come and go, as we all know,” says Fan. “My take is that they provide us with some concrete targets to think: is this expected? Are there new territories/questions in theory or experiments we should cover? No matter whether the LZ event is confirmed, some of these topics would lead to long-term research.”

Simeon Brown acknowledges ‘the pressure is real’ but health targets moving in right direction

New Zealand Herald September 22, 2026

Simeon Brown has acknowledged the stress on the health system but says things are getting better. Photo / NZME

Health Minister Simeon Brown has acknowledged that a tough winter flu season has meant “the pressure is real” in the health system, but says it is moving in the right direction.

In a speech to BusinessNZ, he acknowledged the stress on the health system, both the real pressure in terms and political pressure in terms of the increased salience of attacks.

But Brown claimed some of the criticism on the health system did not reflect the reality.

“Now, like every winter and every election season, health has not exactly been quiet. If you have followed the news about our health system in recent months, you could even be forgiven for thinking it had stopped working.

“The pressure is real. Our hospitals are busy, winter has been hard, and people are still waiting too long for a GP appointment. I’ve never said otherwise.

“But there is a long way between a system under pressure and one that has failed. Under successive governments, negative claims are made about the state of our health system.

“The claim gets made, it gets reported, and then it quietly recedes until it is politically useful again. But that is not what patients are describing to me.

“Not a week goes by without someone telling me they expected the worst, because of what they had read, and instead they were seen quickly, treated well, and looked after by people who could not have done more for them,” Brown said.

Brown said health had been “treated as a political football” for as long as he had been in Parliament.

He said that that the people making the loudest claims about the system did not deal with the consequences of their attacks, which were carried by patients who become “worried about the care they will get”.

Brown himself did not fully abstain from politics in the speech, noting that the Greens’ plan to increase income tax at the top end of the income spectrum would risk sending nurse practitioners offshore.

He published data this morning showing five of the Government’s general health targets are heading in the right direction.

Brown defended the Government’s decision to restore health targets, which Labour had scrapped when it came into power in 2017.

“That is like taking down the departures board. The trains are still late.

“The passengers are still waiting. They just have no idea how long for, and nobody has to explain the delay.

“We can see now what that cost. Accountability was lost, performance declined, and waitlists blew out,” Brown said.

Health targets

Compare district performance across five health measures for April to June 2026.

2030 target: 90% of patients receiving cancer treatment within 31 days of the decision to treat. Compared with the previous quarter.

Source: Ministry of Health, Health Targets Report Card, April–June 2026. Compared with the previous quarter.

Brown said “87% of patients began treatment within 31 days of a decision to treat, up from 85% three years ago”.

“Behind that number are thousands of families getting answers and starting treatment sooner. A mother beginning breast cancer treatment. A grandfather starting care for prostate cancer. A young person newly diagnosed with leukaemia,” he said.

He noted that some regions had already hit the Government’s target.

Brown said that childhood immunisations had improved, saying “84% of children are now fully immunised by the age of two, seven points higher than the 77% we inherited three years ago”.

Brown said the Government’s Elective Boost, which attempts to reduce waitlist by funding more surgeries including in private hospitals, was working.

Brown produced data showing a dramatic reduction in the number of patients who are waiting more than four months for an elective procedure

Brown noted that for years the number of people waiting more than four months “only went up”, peaking at 34,566 early last year.

“Now, simply stopping a climb like that would have been an achievement on its own. But this line did not just stop climbing. It has turned around.

“Today there are more than 14,000 fewer people on that list than at the peak. That is a reduction of 41%, and the lowest it has been since November 2021,” Brown said.

Sunk cost of MBIE’s botched IT project rises to more than $50m

New Zealand Herald September 22, 2026

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley appeared before a Parliament select committee. Photo / Mark Mitchell

Fresh admissions from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment reveal an additional $10 million swallowed by its botched immigration IT project, taking the total known sunk cost to almost $51m and counting.

Ministry chief executive Nic Blakeley, appearing this morning before Parliament’s Education and Workforce select committee and accompanied by several officials, revealed extra spending had been discovered related to the Biometric Capability Upgrade project, which was scrapped late last year after years of delays amid persistent bugs.

Blakeley admitted the project had been “incorrectly capitalised” in June last year and MBIE had also recommended to ministers to write off the cost of the associated In Person Enrolment (IPE) project, which was split from the BCU project, because it was “now considered unusable”, he said.

Blakeley then revealed how the latest assessment of the cost was $42m for the BCU project and $8.7m for the IPE project, totalling $50.7m.

However, he admitted he was still not confident that was the final total costs, raising concerns about MBIE’s financial controls.

It comes as the Public Service Commission continues its review of the IT project, led by Michael Heron KC, which was initially intended to conclude before the election but is understood to be facing delays.

The ministry has been unable to establish the overall cost of the project, which was ongoing for seven years, and has engaged an independent financial auditor to figure it out.

However, this is the latest in a series of updates showing more money than was known had been wasted on the project, which was designed to upgrade New Zealand’s biometric identity management system.

In June, Immigration Minister Erica Stanford was first to reveal about $33m had been wasted on the defunct project, while also accusing ministry officials of misleading successive ministers and using “creative accounting” in splitting the project to avoid Cabinet scrutiny.

That cost estimate was revised in July when Stanford again revealed a further $6m had been discovered as being spent on the project.

In the week before that revelation, MBIE told Stanford that staffing costs for that year were zero and just $236 had been spent on contractors. After being challenged by Stanford’s office, later informed Stanford he had discovered the extra $6m.

At that point, Blakeley couldn’t guarantee about $40m was the final sunk cost and announced the financial audit.

However, today’s admission was yet another revision, taking the known cost to $50.7m.

The saga includes Blakeley offering his resignation, which was declined, after Parliament’s Privileges Committee found he had deliberately misled a select committee over the project. In March, Blakeley and former Immigration NZ head Alison McDonald did not reveal the project had been canned months earlier when asked about its progress.

The pair apologised to the Privileges Committee at their hearing, arguing they hadn’t deliberately misled MPs, but the committee made up of cross-party MPs decided otherwise while not calling for any further sanction.

Blakeley said he had offered his resignation to Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche following the committee’s findings but Roche hadn’t accepted it, saying it wouldn’t be fair or proportionate.

“Mr Blakeley was only six weeks into the chief executive role when this occurred. That does not excuse what happened, but they are factors I considered in reaching my decision about his position,” Roche said.

In June, Roche said the commission’s review would take about three or four months, telling the Herald he expected it to conclude ahead of the November 7 election.

However, the Herald understands from those with knowledge of the review that it could continue after the election, given the extent to which new information is coming to light.

The Herald has approached the Public Service Commission for comment.

The review is separate to the review into the MBIE-run, $336m Our Future Services programme; a seven-year visa processing rebuild that began last year, had failed to meet its targets and had been due for completion between June and December last year.

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

A North Canterbury high school is mourning the loss of a “much-loved” teacher who has died after a battle with breast cancer.

In a statement, Rangiora High School said Kathryn Cunningham “was an excellent educator who inspired many students with her love of science and the natural world”.

Cunningham had begun teaching in the school’s science department in 2010 and was also “a proud ex-student” of Rangiora High School.

A Givealittle page set up to support Cunningham and her family said she discovered a lump while breastfeeding her daughter in late 2022.

The page read that a week before Christmas of that year, Cunningham received the diagnosis of Stage 3 breast cancer.

“Throughout 2023, Kathryn fought through intensive treatment, including chemotherapy, surgery and radiation,” the page read.

“Things were looking positive, and she transitioned to hormone blockers with a real sense of hope for the future.”

Despite this, in July last year, Cunningham was diagnosed with Stage 4 incurable cancer, which spread to her bones and liver.

Email us

The page read that while initial targeted therapy provided six months of stability, several hospitalisations for infections meant Cunningham had to switch back to chemotherapy and radiation.

Cunningham had also hoped to return to the classroom, but ongoing health setbacks including exhaustion and chronic pain meant she had been unable to do so.

“For anyone who knows Kathryn, you know she is the first to help others and the last to want a fuss made over her,” the page read.

“However, she has humbly allowed us to create this page as a way her community can support her.”

Rangiora High School said Cunningham was “much loved” as a colleague, teacher and friend and will be “deeply missed” by our school community.

The school extended their condolences and love to Cunningham’s family.

New Zealand Herald September 22, 2026

Taxpayers’ Union executive director Jordan Williams says it is “very tempting” to want to sue Nicky Hager over his new book, Dirty Work.

The book, released at an event in Wellington last night, made several claims against the group and its co-founders, Williams and David Farrar. That included that the group had an internal dispute in 2022 over whether it should move beyond tax and economic issues and campaign more heavily on Māori and co-governance issues.

Hager told a crowd of hundreds last night that it was an exposé of the “latest front for New Zealand’s hard right”.

It also claimed the TPU settled an employment dispute involving allegations of sexual harassment against Williams. He rejects the allegation.

“This really came from nowhere,” he told Ryan Bridge TODAY this morning.

“The suggestion that there is a settlement of some kind, or the allegations in relation to that were settled, is totally false. My chair Ruth Richardson has dealt with that, she’s checked with every of the historic chairs and the co-founder who sat on the board until 2022. It is totally wrong.”

Williams said the book was “full of inaccuracies”. He alleged Hager failed to put the book’s allegations to them, seek an interview, or give them a chance to respond before publication.

When asked if he will sue Hager, Williams said, “It’s very tempting and a lot of people are texting me in relation to that. But the book’s primary objective is to derail me, to derail David, and to derail the Taxpayers’ Union.

“And we have the most important work over the next five or six weeks. We’ve got to show New Zealanders the extent to which we are on an unaffordable path.”

Hager also joined Bridge later in the show and was asked if he was worried about being sued.

“I’m not at all worried about being sued, but my lawyers would say to me to be suitably careful in what I’m saying, which is why I am.”

Williams said the TPU would be launching election campaigns over the next few weeks.

“This is the most important work of every three years, and I’m not going to let a far-left activist successfully derail. What I’m saying is it’s a question for later.”

The book also claimed Farrar used access to a National election database to send mailouts to homes occupied by “wealthy National and ACT voters”.

Williams said this was “totally wrong”.

“I’m going to dig out the invoice. We purchased that data from a property data company... it’s such a serious allegation and poor old David, it was never put to him because despite having said to Nicky Hager, ‘We will not injunct you, come and talk to us, we’ll be open’, that is just an example of the way this far-left activist works.”

Hager told Bridge, “I was told this by a National Party source and someone who was working in the Taxpayers’ Union office.”

He said he wasn’t as “rock solid” on the claim as he was about the sexual harassment claim.

Bridge asked him if there was anything else he wasn’t rock solid on.

“When you’re investigating a subject which is secret and has deliberately been kept secret, there’s a chance that sometimes there’ll be something wrong.

“But overall, I was working with really reliable people and what’s happened is that they have gone through the book overnight and found one or two or three things that they can draw attention to, whereas there’s this huge weight of evidence apart from that which they’re conveniently not mentioning.”

Hager claimed in the book Farrar wanted the Taxpayers’ Union to “weigh in on these Māori issues more”, while staff pushed back, saying: “That’s not our mission” and “we’re here to fight about tax rates and economics”.

Hager wrote that the dispute went to the board, which changed the TPU slogan from “Lower taxes, less waste and more transparency” to “More Accountability”. One staffer quoted in the book said the change “legitimised a move towards race”.

Responding to this section yesterday, Farrar said: “I can’t speak to anything other than what is attributed to me, but I can say it is categorically wrong in relation to me.”

Hager says then-chairman Ashley Church resigned because he opposed the organisation’s direction. Williams’ own 10th-anniversary history confirms Church resigned over the otherwise unanimous decision to take on Three Waters and “the way it was done”.

In Dirty Work, Hager claims British American Tobacco external affairs managers Elliot Steel and later Stu Mullin met Taxpayers’ Union staff privately, gave instructions and discussed campaign plans.

Those involved included Williams and successive TPU campaign managers Louis Houlbrooke, Connor Molloy and, Hager claims, probably Callum Purves. Hager says BAT paid the TPU, which in turn paid Williams’ Campaign Company to produce campaign messages, petitions, advertisements and websites.

Molloy later travelled to Panama for the WHO’s 2024 tobacco-control conference, where he promoted lighter regulation of alternative nicotine products and joined the US Taxpayers Protection Alliance at its GoodCOP counter-event.

Houlbrooke later became an Act senior press secretary, Purves is Act’s general manager and party secretary, and Molloy is now Act’s deputy campaign director.

Hager told those at the launch event at Unity Books in Wellington that Dirty Work was largely based on insiders; former TPU staffers and National Party members who were “unhappy about the state of New Zealand politics”.

Bridge asked Williams this morning if the group had taken money from a tobacco company and had they paid for free flights.

He said they had taken “one of the lowest percentages of any taxpayer group in the world”.

“We’re really open, and we’ve been open for more than a decade, that less than 3% of our revenue is from industry. That’s booze, that’s sugar, that’s nicotine.”

Hager pointed to some stories in the book, which included recounting Act leader David Seymour’s becoming what Hager described as “Mr anti-Treaty” and on what he said was a “hit-job” on former 1News political editor Maiki Sherman, who resigned earlier this year.

One of the key allegations of Hager’s comments was that the TPU public statements opposing government waste did not reveal the group’s main purpose.

He challenged claims that the group had a wide-ranging supporter base, which he alleged were “angry old men in their 70s and 80s and sometimes their late 60s who have bought into their idea and believed their untruths” about the threat of evolving Māori rights.

Asking himself why publish a book before the election, Hager said there were two reasons; the first being elections were the time we should be thinking about politics: “What better time?”

He then claimed coalition ministers had benefited from the work of groups like the TPU.

“They should be held accountable by the public.”

Asked during a media stand-up how the book showed links between political parties and lobby groups, Hager claimed there are politicians in all the main right-wing parties that tolerate or collaborate with the TPU.

“I don’t think they even realise what a terrible decision they’re making.”

Asked what made the TPU’s relationship with parties distinct from other lobby groups’ relationships with parties, Hager claimed there was a “phony, fake, misleading network, a spider’s web” of groups that were “filling up the political space”.

“I think that if the Taxpayers’ Union and its key members were looked at critically a lot of their power would disappear.”

Hager said he didn’t find explicit instruction from the National Party to TPU over any matters but then claimed it wasn’t necessary because they were aligned.

Williams, who also featured in Hager’s 2014 work, Dirty Politics, said the organisation had been targeted specifically because of its success, noting they have built “the largest taxpayer movement in the English-speaking world”.

He said in his email to members about two-thirds of donations come from grassroots donors, while less than 3% came from “industry memberships and donations (including alcohol and nictonie) [sic]”.

The email repeatedly asked supporters to donate.

“The next few days are going to be hard. I’m not going to pretend otherwise. But we can’t let him win,” the email ends.

In 2018, the police apologised and paid “substantial damages” to Hager after unlawfully searching his home during the investigation into the hacking that led to the Dirty Politics book.

The settlement came almost four years after the publication of Dirty Politics, which alleged the office of former Prime Minister Sir John Key ran a dirty tricks campaign through right-wing bloggers.

Hager wrote the book after an anonymous source known only as Rawshark provided information said to have been hacked from Whale Oil blogger Cameron Slater. Police launched an investigation into the identity of Rawshark after Slater complained about being a victim of hacking.

That complaint led detectives to search Hager’s home on October 2, 2014, taking computers, paperwork and other material. In the settlement that followed, police apologised for a range of breaches of Hager’s rights, including wrongly using an exception in the Privacy Act to access 10 months of Hager’s banking data from Westpac.

“This sends a vital message that people can share important information with journalists with confidence that their identities will be protected,” Hager said.

Hager’s publications also include 2006’s The Hollow Men and 2011’s Other People’s Wars.

Dolphin found dead on Invercargill beach died from toxoplasmosis

New Zealand Herald September 22, 2026

The deceased Hector's Dolphin found on a beach in Invercargill. Photo / DOC

By RNZ

A pregnant Hector’s dolphin found dead on an Invercargill beach died from toxoplasmosis.

The dolphin was carrying a male calf when it was found on Ōreti Beach on August 20.

The Department of Conservation (DoC) said toxoplasmosis is a parasitic disease that reproduces in cats and is a significant threat to dolphins.

DoC marine species manager Michelle Boyle said the loss of the female and her calf was significant for the threatened species.

“Hector’s dolphins are found only in New Zealand waters and every individual is important to the population and its recovery,” she said.

Around 15,000 Hector’s dolphins over the age of one remain.

Cats are the only host in which the parasite can reproduce sexually and produce eggs.

Boyle said the microscopic eggs could survive for months or even years, depending on environmental conditions, giving them time to enter waterways and the sea through contaminated soil and freshwater run-off.

“Hector’s and Māui dolphins spend much of their time in nearshore waters, which can bring them into contact with contaminants entering the marine environment from the land,” she said.

“This case is a reminder that threats to our native marine species don’t only come from activities happening at sea. What happens on land can also affect the health of our marine environment.”

Timely reports of dead animals were valuable because examination helped DoC understand causes of death and threats faced by vulnerable species, Boyle said.

Caesar the kiwi hatches at Taupō’s Gallagher Kiwi Burrow

New Zealand Herald September 22, 2026

Casear, the kiwi chick, hatched on September 11 and is now being raised at the Gallagher Kiwi Burrow in Taupō. Photo / Tom Eley

Caesar may have an impressive name, but the kiwi’s origins are less regal.

The chick takes his name from the Caesar cut, a short, forward-combed hairstyle named after Roman ruler Julius Caesar and popular in the 1990s.

The chick hatched on September 11 at the Gallagher Kiwi Burrow in Taupō where the first eggs of the 2026 breeding season arrived from Cape Sanctuary and Maungataniwha in Hawke’s Bay.

Kiwi chicks at Cape Sanctuary are named after hairstyles.

The inspiration came from Prize, a male kiwi at Cape Sanctuary who often got carried away while preening his chicks, leaving some with distinctive “haircuts”.

Prize is Caesar’s father, but the chick has escaped the over-zealous grooming but still got the name.

Cape Sanctuary is New Zealand’s largest predator-fenced, privately owned and funded wildlife sanctuary. Andy and Liz Lowe and Julian Robertson founded it in 2006 and it operates in partnership with Ngāti Mihiroa.

National charity Save the Kiwi operates Kiwi Burrow.

The Waikato Herald was given a behind-the-scenes look at the Gallagher Kiwi Burrow at Wairakei Golf & Sanctuary as the facility began its seventh breeding season.

For the facility’s keepers, the journey from egg to kiwi starts well before the first crack appears in the shell.

They check and measure eggs before putting them in an incubator that automatically rotates them. This mimmicks the movement of an incubating male kiwi.

Keepers also candle the eggs, which involves shining a light through the shell to see the developing chick inside.

The eggs are one of the most fascinating parts of the job for Save the Kiwi’s senior kiwi keeper Kim McGuire and husbandry manager Helen McCormick.

“Most people probably think the birds and chicks are our favourite part, but I think for both Helen and I, it’s the eggs,” McGuire said.

“You have this thing that is just, add a bit of heat and they totally develop into those chicks.

“Just phenomenal.”

As hatching approaches, the keepers watch closely for the chick’s position.

At one end of the egg is an air cell, a pocket of air separated from the rest of the egg by a membrane.

The chick needs to get its bill towards the air cell so it can begin breathing.

If it is facing the wrong way, it can struggle to hatch and keepers may need to intervene.

The best hatches were the ones where keepers did not have to intervene, McGuire said.

Once the chicks are out, staff weigh and check them daily. The yolk absorbed before hatching provides nourishment while they learn to feed themselves.

Keepers did not immediately know whether a chick was male or female, McCormick said.

Feathers are collected while the birds are at the Burrow and sent away for sex testing.

After about three to four weeks, the chicks leave the Burrow for a kiwi crèche or predator-controlled sanctuary.

There they continue growing towards about 1kg, known as the “stoat-proof weight”, when they have a much better chance of surviving introduced predators.

Wairakei Golf & Sanctuary general manager operations Warren Collett said about six or seven kiwi were currently roaming the property, although a couple had lost their transmitters.

“They’re roaming around out there having a ball,” Collett said.

A part-time ranger checks the sanctuary’s external predator fence, while about 250 traps are maintained across the property.

The Gallagher Kiwi Burrow has hatched more than 450 kiwi since opening in October 2019, with eggs arriving from conservation projects throughout the North Island.

Keepers avoid treating them like pets, despite spending weeks caring for them.

“These are wild animals and we don’t cuddle them,” McGuire said.

Some chicks quietly tolerate their daily checks. Others are more vocal.

“Some can be very, very vocal,” McGuire said.

“They really tell us what they think of us.”

Caesar still has plenty of growing to do. At his latest weigh-in, he tipped the scales at just 300g.

For now, the young kiwi remains under the watchful eyes of his keepers, who weigh him, check his progress and make sure he is growing as he should.

If all goes to plan, he will leave Taupō and take his place in the forest.

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Hawke’s Bay teen Lily Moore awoke the morning of Smokefreerockquest as an aspiring doctor who liked writing songs on her guitar.

By late Thursday evening, the Havelock North High School Year 13 student was a national songwriting champion.

Moore had planned medical study in 2027.

Her Smokefreerockquest win has thrown that up in the air as she now treads the same path wandered by Bic Runga, Marlon Williams, Anika Moa and more.

Smokefreerockquest is a nationwide youth music event and songwriting competition for high school students that started in 1988.

The final was held at Massey University’s Great Hall in Wellington and Moore won the solo/duo category at Smokefreerockquest 2026.

She beat six acts from around the country and won a NZ On Air recording, video and promotion package worth $10,000, plus $3000 to spend at the Rockshop.

Moore, 17, said her songwriting was emotion-based with texture-focused lyrics, influenced by Adrianne Lenker, Pinegrove, Phoebe Bridgers and Lizzy McAlpine.

She entered Smokefreerockquest in 2025 in duo Heaps Moore, but went solo this year to see if she could do it.

“I never knew if I could,” she said.

“I have been songwriting alone for a long time, but I’ve never truly taken on the role of performing my own original songs.”

She was extremely nervous going into the final, competing against other top young songwriters.

“I was kind of at peace with the fact that they were so incredible and that I was just going to go out there and try my absolute best and just have a great performance on a stage.”

When Moore was announced as the winner, she was shocked.

“It really took me a moment, and it still hasn’t quite hit me yet.”

Moore’s win has her rethinking heading to the University of Otago next year. She is now considering a gap year in the United Kingdom to try her luck in the music scene.

“Otherwise, I’ll just have fun with music for a year and try to get out what I can,” she said.

In the band category, Havelock North High School nu metal band Trolley won the Rockshop Electronic Assist Award and the band’s DJ, Finn Clark, was awarded the Chloe Wright Scholarship, supporting up to three years of tuition at any New Zealand institution.

Clark said winning the scholarship had changed his life, and he planned to study music at Victoria University in Wellington with dreams of a master’s degree or PhD.

The band was also proud to have worked up a mosh pit at the final while they were performing.

Moore and all Trolley members agreed entering Smokefreerockquest was one of the best things budding musicians could do.

“Rockquest really pushes you into performing original material,” Moore said.

“I wouldn’t have gotten into music if it wasn’t for Rockquest,” said Trolley guitarist Arya Chebbi.

Havelock North High School principal Joel Wilton said the result wasn’t bad for a little school in the provinces.

Jack Riddell is a multimedia journalist with Hawke’s Bay Today and has worked in radio and media in the UK, Germany, and New Zealand.

Wallingford Homestead earns 2 Michelin keys for an exceptional stay

New Zealand Herald September 22, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

The “David and Goliath” wins keep coming for a boutique rural accommodation venue in Hawke’s Bay.

Fresh off receiving the first hat for a Central Hawke’s Bay establishment in the Cuisine food awards, Wallingford Homestead has now been given a nod from Michelin.

Wallingford is one of four businesses in Hawke’s Bay and 28 nationwide to win Michelin key selection – the equivalent of a restaurant star for the accommodation industry.

Craggy Range’s luxury vineyard retreat and The Manse in Maraekakaho were each awarded one Michelin key, while Wallingford and Rosewood Cape Kidnappers were awarded two. Rosewood also received two in 2025.

Wallingford Homestead owners Chris Stockdale and Jeanette Woerner said they were overjoyed with the recognition.

“It feels a bit like a David and Goliath story, to be included in such a category,” Woerner said.

“We are dumbfounded, if I am honest, bedazzled, numb, very grateful.

“At first we thought it was a hoax, then we thought it was for the Wallingford in the UK.”

The Michelin Guide’s hotel selection is based on the work of its inspectors, who travel anonymously and independently to identify hotels offering outstanding experiences.

The selection spans properties from historic landmarks and grand hotels to independent boutiques, remote retreats and innovative new openings.

Hotels are awarded one, two or three keys, according to the level of experience they offer.

One key is a very special stay, two keys is an exceptional stay and three keys is an extraordinary stay.

Woerner said they offered an old-world experience and their calm, rural setting was often used for milestone birthday celebrations, couple destination stays and elopement weddings.

As a former chef, Stockdale oversees the “estate-to-plate” tasting and sharing menus at the hotel’s restaurant, which celebrate seasonal ingredients sourced, and even foraged, from local producers and artisans to offer a taste of the terroir.

Woerner focuses on guest experience, alongside her small team, who she says use their intuition to pick up on what guests may want to enhance their stay.

Woerner said over their eight years at Wallingford they had worked hard to create an intimate and personal guest experience.

“We do quite a bit of work before the guests get here ... It’s not a cold-call relationship; there is this preamble beforehand where we really feel like we know who is coming.

“If they really love a certain flower, we make sure that’s in their room, or somehow included in the welcome letter.

“If they want a cup of tea or a glass of champagne, we generally serve that on the balcony or by the fire, so it’s a really old-world relationship.

“Our numbers are tiny; the house is full at 10, we have just the five ensuites, and all of [the lodgings] have verandas that you can just walk out on to.”

She said they were proud to put Central Hawke’s Bay on the map.

“When people come here from New Zealand nationally and internationally, the one comment we always get is ‘I just never would have thought of coming here’, it’s got exposure to the world as a place to come and pulling a little bit of a spotlight on this very beautiful part of New Zealand.”

International Director of the Michelin Guide, Gwendal Poullennec, said the growth of the hotel selection came at a particularly interesting moment for the industry.

As the guide expands its presence across hospitality and lifestyle, he said the role of independent and boutique hotels was keeping the sector moving forward.

“This second global selection of the Michelin keys reflects the extraordinary momentum driving the hospitality sector once again this year.”

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

How a regional river became the centre of a political storm and international intrigue

Sydney Morning Herald September 23, 2026

Standing on the banks of the Fitzroy River, it is easy to see why Rockhampton has a reputation for rowing. But fitting tens of thousands of Olympic fans remains a test.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

As the boats get closer to the finish line, the barracking from parents and supporters on the riverbank starts to drown out the crews’ voices being carried over the still water.

It’s an idyllic setting. Paperbarks line the river, a sea of green either side of the brown Fitzroy River.

On any other day, this would be prime real estate for a quiet picnic surrounded by the sounds of the Australian bush.

This weekend, though, Rockhampton’s Ski Gardens is a hive of activity for the Queensland Schools Championship Regatta. There are 800 kids competing, with hundreds more parents and volunteers lining the shores.

All things going well, in six years’ time, it will host the Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoe sprint events.

Now, the place is packed. Just imagine the tens of thousands jammed in here in 2032.

But that’s a puzzle for the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority and the Brisbane 2032 organising committee to solve, after World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide signed off on the field-of-play technical report last week.

LNP politicians are hard to avoid. Senator Matt Canavan, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and local MPs are all spotted doing victory laps of the venue after news of the report – yet to be made public – filtered through.

This normally quiet river reach has found itself at the centre of a political storm and intense international intrigue.

This week, the BBC was forced to remove a video claiming the body of water was home to 500 crocodiles, after Canavan pointed out the footage was actually filmed in Western Australia.

It’s all been a bit much for Sarah Black, president of the Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club, who just wants to enjoy the moment.

She remembers “just being absolutely in awe” when the Olympic plans were first announced.

“The announcement came out and I was just bombarded by texts and emails – people just so excited – Rockhampton’s got the rowing!” she says.

“It was phenomenal. It was an amazing moment to be part of, and just to be present for.”

Black was even less prepared for the backlash, which she admits was hard not to take personally.

Some reporting, she says, was based on misinformation. For example, there was little mention of the Fitzroy River Barrage, a concrete structure that separates the downstream tidal saltwater section from the upstream freshwater section, where rowing is held.

“I do feel that, in time, people will understand the location better,” she says.

“A lot of people didn’t know about the Fitzroy River Barrage, and that’s out there now – that it’s not tidal. The course itself is in the fresh water.

“As a club, we were unprepared … we don’t have a lot of information on our website about the venue, so I guess the misinformation, once it gets reported once, people repeat it.”

Black wasn’t alone in getting her back up about criticism seen as emanating from down south in Brisbane.

“If you want to stir me up, start reporting half-stories like that,” Capricornia Chamber of Commerce president Jason Foss says.

“I wouldn’t be the only one either. There were a few people who had the shits with the way things were being reported.”

Foss says intrastate rivalry is at play, and central Queensland is justified in having a bit of a chip on its shoulder.

“Brisbane looks after Brisbane, and Brisbane doesn’t care about the rest of Queensland too much,” he says.

“It’s about time that regional communities made a stand and said, ‘Look, no, SEQ doesn’t get everything.’

“We pump a fair bit of money into the state’s coffers. How about something back from time to time?”

Foss says rowing is the perfect way to do just that.

“It’s going to put us on the map, really put us on the world stage, and everybody’s really excited about the possibilities,” he says.

“We’ve got a whole bunch of local smaller family businesses who are super keen to get involved in any way they can.”

Concerns about an accommodation shortfall are warranted, Foss says, but he’s confident the region can rise to the challenge.

“The thing I like about having that 2032 target is there’s a date for us to all be ready for,” he says.

“Every town in the country has a shopping list of things they would like to see happen, but having that hard date in 2032 where everybody’s coming, that makes a big difference.”

Foss says the financial opportunity for the businesses he represents – and Rockhampton more generally – is hard to quantify.

“How are they going to deal with the extra money? Will we see a few Ferraris driving around in town afterwards? Maybe, maybe not.”

Robin Adams is the managing owner of CocoBrew, which has three outlets in Rockhampton, including one fronting the Fitzroy River.

A sports tragic, he’s giddy at the prospect of Olympic competition being held just a couple of kilometres upstream, and he can already paint a picture in his head of Rockhampton in 2032.

“I see people walking up and down the river. I see a buzz in cafes, hotels, motels,” he says.

“People buying things in shops and enjoying the beautiful weather – have a look at it out there, absolutely gorgeous.”

A crowd is building to watch the NRL finals on his venue’s big screen, but Adams says the buzz around town would be orders of magnitude more for the Olympics.

Premier David Crisafulli has been steadfast in his government’s captain’s call to host rowing in Rockhampton – against GIICA’s recommendations – as a show of faith in regional Queensland.

“We like to get things done, and I’m really proud of what Crisafulli has done,” Adams says.

“He stood tall, taking all the bullets, and said it’s going to be here. He’s made it happen … we’ve just got to deliver it now.”

While glad to see Rockhampton score an Olympic event, former long-serving Labor MP for Robert Schwarten says enthusiasm is far from universal.

“There are probably three groups of people,” he says.

“There are those that have no interest in the Olympics whatsoever – couldn’t care less – battling day to day on the breadline, as we used to call it. The Olympics aren’t going to make much difference to them.

“Then there’s a group of people who see it as a godsend economically, the business people here, and so on. They know what the beef expo brings into the city – there’s a whole flow of income out of that.

“Then there’s another group of people, who are like me and hope we haven’t put all the eggs in one basket, and that is that we’re going to get nothing if this doesn’t go ahead.”

It’s a valid concern. While the course has passed a technical field-of-play assessment, there are still several hurdles to overcome.

The call on rowing, Schwarten says, was more about politics than anything else. He prefers a new indoor sports centre as a legacy, and supports the use of Browne Park for Olympic events.

“Bear in mind, it’s LNP front-to-back here for the first time in 100 years, so they all fell into line,” he says.

“There was no political conversation about it, which there should have been in my view. The voice of other people was lost in that process.”

The south-east Queensland rowing community, meanwhile, remains apoplectic about the Rockhampton choice. It’s been championing a purpose-built Olympic and legacy venue at Lawnton, in Brisbane’s urban outer-north.

Georgie Keily is in Rockhampton to support her son, who is competing for Churchie. A rowing enthusiast, Keily does not expect to be back here in 2032.

“I live in East Brisbane, right near where some of the events are going to be, so I think I’d be absolutely prioritising going to the events where I can stay in my own house,” she says.

As it stands, rowers in south-east Queensland – the region with the overwhelming majority of participants – have to be content with Wyaralong Dam in the Scenic Rim.

“There are no facilities there – just some donga buildings,” she says.

“It would have been incredible to have a venue close to the majority of Queensland rowers.”

Looking around the Rockhampton site, Keily says she does not comprehend how anywhere between 20,000 and 30,000 spectators could fit.

“How many people do you reckon are here? Maybe 1000 – and it’s full,” she says.

“There’s no room. The car park’s full. All the boat trailers. The kids are all on top of each other down there.

“I mean, they’re happy as Larry, but there’s five or six hundred of them, and they’re not racing for an Olympic gold medal.”

And then there’s the natural beauty of the place. The cleared area around Ski Gardens is at the end of the course, looking directly up the lanes. It’s hardly conducive to spectator viewing.

“You can’t tell who’s won because they’re rowing towards you, which is quite bizarre,” Keily says.

“To get any number of spectators in, you’re going to have to clear at least 500 metres of those trees, right? Which is a lot, and they look like they’re holding up the banks.”

That’s exactly what they do, says Capricorn Conservation Council president Sophie George.

George says she’s hopeful the Fitzroy course’s natural beauty and value can be preserved, even if the new Olympic infrastructure gets built.

An environmental scientist and biologist by profession, George supports the Olympic rowing course – as long as it’s done right.

She worries about the “pretty ginormous” floods that Rockhampton can experience, and how Olympic infrastructure would mitigate or manage flooding when it occurs.

“The beautiful old trees – eucalyptus, melaleuca – are all very important in maintaining that ecosystem and maintaining that riverbank, and if you remove those old trees, it’s going to cause an ecosystem collapse,” she says.

“There’s no amount of concrete that can replace what those big old trees do to stabilise the ecosystem, stabilise the soil, and also draw water in.”

Consultation has been positive so far, George says, and already some good ideas have been suggested – like hosting spectators on floating pontoons.

“It is certainly a challenge, but I’m sure it’s nothing that technology and the experts putting their head together can’t resolve or find a solution to,” she says.

Despite those concerns, George remains supportive of Olympic rowing in Rocky.

“Everyone wants this, and it’s going to be great for our region,” she says.

“I’m hoping that the infrastructure that we do get, especially with accommodation, can leave a lasting legacy for our region. We need housing. We need it so badly.”

Rowing club president Black also hopes people can get over the controversy and “just enjoy the rowing”.

“Once you’re here, Rockhampton’s course is unique in that we’re in the centre of town – that’s not necessarily the case with a lot of venues around the country,” she says.

“As a spectator and a supporter, you have the benefit of being able to come and watch some amazing competition, and then just going back into town for a coffee. There’s not even a set of traffic lights between the course and the airport.

“I think people are going to be pleasantly surprised.”
