Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 21:30:06 GMT

Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead

Expectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it.

In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the International Criminal Court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the US decided to withdraw from in July 2025).

His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peace in January (just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the president wondered if his new creation might simply replace.

Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon.

But even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s.

In short, he insulted nearly everyone in the room, from the Middle Eastern countries who are wondering about the validity of US security guarantees, to the European allies he habitually belittles, to Ukraine, whose leader, Volodymyr Zelensky was in the room, undoubtedly wondering why Trump is now asking him to pause his effective strikes on the Russian invader.

A famous episode of Seinfeld introduced “Festivus”, a holiday for the sharing of grievances. It felt like that as Trump outlined his Hobbesian vision of the world, with touches of Rodney Dangerfield added in, from a president who complains endlessly that he gets no respect.

In one stretch, he seemed to be lobbying for a Nobel peace prize while boasting of all the conflicts he has solved, as audience members yawned and checked their phones. He mentioned that these wars had previously been “unendable”, an interesting word that effectively describes two wars today. The Ukraine-Russian war is still going strong despite his frequent promises (including today) to to stop it.

Then, of course, there is the war of choice in Iran that he launched nearly seven months ago. As he has so many times in his social media outbursts, he ranged erratically from threats to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” with car-salesman promises to help Iran achieve greatness if they will just agree do work with him. Which, obviously, they will not, as they continue to defy US threats and even to solidify their position (which has improved markedly with Houthi gains in the last two weeks).

Trump insisted that stocks of American weapons are increasing, when all news reports are they are rapidly being depleted. The price of oil has been rising steadily.

There was a lengthy assault on climate change, claiming (falsely) that the earth’s climate is cooling, and that the science is a hoax when August tied a record for the hottest month ever recorded, and several important science reports in the last week confirmed how dire the situation is. In Tennessee, the temperature on the field of a football game between the Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles reached 157F. Perhaps that is what the president meant when he bragged that the US is the “hottest” country in the world? He may need a new speechwriter – that claim was also made in his 2025 speech to the UN.

Another neologism was “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, a term that the president is hoping will suddenly replace “AI”, much as he tried to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. Time will tell, but it feels unlikely the new term will stick.

On the eve of an important summit and state dinner with Xi Jinping, this might have been an important moment to stake out ways the US and China might cooperate on AI, to mitigate risks and increase the potential for beneficial research into disease and other problems. That opportunity was not seized.

Other topics that were not addressed included our rapidly deteriorating relationship with Canada, once the US’s greatest ally, and now enraged by Trump’s constant insults. Far from bending Canada to his will, they are achieving the opposite effect, as it always Elbows Up now. It will take years to repair the damage to a vital strategic relationship to the North.

Instead, more attention was paid to Greenland. The president claimed the US would now be enjoying basing rights – which we already enjoy – and he also suggested that foreign adversaries would not be allowed their bases. That is hardly news – they have never been allowed bases on Greenland.

While discussing his own vision of sovereignty, including his claims to Venezuelan oil, Trump drew from a sordid page of US history, and quoted a corrupt New York politician, William M “Boss” Tweed, to say “to the victor belong the spoils”. Tweed, the leader of Tammany Hall, was later convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars from the public, and died in jail.

Perhaps the saddest aspect of this speech was its utter lack of American idealism – the very force that led to the UN’s creation. In the 250th year of the United States, there were plenty of themes that might have won over a skeptical audience, But there were no inspiring words about fighting poverty, or reducing nuclear tests or keeping weapons out of space (as John F Kennedy promised in 1963).

Or human rights (introduced as a major theme by Jimmy Carter in 1977), or about reducing tensions with Russia (which Ronald Reagan spoke about in 1988), or the end of the Cold War (which George HW Bush celebrated in 1990), or the need to fight terrorism while avoiding Islamophobia (as Bill Clinton explained carefully in 1998).

It was just raw power; and a power that is likely to diminish in the years ahead. The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations. But the United States is now at historically low levels of approval around the world, as measured by the Pew Global Attitudes project, with only 23% of people (across 36 nations) expressing confidence in Trump’s leadership. The number is unlikely to go up after today’s performance.

Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

Outgoing UN chief says polluters have treated atmosphere like an ‘open sewer’

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 21:19:45 GMT

António Guterres laments world leaders’ inaction and says oil and gas firms ‘must pay’ for climate devastation

For one last time, António Guterres tried to fix the world’s gaze upon the dangerously escalating climate crisis. But the departing UN secretary general found world leaders still largely focused on other issues, even after a painful summer of stunning climate-driven disasters.

Speaking to assembled dignitaries at the UN on Tuesday, Guterres railed against big oil for treating “the atmosphere as an open sewer” and warned again of the catastrophic effects of the climate crisis.

Guterres said: “Three years ago, in the mountains of Nepal, I sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt, warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in. Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers.

“But as tragic events have shown, impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder, and spreading further than many anticipated.”

The UN chief said: “Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay. And to the leaders, cities, civil society and citizens working to hold them accountable – you are on the right side of history. Keep going.”

Guterres has been an unflinching advocate for climate action in his nine years as UN secretary-general, and his departure from the role is set to leave a void in a geopolitical landscape consumed by wars, inflation fears and other economic concerns rather than our rapidly heating planet.

“António Guterres has been the most climate-forward secretary-general in UN history; and this speech shows why,” said Alden Meyer, a veteran climate policy expert at E3G. “He clearly laid out the stakes on the climate emergency – the horrific consequences of inaction and the tremendous opportunities in deploying the available solutions.”

This summer has been roiled by record heatwaves and wildfires across the US and Europe, as well as a catastrophic glacier collapse and landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border. A mounting El Nino event, perhaps the largest in modern human history, is meanwhile set to push global temperatures to new record highs and spur a spike in food insecurity.

Yet the climate crisis has slipped from the agenda to the extent it has been little surprise that this week’s UN general assembly is not expected to bear any major new commitments to slash planet-heating emissions or to accelerate the rollout of a clean energy sector that is, while growing, still not on pace to avert further dangerous temperature rises.

Even Climate Week, an array of events across New York that overlaps with the UN gathering, is not expected to deliver any major announcements. While a record number of people – more than 100,000 – are set to attend Climate Week events, organizers have lamented an outbreak of “climate hushing” among political and business leaders who have determined the public has tuned out of the planetary emergency.

Donald Trump, who has dismantled environmental policies in the US and repeatedly called climate science a “hoax”, has been a major factor in this, even though his UN speech this year dwelled less on the topic than last year’s incendiary version.

But those who advocate for action said there was broader blame to be cast upon the complacency of other leaders who have failed to ensure the world does not blow past previously agreed temperature thresholds. There is still widespread public alarm about the climate crisis, polling shows, despite the disconnect by political leaders.

“We are in a terrible spot. That is the truth, because hypocrisy has won over concrete action,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama, who is pushing for a universal declaration of the rights of nature at the UN this week.

“As to the international arena, it’s a terrible situation. Look at the signs. A war in Iran … the other sign that we have is this forthcoming El Nino. So do we need more signs? No, it’s terrible. But what are people doing? Nothing.”

While Panama has acted strongly to cut its own emissions, other countries are failing, Navarro argued. “The war in Iran, the El Nino – has it had any impact in terms of countries or political leaders stepping up with bold commitments for real change? Zero,” he said.

“All I see around me is hypocrisy, BS, beautiful speeches, zero action. Let’s start telling the truth and start telling the truth to our own citizens. We’re facing climate change and it will have an impact and we’re not doing enough to alter it.”

The rays of optimism at Climate Week so far have centered on relief over the fact Trump is set to become a lame-duck president and also the continuing growth of renewables such as solar and wind. “Climate” may have become a taboo term for some, but investment in clean energy, particularly in China, is booming.

“The economy is built on batteries and the sun in California, which we know is cheaper,” said Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and potential Democratic candidate for the next presidential election.

“You can bottle the sun, you can catch the wind, you don’t have to worry about the sun getting blockaded in the strait of Hormuz. It gets cheaper and cheaper, in the abundance.”

Much of this progress is still being overshadowed, Newsom conceded, by Trump. “He’s trying to take us back to the 19th century,” Newsom said of the president. “He’s doubling down on stupid.”

Mariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against Køge

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 21:10:16 GMT

Mariona Caldentey’s 93rd-minute penalty delivered a win and a hefty dose of relief to fans bouncing behind the goal in the North Bank after the ball hit the back of the net, but Arsenal’s narrow defeat of HB Køge in their Champions League opener left more questions unanswered than answered for the struggling Gunners.

Manager Renée Slegers’ puffed cheeks said it all when the full-time whistle went. If it had been revealed on the final whistle that a forcefield surrounded the opposition goal at Meadow Park, many would have believed it, such was the extent of Arsenal’s ridiculous profligacy in front of goal in their league phase opener.

Exactly what is stopping Arsenal from getting the ball in the back of the net with a swagger reflective of their talent-laden squad is hard to pinpoint. Yes, teams are defending excellently against them, as a battling Køge and goalkeeper Alberte Vingum did on Tuesday night, but this feels like an Arsenal problem: a mentality one, a training ground one, a ruthlessness one.

The shadow of Sunday’s trip to Stamford Bridge loomed large at Meadow Park with eight changes made to the team that salvaged a point against Manchester United deep into added time on Saturday.

Only centre-back pairing Leah Williamson and Steph Catley and forward Stina Blackstenius retained their place in the starting XI for their Champions League opener.

The hope, without being disrespectful to their Danish opposition, was that this game would alleviate the frustration the Gunners are experiencing in front of goal, breaking the mental block several players seem to be suffering from. Unfortunately, the A Liga leaders had other ideas.

Arsenal were dominant in possession, pushing players so far forward that they often looked to be operating with a back one, of Catley or Williamson.

Paris Saint-Germain came from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw at Real Madrid in their Women's Champions League opener.

Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG.

Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – as Benfica dispatched Juventus 2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts.

The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game for Inter with a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish side BK Häcken to a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack. Press Association

Chloe Kelly tested goalkeeper Alberte Vingum early on, cutting onto her right foot and forcing a fingertip save from the 21-year-old. Frida Maanum did the same two minutes later, latching on to a half clearance and lashing the ball goalwards only for Vingum to get her hands behind it.

The message from the bench came loudly from Slegers, the manager yelling “pressure!” as Blackstenius harried a Køge centre-back.

The Gunners’ pressure seemed to have yielded the breakthrough in the 13th minute, when Caitlin Foord kept an attack alive before sending the ball to Taylor Hinds. The full-back fed Kyra Cooney-Cross and the Australian midfielder’s neat flick was turned in by Kelly on the volley with the outside of her leg. It was a fine finish but the video assistant referee intervened to penalise an offside Blackstenius for straying into the line of sight of Vingum.

That the game reached half-time with the game goalless was somewhat inexplicable, but also symbolic of Arsenal’s stuttering start to the season, with just five points from their three WSL games after consecutive draws, against Crystal Palace and Manchester United. Køge, meanwhile, have built some real momentum in the Champions League having earned a 4-1 win over Riga and 2-1 win over Hearts in the second round of qualifying before a 2-1 aggregate win over PSV Eindhoven sealed their place in the league phase.

The scale of the achievement for the visiting team was demonstrated by the buoyant celebrations of their coaching staff as soon as the half-time whistle was blown. Manager Kristian Mørch Rasmussen bellowed “good job in here”, before tripping on a railing and receiving a chorus of boos from the home fans behind the opposition dugout. He walked across the pitch towards the dressing room with a smile on his face and a finger to his lips shushing the crowd.

after newsletter promotion

Blackstenius made way for Alessia Russo at the break and the home team continued their push.

The longer the game went without an Arsenal goal, the greater the anxiety of the fans packed into Boreham Wood’s Meadow Park became.

Caldentey and new recruit Lisa Baum joined the battle just before the hour mark but Arsenal still could not find a way though the extremely well-organised Køge backline that just did not seem to tire.

A bursting run from Baum looked promising as she escaped her marker but a brilliant recovery tackle pickpocketed the forward and sent the ball out for a corner in the home team’s best chance of the second half.

The bizarre Disney+ coverage of the match, unbeknown to the fans under the floodlights, quickly became the biggest talking point among fans watching from home, with the bored studio dog and heavily criticised weird advert break while the game was still being played serving as a brief distraction from the tedium on the pitch. It was not any better when coverage resumed, Arsenal were dominating and creating but they are so hugely frustrating to watch when they are not converting, particularly with the attacking talent at their disposal.

Their 21 attempts to Køge’s four told one story, the two attempts on target to one told another.

As the clock edged towards full time, every effort placed high, wide or cut out was wildly celebrated by the Køge substitutes. They were silenced eventually, when Yukina Sakabe upended Selina Cerci in a rare blimp from the visiting team and Caldentey converted from the spot.

Relief filled the stands, but with Chelsea up next, nerves of another wasteful season will not settle.

The Great British Bake Off review – Nigella is wise, generous … and perfect for this national treasure of a show

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 20:30:04 GMT

The newest judge on the culinary competition is a soothing presence who is the ideal complement to Paul Hollywood. Long may the show continue with her on it

There’s a very good argument to be made for requiring a national referendum on whether presenters of shows that are part of our cultural identity should be allowed to leave, followed by – if necessary – a vote on who should replace them. At the very least, this would avoid the parlous state of affairs we face right now: at the very moment the public is grappling with the new-look Strictly Come Dancing (Tess and Claudia replaced by Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe, three whole different people!) we are asked to cope with a change to the order of the tented universe too.

For The Great British Bake Off lineup has replaced Prue Leith (who stepped down after deciding that, at 86, she would quite like to go back to having holidays instead of filming the series all summer) with – the one! The only! – Nigella Lawson.

It is, in TV terms, a big “get” and has been much heralded. And if there had been a public vote, Lawson would probably have won it. So is change always synonymous with destruction, or can Nigella buck the trend for modern enshittification of all things and give us the sanctuary we crave?

Yes, my friends. Yes, she can. She moves through Bake Off dispensing words of wisdom, generous praise and gentle criticism, just as confident as Leith but a much quieter, more soothing presence that works perfectly with Alison Hammond’s ebullience and Paul Hollywood’s teacher-ish vibe. She has a streak of romance that complements Hollywood’s ever-practical approach too, which enables her to enjoy contestants’ flourishes (the mirror, for example, that drag performer Gabe makes to decorate the “self-portrait” showstopper challenge behind which hides his alternative persona) in a way that Paul – a man without whimsy – does not.

The producers wisely do not give Lawson a big introduction on the show itself. Hammond welcomes her, she is lightly ribbed over “sumptuous” (attached to the chocolate stout cake that presents the first challenge) being a very Nigella word (though “ferrous tang” a bit later on has got to be up there too) and then we’re straight into business.

The key to a successful stout cake is slow cooking on a low heat and leaving enough time for it to cool before decoration. The contestants all understand this, which reminds you that the greatest attraction of Bake Off was, is and (God willing) always shall be the opportunity to watch competent people do things well and be celebrated – instead of seeing foolish people get humiliated on screen, then destroyed on social media.

Accordingly, the tent soon fills with cherry compotes, Swiss meringue and ambition. We move with the presenters, Hammond and Noel Fielding, round the work stations to get our first look at the cakes and contestants. Is everything going OK, Noel asks young Danni. “Indeedaroonie!” Danni replies. “You’re already my favourite,” says a grinning Noel.

Everywhere you look, people are doing clever things with buttercream, cardamom and something called malt mascarpone because people are amazing. Clara, from Portugal, who began baking two years ago, is trying and failing to make a sugar dome, but true disaster befalls Molly when her perfectly baked cake is taken out of the oven and drops in truly irrecoverable fashion to the floor. She takes a moment, then starts again, this time in sandwich rather than bundt tins so the new bake time will be shorter. Molly, our hearts are with you.

Judgment time. Connie, who runs a music centre and brings cakes in for her students, has provided “fascinating flavours” but overbaked. “The fear of unmoulding seizes one,” says Nigella, sympathetically. Hairdresser Tom has gone too heavy on the bicarb. But law student and calisthenics fan (this is the other great feature of Bake Off – everyone hints at multitudes) Mo’s peanut and caramel creation is “sensational – I’m in heaven” (Nigella) and “spot on – I love it” (Paul).

The technical bake hinges on replacing the right amount of flour with the right amount of crushed walnut and providing a strong enough coffee hit. Tom redeems himself (“My dream cake,” says Nigella), Gabe and Gary (smallholder, took up baking five years ago) make good showings, but Molly’s is deemed lacking. We fear for Molly, until … showstopper challenge triumph! Oh yes. Roaring back she comes, with a “light, tart beautiful bake” replete with mango and lemon curd and honour is restored.

My screener contained the star baker reveal but not who was sent home. Assuming it was the contestant who deserved it (although none of them deserves it – they are all magicians to me, conjuring this edible art from nowhere) I pronounce the good ship Bake Off fully seaworthy. Long may she sail with Nigella and crew at the helm.

The Great British Bake Off is on Channel 4

Trump praises relations with Burnham despite tensions over AI and Iran

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 19:50:36 GMT

US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York

Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos islands and the war in Iran.

At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister.

Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran.

UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead.

On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure.

Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US.

Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.

Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops.

In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year.

But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.

“Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution.”

Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks.

In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.

“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said.

But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”.

However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK.

UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial.

But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.

“I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”

Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.

In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.

Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade.

“Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said.

Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

First blood to England in ODI series after Will Jacks helps see off Sri Lanka

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 19:34:46 GMT

All-rounder takes five wickets after vital 46 not out

Harry Brook top-scores with 67 in comfortable win

Harry Brook had called on his ­England players to continue the “high-octane” cricket witnessed during their clean sweep in the Twenty20s but this latest victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international was more of a slow-burn affair.

Gone was the neck-arching carnage of the previous week and in its place, on a tired end-of-season surface, England were bowled out for 265 in 48.1 overs. Brook top-scored with 67 under a warm September sun, before his bowlers rolled the tourists for 176 to take a 1-0 lead into Thursday’s second match at Headingley.

Familiarity with conditions doubtless played its part and Sri Lanka, on the wrong side of the toss, never truly felt in the hunt. For Brook it was an 11th victory as England’s ODI captain, nudging him into credit after 10 defeats and continuing what has been a quiet resurgence in the format this year.

The volume will need to increase over the next 12 months as England build towards the next 50-over World Cup. But while hugely relevant lessons were never going to be learned in Chester-le-Street, the role played by Will Jacks was significant on the day and, as the new vice-captain, underlined his centrality more broadly.

Without Jacks’s unbeaten 46 in the first innings, including 18 runs taken off the 48th over, Sri Lanka might well have had a sniff here. Indeed, since returning in a lower middle-order role last year – one that has taken adjustment given his preference to bat in the top three – Jacks has averaged 43 and struck at over 100.

His off-breaks are also developing into a handy tool for Brook, returning five for 22 from seven overs here – including the top-scorer, Dunith Wellalage for 45 – as he mixed up his pace and angles. Only Vic Marks, five for 20 against New Zealand in Wellington way back in 1984, boasts better ODI figures by an England spinner – not that the man himself would ever boast about such things.

“[Jacks] is not a part-timer, he’s a very good off-spinner,” said Brook. “He can spin the ball big and contain. He could have moaned and groaned about playing as an all-rounder but he’s accepted that and become a very vital player for us over the past 18 months. He’s a very good leader, with bat, ball and in the field.”

Save for Jofra Archer, who took a bit of tap at the end of his all-format summer, Brook’s attack suppressed their opponents to defend a sub-300 total for the first time since 2022. Jamie Overton picked up two wickets bowling cross-seamers, while the loss of Adil Rashid – out of the series with a hand injury – was not felt.

England bowler Mark Wood has announced his retirement from international cricket. The 36-year-old paceman played 38 Test matches over an 11-year England career, taking 119 wickets.

“My stats won’t read I was the best bowler ever – but I hope my teammates think I was someone who tried my best every time,” he said.

Wood last played for England in an eight-wicket defeat to Australia in the first Test of the 2025/26 Ashes series. He made 70 one-day international appearances and was part of England’s 50-over World Cup-winning squad in 2019.

The Northumberland-born bowler played 38 T20s and was in the England squad which won the World Cup in 2022, although injury ruled him out of the semi-final and the final.

Injuries ultimately cost Wood more caps, and a knee problem has prompted him to call time on his international career.

“When you speak to other people, they say it hits you in the face, there’s a big feeling around that being it, ‘you’re done’,” he told Sky Sports.

“I’ve never really had that, I love playing cricket, I love playing for England, that’s been something I’ve felt really strongly about and proud to do. But I’ve had a lot of injuries.

“I’ve always found a way where I’ve believed I’d come back and had that resilience where I’m going to come back again, or I’ll be better, or I’ll prove somebody wrong again, but this time it’s just ground me down really.

“I never really wanted to give up England, but the lads that are coming through are doing a fantastic job and the news should be about the lads going to get their contracts and I can just focus on other things.”

Arguably England’s fastest-ever bowler, Wood clocked 97.7mph in the 2021/22 Ashes series. He took the final wicket at Trent Bridge when England regained the urn in 2015.

WinViz actually had Sri Lanka as marginal favourites at the halfway stage but looking on, there was a nagging sense England had plenty. After an initial 10-over power-play in which the hosts reached 61 for one – Tom Banton the man out, bowled by a beauty from Asitha Fernando – batting had started to become trickier.

Although just as relevant to England falling short of 300 was a sparkling debut from Sachindu Colombage, a 28-year-old wrist-spinner with a jerky, quirky action who claimed three for 44. Colombage was playing for Downham Stow in the East Anglian Premier League last summer and has an unremarkable domestic record. But Gary Kirsten, Sri Lanka’s head coach, looked beyond the numbers.

What Kirsten saw was the drift and dip that can trouble the best and in Joe Root and Jos Buttler, Colombage undid a couple of them here. Both were trapped on the back foot, Root hearing his off-stump rattled for 44 and Buttler pinned lbw for 31 by one that straightened. The less heralded Overton was later bowled by a leg-break that went above the eyeline and spun sharply.

Root’s removal in the 23rd over was the first time he had been dismissed in ODI cricket for some 416 deliveries – a streak of 404 runs that goes back to England’s 2-1 win in Sri Lanka last winter. The key wicket was Brook, however, having looked pretty much immovable until he went to charge the seamer Dushmantha Chameera for one of his inside-out scythes and skewed the ball to deep point.

It was one of the rare times that ­England had looked to clear the rope in what became their first ODI innings for more than seven years without a six. Brook’s demise also triggered the loss of four wickets for 29 runs in 46 balls, as a promising 182 for three became 211 for seven and tempered ambitions with it.

As well as the end of Buttler, this mini-collapse included Rehan Ahmed run out by a direct hit from Charith Asalanka in the ring. England’s new mentor, Kevin Pietersen, had stressed the need for better strike rotation before this match. But there was never a single as Ahmed set off, realised his error, and then pretty much gave up.

Watching all this unfold was Jacks, who with a bit of support from Gus Atkinson steered England to a defendable total. His work had only just begun, however, repeatedly punching holes in Sri Lanka’s lineup before sealing a comfortable win – and his first five-fer – with a ripper to bowl the No 11, Dilshan Madushanka.

Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 19:18:40 GMT

Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump

US politics live – latest updates

How do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby.

Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand.

So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover.

The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at the United Nations general assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident.

All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed?

And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”?

Taking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water.

It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that.

Burnham then bigged up the deal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual.

Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

On we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old.

Then a question on the sanctions imposed on illegal settlements in the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal.

There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting?

Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.

Will anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacle

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 19:00:03 GMT

Fifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge him

For Gianni Infantino there is no international break. The Fifa president is widely expected to make an appearance at the United Nations general assembly this week in New York, where he will lobby heads of state for their federations’ support as he continues his campaign to be re-elected next year.

Infantino has not been idle during the lull since Fifa abandoned its World Cup sell-off plan last month, instead crisscrossing the globe on a private jet provided by Qatar Airways as part of its sponsorship deal with world football’s governing body.

From his strongholds in Doha, Rabat and Miami, Infantino has also visited Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Kyrgyzstan and various other countries, his trips often coinciding with the approval of funding for development projects worth millions of dollars. His would-be opponents have been conspicuous by their silence.

Whether Qatar Airways facilitating Infantino’s re-election campaign should be considered legitimate Fifa presidential business is a moot point, which neatly encapsulates the huge incumbency bias that will benefit Infantino if a vote takes place at the Fifa congress in March. That ballot appears to be in doubt, with multiple sources involved in the push to remove Infantino telling the Guardian they are running out of hope of finding a candidate to beat him.

Although dozens of the 200 member associations that had submitted letters of endorsement for Infantino withdrew them after the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise sale plan in July, the prevailing view is that the silent majority remain steadfastly behind him.

A meeting with the Caribbean Football Union, where funding projects were approved, may have splintered the vote at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and there are increasing concerns that the European alliance may not be watertight.

“As long as Gianni is running, I don’t think anyone else will raise their hand,” one source said. “They would effectively be running against Fifa the institution. Fifa declared his candidacy, provides staff, aeroplanes and cars, even a personal video team.

“If he doesn’t step down before March, the election will not be contested. Uefa and others could stage a boycott so the victory would be tainted, but Gianni will win a clear majority of whoever shows up.”

Infantino first declared at the April congress in Vancouver his intention to seek a fourth and final term of office. Fifa statutes limit presidents to three full terms but under a recent change he will be permitted a fourth because his first term lasted three years, rather than the usual four, after his 2016 election to replace the disgraced Sepp Blatter.

The 56-year-old reasserted his intention to stand after attending the first match of the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland a fortnight ago. That came via a statement issued by Fifa’s media team.

As it stands Infantino does not have an opponent, despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to go. Beyond the obvious difficulties of taking on an incumbent who controls the machinery of office and funding budgets – the last Fifa president beaten at the ballot box was Sir Stanley Rous in 1974 – there are specific reasons why none of the would-be candidates have declared.

The most credible challenger is regarded as Concacaf’s president, Victor Montagliani, but the Canadian is committed to standing for re-election at his confederation, and the vote is due to take place in February. Standing in both elections is not regarded as feasible, and Montagliani is understandably reluctant to walk away from Concacaf in favour of fighting a potentially losing battle against Infantino.

The AFC president, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, was beaten by Infantino in the 2016 election, the only time Infantino has faced an electoral opponent, and is further hamstrung by the fact that his confederation’s main powers, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are backing Infantino. Qatar’s position would also appear to rule out a challenge from Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, and an openly European move led by Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin, would have no chance of success. Ceferin, in any case, has his own presidential contest in March to focus on.

To compound the difficulties for Infantino’s would-be challengers, any election would be a secret ballot, making any promises from member associations during the campaign period all but worthless. As a result, Uefa is focusing most of its efforts on legal avenues to remove Infantino, accusing him of “criminal mismanagement” in a 56-page document lodged with US state courts in New York, Miami and Colorado last month seeking the disclosure of all documents relating to FFE.

Fifa responded strongly the week after Uefa made its legal complaint, filing a response in New York in which it sought to block the discovery process. Its submission accused Uefa of mounting a smear campaign against Infantino in the absence of any evidence of wrongdoing.

Fifa’s submission said: “Uefa’s application suffers from a fundamental defect: Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate.

“While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of Uefa’s smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership.”

Although there is widespread confidence that at least one of the three jurisdictions will grant discovery, the process grants Fifa the right of appeal, so there is little prospect of new material being made public before the 18 November deadline for presidential candidates to come forward.

An initial decision from the courts is expected next month, but an appeal from the losing party appears inevitable whatever the outcome.

“The issue with discovery is that it takes a long time,” a source said. “It’s likely to run beyond the date of the election in March. If the process is under way by then, Fifa congress could decide to wait until we find out what the courts discover and postpone the election. But there would still have to be a vote on that.”

Uefa’s not-so-secret hope is that the discovery process finds evidence that FFE was deliberately undervalued at $20bn (£15bn) to provide a guaranteed future windfall for Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, which had seemingly agreed to pay $4.2bn for 21% of the new commercial venture, giving it a significant share of future Fifa revenues.

Thrive subsequently bought 20% of the LA Lakers last month as part of a larger transaction with the former Disney chief executive Bob Iger that valued the NBA franchise at $12.5bn, a deal that has further highlighted Infantino’s valuation of the World Cup.

after newsletter promotion

Fifa’s revenues for the four years to 2026 were $15bn, a figure projected to grow to $18bn over the next four-year cycle owing to larger broadcast deals, without accounting for any expansion of the World Cup and Club World Cup, which remains on the agenda.

A corporate fraud lawyer said that undervaluing FFE could potentially constitute a criminal offence by Fifa, a case Uefa would take to the Swiss courts. “If you’re doing a deal that is way off market then you are deceiving the stakeholders, in this case the member associations,” the legal source said. “That is criminal. If Uefa has a criminal case that’s where it will be. It’s about how the valuation was done, by whom, and what conflicts were there.

“All of that should come out during disclosure. If beyond that there were personal deals being struck on the side, that could also be criminal. All those details should be disclosed.”

Beyond the $20bn valuation, the identity of the would-be investors and Fifa’s claim that it would retain control over governance, very little has been made public about the development of FFE, with a sales deck produced by the US bank JP Morgan containing no details of a tender process, voting rights or future exit terms. A senior investment banker who has been involved in similar deals said it is inconceivable such details were not agreed before Thrive agreed to commit $4bn, albeit much of the funding was due from other investors.

“I don’t think Thrive was going to be involved with Fifa for the next 25 years,” they said. “This looks like a quick in-and-out play. The plan would have been to buy it low and sell it high. I think the investors saw an amazing deal.”

There is no evidence of any wrongdoing or criminality on the part of the any of the parties involved in the proposed FFE deal.

Thrive has revealed little about its intentions beyond a statement issued last month in which it presented FFE as a proposal to be voted on by Fifa’s members, rather than a done deal.

Significantly, however, it also expressed an element of regret at getting involved given the political backlash, which many within football have interpreted as an attempt to distance the firm from Infantino.

“It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination,” Thrive said. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved.”

Uefa and Concacaf, in particular, appear prepared to dig in for the long haul, despite concerns that Infantino will be re-elected. The two confederations are continuing to work together to develop a unified Nations League competition, revealed by the Guardian last month, and last week wrote a joint letter to Fifa demanding that it release funds from its $6bn reserves to fund an additional payment of at least $10m to each of its 211 member associations during the next four-year cycle.

Some sort of payment appears inevitable given Infantino promised to provide $20m more to the member associations via FFE, but Uefa and Concacaf are hoping Infantino does not accrue political and electoral credit for it.

Ceferin and Montagliani are expected to meet at next week’s general assembly of the European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, where Infantino may also make an appearance. Infantino addressed the EFC’s 900 members at last year’s EFC meeting in Rome, where his suggestion that more international tournaments should take place during European winters to accommodate the global south caused controversy, although that pales compared with his pronouncements and plans since.

Uefa has made one accommodation with Fifa by withdrawing its threat to boycott the Under-20 Women’s World Cup that finishes on Sunday, and Infantino has agreed to its demand to commission an external governance review, which he communicated in a letter to the member associations this week. Suggestions that this move could lead to a truce with Uefa are given short shrift by those close to the leadership.

Despite the electoral gloom, those agitating for change are also clinging to memories of the fate of Infantino’s predecessor, Blatter, who was forced to resign in 2015 amid an FBI corruption investigation days after winning a fifth term against Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan. Blatter himself has never been charged in relation to the investigation.

For those looking to remove Infantino, the presidential election is not necessarily the end of the process. “This is a fight to the death now and we have to keep going,” one source said.

“The fact that Gianni is the only guy running at the moment does not mean it’s over. Look what happened to Blatter. He was re-elected in May 2015, but was gone in June. Eventually the truth will come out.”

Wamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern Munich

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 18:58:04 GMT

Manchester City produced a gutsy performance to fight back and earn a valuable 2-2 draw away at Bayern Munich on their return to the Champions League. José Barcala’s side took the lead through Giulia Gwinn and an unfortunate Kerstin Casparij own goal but Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser earned the visitors a hard-earned point.

City’s head coach, Andrée Jeglertz, was pleased with the resolve of his side after a difficult first half. “It [a comeback] has happened before because we know the quality is there,” he said. “The mentality of ­winning and the belief is there. It shows ­something about this group again.

“There were definitely two phases of this game. In the first half, Bayern were very good. I think we were a bit slow on the ball … It was almost like we were surprised by the tempo. I know we weren’t but it looked like that. At the end of the first half, we got a little bit back. The trust and the belief at half-time was good so I felt that this is still possible.”

It was always going to be a challenging start for the English champions against a Bayern team who have historically thrived in the league phase of this competition. They came into this unbeaten in their last 15 home group-stage matches and on the back of a semi-final run last ­season that, according to Gwinn, had left them “even hungrier and eager for more”. Not only that but the German team have kicked off the defence of their Frauen-Bundesliga title in stunning fashion with five wins from five.

City also arrived in Germany full of confidence after an equally impressive start to the season. Their 4-2 win over Liverpool on Friday had been a further sign of their mettle, finding a way to win despite not being at their best.

Paris Saint-Germain came from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw at Real Madrid in their Women's Champions League opener.

Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG.

Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – as Benfica dispatched Juventus 2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts.

The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game for Inter with a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish side BK Häcken to a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack. Press Association

European football, however, presents a different test altogether and they came into this game with plenty of unknowns. How would they measure up after a year out of the competition? Could their injury-hit squad juggle the load of European football and domestic challenges?

Reality hit in a first half during which a refreshed Bayern took control of proceedings. Barcala had been able to make five changes to his starting XI, having completely rested Klara Bühl and Gwinn against Köln on Saturday, and they looked full of energy.

Bühl immediately stretched every sinew of City’s fragile-looking defence with her pace and guile. The 25-year-old was at the heart of everything Bayern created early on, firing a volley wide before setting up the equally prolific Pernille Harder for a half chance.

It did not come as a surprise, therefore, that the hosts broke the deadlock with 11 minutes on the clock. It was a move that cut through the heart of Manchester City as Linda Dallmann broke clear to send Gwinn on her way. The full-back saw the pitch open up in front of her, dispatching a cool finish past Ayaka Yamashita in the City goal.

It was moment when the 4,291-strong crowd raised the decibel level, buoyed by their team’s domination and, perhaps also, the Oktoberfest celebrations. This was Bayern’s first outing at Sportpark Unterhaching and the raucous crowd seemed to settle in straight away at their new home.

The pressure on City continued. Struggling to find space in possession, they were guilty of playing into Bayern’s hands, channelling their attack centrally rather than trying to exploit the wide areas. Things got worse when an unwitting Casparij diverted a dangerous Harder cross into her own net to double the score.

This City side are made of stern stuff, however, and Jeglertz’s ­players were handed a lifeline just before the break, albeit in controversial fashion. As a blue smoke flare blazed on the pitch, the referee allowed play to continue while Casparij burst forward. Her cross was met by Khadija Shaw, whose shot was deflected into the path of Mead, who tapped home.

The second half was a much more even affair as the pendulum of momentum swung between the teams. City should have had an equaliser when Aoba Fujino was brought down by Ena Mahmutovic only for the goalkeeper to step up and save Shaw’s penalty.

Despite the hosts still looking potent going forward, City could sense that the tide was shifting and found an equaliser with four minutes to play. Wamser, signed from Bayer Leverkusen this summer, arrived unmarked on the edge of the box to rifle home a finish on her return to Germany.

The substitute Edna Imade had two big chances to win it for Bayern late on but the visitors held strong. With one of their most difficult games out of the way, they face Real Madrid next week in Manchester with a chance of making another statement on the European stage.

I read 163 novels and these are the six best: Mary Beard on judging the Booker prize

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 18:57:06 GMT

I found being a Booker judge hugely rewarding. All the works on our shortlist will change how you see the world

This year’s Booker prize shortlist

As a Booker judge, I think I have worked harder than I have ever done before. Reading 163 novels in six months, making careful assessments, being ready to argue for your judgment, going back to check you haven’t got it wrong … in some ways it took more energy than actually writing a book. But it was also hugely rewarding and fun. I shall never forget the discussions in our regular judging meetings, and the pleasure of discovering how we had sometimes reached almost exactly the same view of a book, and sometimes dramatically diverged. There were no big newsworthy squabbles, but a lot of discussion, a lot of listening and re-reading.

When each new batch of 30 or so novels arrived at home, through the spring, I plunged in and picked them out at random (only occasionally cheating by selecting a slim volume when I felt I needed to get my total up!) But so that you have more to go on, here is a quick guide to each of the books on the shortlist – in strictly alphabetical order.

In M John Harrison’s The End of Everything, we enter the dystopian world of Kent, sometime in the near future. There’s been a catastrophe of some undefined sort and the survivors have been reduced to scavenging and “making do” after most of the rules of social order have collapsed. Expect an unexpected random shooting or two, and an alien visitor to be managed. But the book is not (just) weird. It is also about us and about now – a gripping read and often funny in the most surprising places. If you can’t always make out exactly what is going on, that’s part of the point.

Also with the hallmarks of dystopia, but inspired by a rumoured real-life violent incident in Jamaica in the 1980s, Marlon James’s The Disappearers explores a vicious killing and its long, unsettling aftermath. While rehearsing for a play, some gay men are attacked by homophobic thugs: one actor is left dead; another has both eyes gouged out; all are scarred in different ways. Later one of the survivors sets out to find the others and reckon with what happened. A hugely ambitious novel, it is told over different times, in different voices and registers (diary extracts, media interviews etc). The characters stick in your head, the wit is sharp, the rawness unforgettable.

In contrast, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag starts from an hilarious premise. A struggling actor takes a job in a university psychology department, where he must attend classes dressed in a black leather bag. This is based on a real-life experiment from the 1960s, which aimed to discover how the other students would react to the “bag man” in their midst. Beyond its surreal humour, which will have you laughing out loud even on a second read, Black Bag raises big questions about identity, ambition and human frailty, as well as conjuring up some truly absurd sex scenes (in the bag, of course).

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry has its surreal aspects, too. The narrator, a self-effacing museum curator, specialises in re-creating historical tableaux, with horribly accurate fake fruit and plastic joints of meat. During one assignment, the curator uncovers the story of a forgotten medieval king, trapped in a treacherous court – a reluctant and unsuitable occupant of the throne who came to power as the last option after the death of his brothers. Perry elegantly intertwines present and past to question the boundary between history and fiction, and to ask whether the past can ever be a safe refuge from the here-and-now.

Artie Dam, in Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, has no safe refuge anywhere. A much-loved, fiftysomething history teacher in an American high school, who likes messing about in boats, Dam sees his apparently comfortable world gradually collapse. We find him with thoughts of suicide, trying out shoplifting in a bout of madness, facing a new US president – and weighed down by the discovery of an almost unbearable family secret. This is a seductively understated book, which unpicks the silences and shame of family life, while also unpicking the new world of Trump’s America, without ever once haranguing the reader.

Silences and shame also underlie John of John by Douglas Stuart. Here a student – at the end of his course and with no job – returns “home” to the tiny Hebridean island of Harris. Stuart paints the island landscape vividly, but it’s far from the romantic, untouched world of the tourist brochures and it’s a disconcerting sort of home. This is a world of violence, feuds, discontent, hypocrisy, secret sex and isolation that is not only geographic. Yet there is a rough tenderness in the story that Stuart weaves, as well as tremendous emotional depth, and in the end, almost unbelievably, a sense of hope.

Each of these books can change how you see the world. So, plunge in and enjoy the ride.

Previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart shortlisted for Booker prize

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 18:55:24 GMT

The two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelist

Booker judge Mary Beard on this year’s shortlist

This year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison. Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November.

James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time for The Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list.

Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in a Guardian review.

The End of Everything by M John Harrison (Serpent's Tail)The Disappearers by Marlon James (Hamish Hamilton)

Black Bag by Luke Kennard (John Murray)

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry (Granta)

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout (Viking)

John of John by Douglas Stuart (Picador)

Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! This year, she is shortlisted for The Things We Never Say, which departs from the well-known cast of characters in her previous novels to introduce the history teacher Artie Dam, whose comfortable life on the Massachusetts coast is threatened by a secret, and by the realities of a changing US.

Harrison, who judged the prize in 2022, is shortlisted for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in an unnamed Kent coastal town. The book, “as its title suggests, is about everything”, wrote Michel Faber in the Guardian. “It burrows deep into our psyches – into the psyche of our civilisation – and exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now.”

The shortlisted books “took risks”, and they “could not be replicated by artificial intelligence – these are very human books”, said the writer Raymond Antrobus, who is on this year’s judging panel alongside the chair Mary Beard, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, the writer Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu.

Kennard made the list for Black Bag, his comic campus novel about an actor in his late 30s who takes a job involving attending lectures in a black leather bag as part of a psychological experiment.

Completing the shortlist is Perry, the sole debut novelist, with May We Feed the King. The book – which won this year’s Waterstones debut prize – is about a modern-day curator tasked with dressing rooms in historic houses, who becomes increasingly obsessed with the life of a medieval king.

Four of the shortlisted titles are by men, and three of them – Black Bag, The Disappearers, and John of John – explore masculinity and male sexuality. That the shortlisted authors are predominantly male is “quite surprising, because generally speaking the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”, said Cocker. The masculinity theme may come down to men “having to rethink their role”, he added. Beard said she doesn’t think it’s a “very masculine” shortlist, while Lockwood half-joked that “all these books are gay”.

Among the surprises on the shortlist was the absence of American author Emma Cline, whose novel Switzy, which follows a man suffering from dementia travelling to a euthanasia clinic, received positive reviews across the board, amid predictions that it could win the overall award. British author Gwendoline Riley also failed to make the cut with her longlisted novel The Palm House.

The judges said the shortlisting meeting lasted approximately three hours. The five other books that didn’t make the shortlist were The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis, Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman, The Renovation by Kenan Orhan, All Them Dogs by Djamel White, and The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams.

This year’s prize was open to books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

Last year’s prize was awarded to David Szalay for his novel Flesh. Recent winners include Samantha Harvey for Orbital, Paul Lynch for Prophet Song, and Shehan Karunatilaka for The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 18:10:53 GMT

Lian Yunzhi solves 3x3 puzzle on several occasions in average time of under 4.5 seconds, according to state media

A six-year-old Chinese girl has set a new women’s world record for solving a Rubik’s Cube in just over four seconds, state media reported.

“Speedcuber” Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice this month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday.

She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving the Rubik’s Cube five times.

The girl, who is from Chengdu, is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”, CCTV said.

A video posted by the broadcaster showed her wearing a red gingham bow on her head as she deftly turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube.

After solving the puzzle she was seen placing the cube on the table, clapping her hands and pumping a fist in the air.

Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, the six-year-old was introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class – alongside various other extracurricular activities such as dance and music lessons, her mother, Lin Yangxi, told local media outlets.

Lin “gradually realised” that cubing was an “excellent activity for fostering a child’s comprehensive abilities” and shifted her focus towards it, she told Chengdu’s Red Star News.

Her daughter has now mastered more than 1,300 Rubik’s Cube solving algorithms, practising daily for two to three hours, Lin said.

Photos from Red Star News showed the girl’s trophies displayed on a shelf in her home.

“Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing,” Lin said.

“It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions,” she added.

EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 18:07:19 GMT

Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the bloc

The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years.

With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.

France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.

Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.

The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.

Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”

The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense ‌of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.

In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.

A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”

A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.

Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.

Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.
