The Guardian view on the Lib Dems: Ed Davey wants Tory voters without losing the left

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 17:51:32 GMT

The party leader offers social liberalism and lower taxes, hoping opposition to Reform UK will hold together voters with competing economic interests

Sir Ed Davey’s speech at the Liberal Democrat party conference was a calculated appeal to voters who recoil from a rightwing bloc associated with Brexit, nationalism and reactionary politics. That’s not a bad place to start. But he wants this message not to be lost in the headlines about his party’s £17bn tax giveaway aimed at disillusioned Conservative voters. To walk that line, his address sought to present Reform UK’s politics as an existential threat to Britain, appealing directly to left-leaning tactical voters. At the same time, he told moderate Tories that only a vote for the Lib Dems can reliably block both Reform and a Conservative-supported Nigel Farage premiership.

It’s a clever strategy. Too clever, think some in his party, who yearn for clearer dividing lines. Yet the Lib Dem leader is nothing if not ambitious. He claims that his party could have more MPs than the Conservatives after the next election. In 2024, the Lib Dems won 60 of their 72 seats from the Tories; they were also second in a score of Conservative-held seats. That electoral geography pushes the Lib Dems as replacing the Conservatives as the respectable, pro-market opposition, while Reform occupies the space of the nationalist right. The logic is that in a multiparty system under first past the post, it may no longer be necessary to be a national party. Sir Ed might become kingmaker as the parliamentary expression of a liberal southern tendency.

Rejoining the single market would be in Britain’s interests. But presenting the move as a frictionless growth policy obscures the major change involved in accepting common rules and institutions. Sir Ed’s tax cuts may be smart politics, parking Lib Dem tanks on Tory territory. But they are a world away from his 2024 election image as the champion of carer’s allowance, NHS funding and local sewage protests. That leftwing stance importantly allowed him then to tap into tactical anti-Conservative voting.

Raising the personal allowance to £15,000 allows Sir Ed to speak to almost every taxpayer in a cost of living crisis, while increasing the higher-rate threshold to £56,000 targets professionals in the south on whom his electoral strategy depends. The trouble is that the tax cuts are a promise, but the growth – from closer ties to Europe – that “pays” for them is a forecast. Choosing tax cuts over public investment leaves the Lib Dems exposed to competition from the left, from Labour and the Greens.

Sir Ed is trying to detach economic liberalism from the socially conservative nationalists and link it to a pro-European and socially liberal party. He’s right to say that “people feel powerless”, but the examples that Sir Ed uses to demonstrate their lack of agency – unsafe maternity care, inadequate disability provision and polluted rivers – largely arise from failures of collective provision or state regulation. Their solutions require capable public institutions and more resources.

The political scientist Paula Surridge wrote that continued Lib Dem success depends on them being seen as a safe alternative for liberal-left voters. The cultural and social liberalism he sells would reassure this group. But tax cuts might disquiet them. Sir Ed is betting that these tactical voters care more about defeating the nationalist right than the Lib Dems’ economic programme. That was the case in 2024. After years of the public dealing with high prices, it may be harder to land that message next time.

The Guardian view on Keynes in the West End: James Graham’s latest play captures the zeitgeist

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 17:50:31 GMT

As the chancellor, John Healey, ponders options ahead of his first budget, the playwright’s new work offers lessons from the past

Still only 44, James Graham has become a formidable chronicler of our national story. On themes such as the rise of Rupert Murdoch, social upheaval in post-industrial Britain and the neuroses of the England men’s football team, the playwright and screenwriter has made it his vocation to read the signs of our times and write them up for the stage.

Graham’s new play goes a bit further back in history, but its subject matter is characteristically of the moment. Opening this week in the West End, The Standard of Living offers a portrait of the sentimental and intellectual passions of John Maynard Keynes (played by Rory Kinnear), as the great economist makes his name between the first and second world wars. As Keynes rails against the laissez-faire ethos of the age, he seeks to devise a theory of growth that justifies state intervention on people’s behalf in the wake of the Great Depression.

A month out from the first budget to be delivered by Andy Burnham’s government, the contemporary relevance is not hard to spot. Ever since the prime minister pledged to bring an “end to 40 years of neoliberalism” and launch a new era of public investment to bring about growth, his opponents have sought to characterise that project as a reckless Labour version of Trussism. Discussion of the nation’s political direction has been reduced to a numbers game relentlessly focused on bond yields, debt levels and what markets will or will not countenance.

John Healey may or may not take a seat in the stalls during the play’s scheduled run. But just as Graham’s Labour of Love presciently addressed the Labour party’s problems in its red wall heartlands, and Dear England explored a nation’s insecurities through sporting anxiety, his latest offering captures the zeitgeist in a way that goes beyond the contents of the chancellor’s budget briefcase.

The economic historian Robert Skidelsky, who died this year, observed that “our age has eerily come to rhyme with Keynes’s”. In the aftermath of the 2008 crash, nationalist threats to the global order have multiplied and the far right has been able to mobilise popular discontent at declining living standards. Whether progressive governments can negotiate the fiscal room for manoeuvre to allow them to respond effectively is a key issue of our time. Meanwhile, the existential threat posed by unregulated artificial intelligence has taken the laissez-faire debate on to new and alarming territory.

Graham and Nicholas Hytner, the director of The Standard of Living, are too skilled to allow such echoes to add up to a sombre night out. Keynes’s marriage to the Russian ballerina Lydia Lopukhova, for example, is deftly exploited to make dance a metaphor for what a graceful balance of economic forces might look like. Perhaps the highlight of the evening thus becomes a vigorous pas de deux across the stage involving Keynes and his free-marketeering rival, Friedrich Hayek, choreographed to the rhythm of an argument about interest rates.

Ideas, art, love affairs and the bohemian excesses of the Bloomsbury set all compete for audience attention. At a time when the common good risks being undermined by market imperatives, algorithmic abstractions and rogue AI agents, Graham has once again produced a play that poses the right question at the right time: how can humans take back control?

Police believe they have foiled ‘imminent’ attack on Manchester’s Jewish community

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 17:50:25 GMT

Counter-terrorism police say ‘long-running investigation’ disrupted alleged plot days after two men arrested on eve of the holy day Yom Kippur

Police believe they have stopped an imminent plot to attack Jewish communities in the Manchester area.

The announcement on Tuesday follows the arrest of two men on Sunday at 2.45pm in Manchester and comes during the Jewish holy month.

Counter-terrorism investigators were unusually explicit about the alleged attack plot, which was halted after an operation lasting several months. Police believe they have detained the main suspects and any materials they may have been planning to use.

Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.” The arrests and official confirmation of a suspected attack plot comes almost a year after an Islamist-incited attack on a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur left two people dead, with the attacker shot dead by police.

Arrests were made hours before this year’s Yom Kippur started, with police fearing any plot might be “imminent”. The Jewish festival of Sukkot falls on Friday, with other holy days to follow.

Evans added: “We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy Day period.

“I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester police and partners to ensure we’re doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe.”

The two men in their 30s were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act, meaning police suspected they were terrorists. Police will not officially say what the motive was, nor the nationality or ethnicity of those detained.

The Guardian understands that a far-right motive is thought to be unlikely. Sources stress the investigation is at an early stage. Islamist extremism is among possible motives under consideration, and given a spate of recent attacks against Jewish targets, investigators are searching for any sign of a state link. Investigators are increasingly finding it difficult to determine motive until much later in an investigation, if at all.

The UK’s terrorism threat level is now at its second highest level of severe.

The investigation was led by CTP in London and the two men arrested have been taken to a police station in the capital for questioning.

Warrants for their further detention have been granted, meaning they can be held until Sunday.

The arrests led to searches in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford, which police say have now been completed. Examination of electronic devices such as mobile phones is under way.

Evans added: “Counter Terrorism Policing continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities.

“As we have shown with these arrests, where we suspect there could be a threat to the public, then we will not hesitate to investigate and take action.

“We are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry and we anticipate these will continue over the coming days as this investigation continues.

“Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns.”

The Community Security Trust (CST), which works to keep Jewish communities in the UK safe from attack, said: “This is utterly chilling, coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year, and is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time.

“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and alert, and to report any suspicious activity to police on 999 and then to CST.”

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 17:22:55 GMT

Entire £233m budget for 2026 allocated in less than a day, leaving thousands of farmers disappointed

Thousands of farmers have been left empty-handed with the government’s 2026 nature funding spent in just six hours.

The £233m sustainable farming incentive (SFI) scheme opened for applications from farmers at 10am on Tuesday.

SFI is part of a package of payments that replaced the EU’s common agricultural policy, paying farmers to look after nature, soil and other public goods, rather than simply for farming and owning land.

But by 4pm on Tuesday – just six hours after it opened – the government confirmed that the 2026 SFI scheme was closed for applications, with all of the budget allocated.

For many farmers this was their first opportunity to apply to SFI since the scheme’s sudden closure in March 2025. The next opportunity to apply for funding will be in 2027.

“Vicki Hird, the strategic lead on agriculture at The Wildlife Trusts, compared the scramble for SFI funding to “the scramble to get Oasis tickets” and said it was shocking to watch the funding disappear so quickly.

“The government really needs to get the budget in order to ensure farmers have the funding they need for nature, food security and national security,” she said.

Alice Groom, the head of sustainable land policy at the RSPB, said it was “unprecedented” for the budget to be used up so quickly. “We thought the money would go quickly but not necessarily in one day,” she said.

“Defra doesn’t have a way of managing the budget. SFI is supposed to be spent on meeting environmental goals and transitioning to environmental farming, but it’s now first come first served.

“There will likely be thousands of farmers who haven’t been able to apply for any funding, which will have implications for their ability to deliver for the environment on their farm,” she said.

Throughout the day, farmers who had been experiencing problems with their SFI applications had to wait up to five hours to speak to someone to get help. Martin Lines, the CEO of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said this will have meant they won’t have spoken to someone until after the scheme had closed.

This year has been extremely challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. The SFI funding will have been seen as a way for many farmers to invest in the future of their businesses, he said.

Lines said the fact that thousands of farmers would inevitably miss out on funding was “terribly sad” and showed the “desperation” many farmers were experiencing.

Sex-based discrimination in medicine costs lives

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 16:58:22 GMT

Readers respond to an article on women being less likely than men to be offered active treatment for the same conditions

As head of pharmacovigilance at a clinical trials technology company, I was not surprised that a review of global research found that women are less likely than men to be offered active treatment for the same conditions (Women with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’, 16 September).

This inequality costs lives. A British Heart Foundation-funded study found that women were less likely than men to receive recommended care after a heart attack. Research in 2018 estimated that more than 8,000 women’s deaths may have been prevented over 10 years had they received the same standard of care as men.

The problem starts long before a patient reaches the hospital, however. For years, women have been woefully underrepresented in clinical trials, initially because policy excluded women who might become pregnant. However, women also have busy lives, typically managing home and work, which makes taking time off a challenge that many find impossible.

Yet without representation in the trials that give us safer, more effective medication, women’s specific needs are sidelined – which is unacceptable given that women experience 50%-70% more side-effects from drugs than men. Including women in more trials would go a long way towards addressing the health inequality between women and men. Claire WilliamsNorthWest EHealth

Sex-based discrimination is not new, but the fact that women with the same health conditions as men – from kidney to heart to liver problems – are less likely to be offered treatment continues to shock us. These are not just men’s issues, as they have historically been treated, but conditions that significantly affect women.

This new research is significant because it goes beyond gynaecological conditions. It illustrates that medical misogyny is not just rife in “women’s specialities”, where conditions are dismissed as “women’s problems”, but across fields, contributing to women receiving less treatment and less help for their health problems.

A fundamental shift in attitude is needed. Addressing this requires mandatory education in women’s health and in sex- and gender-sensitive medicine to eliminate bias throughout the training and continuing professional development of all healthcare professionals. Education must also begin in schools, with stronger sex and health education to challenge stereotypes and improve understanding of women’s health.

The renewed women’s health strategy and the 10-year health plan for England provide an opportunity to act. Women are not asking for preferential treatment; they need equal access to timely diagnosis, appropriate investigation and effective care. Prof Geeta NargundHealth Equality Foundation

I was delighted to see more discussion of endometriosis and other women’s health issues (‘It makes you feel helpless’: patients and doctors cast doubt on standard treatment for endometriosis, 15 September). However, there remains a woeful disregard of many of the issues women face.

Pelvic pain is experienced by many women, as the article pointed out. In my case, as extreme pain came to dominate my life, I saw several top (male) professors of gynaecology and urinary disease before – thanks to a Guardian article – I saw a female gynaecologist who pointed me to a solution. This was physiotherapy specifically directed to dealing with women’s health issues, and pain in particular. These techniques need to be far more widely available and known. Prof Sophie WatsonThe Open University

Minority ethnic NHS staff pay a heavy price for speaking up about patient safety

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 16:58:17 GMT

Providing psychological safety to Black, Asian and ethnic minority staff so they can raise concerns about patient care without fear would save lives, write Dr Jennifer Creese, Dr Joy Spiliopoulos and Prof Carolyn Tarrant

Your report (One in five black, Asian and minority ethnic NHS managers in England plan to quit amid racism, report finds, 15 September) rightly highlights racism, exclusion and blocked career progression in the NHS. But it also points to a wider risk: patient safety. Care mistakes already cost the NHS £14.7bn a year.

A March 2025 report by the NHS Race & Health Observatory notes that Black, Asian and minority ethnic (BAME) staff, who make up more than 40% of the medical and dental workforce, still face harassment and discrimination in promotion, everyday work and disciplinary processes. This fuels stress, burnout and poorer mental health. Bullying and harassment are estimated to cost NHS England £2bn a year through staff turnover, sickness and lost productivity. In such environments, BAME staff are less likely than white colleagues to speak up about patient safety, fearing that their concerns will not be understood or taken seriously.

In recent research funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research, BAME NHS staff told us that racism, exclusion and barriers to progression affected not only their wellbeing but also whether they felt able to speak up when they saw patient safety issues. Staff in medical, nursing, midwifery, psychological therapy and patient safety roles described not being heard, unclear routes for raising concerns, fear of backlash, exclusion and bullying. Visa-dependent staff described particular anxieties. The result was reduced trust in organisations, diminished professional fulfilment and, in some cases, staff leaving.

NHS England’s pledge that new staff standards will require trusts to tackle racism and ensure equal representation, equal opportunities and fair treatment is welcome. But the standards must also require trusts to create psychological safety for BAME staff: workplaces where staff can raise concerns about safety and racism without fear of repercussions. This would support retention and progression, reduce avoidable costs and, most importantly, protect patients’ lives. Dr Joy Spiliopoulos, Dr Jennifer Creese and Prof Carolyn Tarrant University of Leicester

In their unqualified admiration for your democracy, our leaders have done a lot to emulate it: in 1861, Alexander II abolished serfdom; in 1905, Nicholas II allowed the creation of our elected parliament; in 1917, Kerensky allowed women to vote; in 1990, Gorbachev reintroduced a multiparty system; he, Yeltsin and Medvedev resigned in 1991, 1999 and 2020 respectively (like your Wilson, Thatcher, Blair, Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and Starmer in 1976, 1990, 2007, 2016, 2019, 2022, again 2022, and 2026 respectively).

But ordinary Russians are up to their ears in their age-long que será, será approach to politics. So there has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch. Had Mr Behr lived in our provincial towns instead of Moscow in the 1990s, he would have produced a very different article. Mergen MongushMoscow, Russia

Anti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led by Reform UK ended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card.

Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader of Sunderland city council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”.

Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding.

The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”.

Bennett, who became only the second black player in Sunderland’s history when he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996.

The former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years.

Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces.

He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing. For something like this to happen now, we just want to know the reasons why.”

Bennett said the racist riots across many English cities including Sunderland in 2024 showed there was “still lots of work to be done”.

While Britain had come a long way since the 1980s, he said, there remained issues to confront around attitudes towards asylum seekers and migrants.

“You’ve got all different issues going on now. It keeps moving, it’s always something else which causes some form of racism,” he said. “It’s something that is challenging every single day and we’ve got to keep the fight. There’s still lots of work to be done and we can’t just ignore it and think it’s going to go away because it’s not.”

Eynon, whose party gained control of the council in May, said the authority was not “stepping back from its opposition to racism or discrimination” and that “racism has no place in Sunderland”.

He took issue with Ged Grebby, the chief executive of Show Racism the Red Card, describing Reform as a “very dangerous organisation”.

Grebby defended his right to express personal views and said the charity had support across the political spectrum.

Separately, Reform UK has been accused of “vice signalling” after its councillors in Bradford proposed to pull out of the Local Authority of Sanctuary scheme, which is intended to show a city is a safe place for migrant communities.

The Reform group that runs the council said it would be putting forward a motion at the next meeting in October to end the status, which it said has meant the council had “led Refugee Week engagement and utilised local libraries to celebrate all new arrivals into Bradford”, adding that “public services should instead be prioritised for Bradford residents”.

The Reform councillor Jayne Morgan said the move “may upset oversensitive political opponents” but was firmly in the public interest.

In response, Imran Khan, the leader of Bradford’s Labour group, said: “Reform failed to deliver on various promises they made to Bradford residents this summer, so instead they fall back on their usual toxic recipe of hate, victimhood and division.”

He said pulling out of the scheme would “do nothing to help a single person” in Bradford. “This is vice signalling from Reform and all it does is damage integration and promote division and resentment, which helps no one,” he said.

The great iced coffee debate: is it wrong to take a beverage into a job interview?

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 16:37:07 GMT

It might seem a perfectly natural thing to do. But, on TikTok, a recruiter has expressed her dismay at gen Zs showing up with a takeout drink – and it’s caused a ruckus

Name: Iced coffee.

Age: Colonial troops in Algeria invented a sweetened cold coffee beverage known as Mazagran in around about 1840. However, in Japan, a cold brew was popular among sailors even earlier, in the 17th century.

Fascinating. Isn’t it? But actually this is less about the age of the drink, more about the age of the drinkers. Plus, when it is and isn’t appropriate to drink it.

Go on. It started with a TikTok …

Obviously! From @caitlinrecruiter.

Who I’m guessing has something to do with recruitment? Correct: 16 years’ experience, mostly with Fortune 500 corporations.

Impressive. Where does iced coffee come in? With a candidate at a job interview. This is what Caitlin has noted among some of her gen Z job-hunters. She’s not a fan.

Is it the ice that’s the problem? No, iced coffee is just popular with that generation. The issue is around bringing a beverage to an interview and the casual impression it gives. “It just looks like you didn’t have time to finish your coffee beforehand,” says Caitlin.

Maybe you didn’t. Well, maybe you should have made time! Time management is important. When LinkedIn surveyed more than 1,000 managers about interview no-nos, showing up late came out top.

What else? Using foul language.

You can shove your effing job up your … Yes! Also, dressing inappropriately, looking at your phone, appearing disinterested or disengaged, not asking questions about the job or company.

So act like you care? Yes. Back to Caitlin’s TikTok, she says bringing a coffee to an interview makes it look like “a stop on your list of errands for the day. It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks, now you’re stopping by your interview, then you’re onto the next thing.”

I’m guessing it went viral? 371k at time of writing. She’s calling it the great iced coffee debate.

Comments on both sides of the argument? And across a generational divide. For example: “Professional millennial here. I would never show up with a drink in my hand.” And: “This comment section proves that generation has lost the art of professionalism.”

And some examples from the other (possibly younger) side? “But an interview IS just a stop on my day. It’s not my whole day.” (13k likes) And: “Do you guys need employees or not.” (19.7k likes).

Do say: “Yes, I’d like to know what success would look like in the position.”

Don’t say: “Can we wrap this up, I’ve got things to do. Am I hired or what?”

Meanwhile, The Great British Bake Off star Nadiya Hussain shared a widely circulated video in which the therapist Megan Cooper accused Sheeran of crying “white tears” and playing “the victim”.

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 16:18:13 GMT

Billionaire owner of Ineos says company ‘cannot compete’ with global market despite efficiency of Humberside sites

Billionaire industrialist Sir Jim Ratcliffe is pausing production at three chemical plants in Hull, blaming the UK’s “ridiculously high” gas prices.

Ratcliffe’s chemicals conglomerate, Ineos, said on Tuesday it would “mothball” three chemical plants because the cost made it difficult to compete in the global market.

Production has already been paused at two of the Humberside plants and the third is due to come offline in a few days, according to Ineos. About 240 people are directly employed by the company across the three sites.

Ineos said the number of jobs on Humberside that would be affected by a permanent closure would rise to 4,000 including those employed in the sites’ supply chains.

“I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. “[W]e just cannot compete.”

The Monaco-based billionaire claimed that gas prices in the UK were 12 times higher than in the US and eight times more expensive than the coal increasingly used by chemical plants in China.

The rising cost of gas in recent years has taken a heavy toll on Europe’s chemicals industry, including the Ineos empire, because it is a vital feedstock used to make the chemical building blocks required to manufacture products ranging from textiles and pharmaceuticals to detergents.

Gas prices tend to be higher in the UK than in other parts of Europe due to the country’s reliance on gas for heating and electricity generation. Historically this reliance was met by the UK’s domestic North Sea reserves, but as production declines the UK has become increasingly reliant on imports.

Earl Spencer apologises to Piers Morgan over ‘incorrect assumption’

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 16:03:30 GMT

Brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, says ‘accuracy is important’ as he responds to broadcaster’s threat to sue over claims made in memoir

Earl Spencer has apologised to Piers Morgan for incorrectly claiming in his new book about Diana, Princess of Wales, that the former tabloid editor was behind the publication of intrusive photos of the late royal in the mid-1990s.

Morgan had earlier threatened to sue Spencer over “fabricated inaccuracies” and “examples of brazen falsity” in the book, which was published on Tuesday.

In the memoir, the earl claims Morgan was in part responsible for the publication of photographs taken by an allegedly hidden camera in a gym, of Diana working out in a leotard.

But the broadcaster told his audience on YouTube on Monday that the pictures were published in the Sunday Mirror nearly two years before he became editor at the Daily Mirror and when he was working at the Sun.

Morgan called on Diana’s brother to pulp the remaining copies of his book and said he had instructed his lawyers to demand the work be pulled from sale immediately.

Later on Tuesday, Spencer issued a statement apologising to Morgan and admitting he had incorrectly assumed Morgan had been editor of the Mirror at the time.

“Earl Spencer’s account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate.

“Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister’s funeral,” the statement said.

“The book then records Earl Spencer’s assumption that Mr Morgan’s response was because he was editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group had published highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym.

“The photographs were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. Mr Morgan has pointed out that he did not join the Daily Mirror until October 1995. As an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error.”

In his response to Spencer’s apology, Morgan also wrote he was “neither surly nor annoyed” but had been “very respectful” to the earl during their telephone conversation.

He wrote: “Earl Spencer’s account of our phone call is also deeply misleading.

“I was neither surly nor annoyed, but instead, very respectful to him and his family, as I wrote in my diaries, The Insider. It would seem that Spencer’s recollection of phone calls is very suspect.”

Morgan also doubled down on his threat of legal action, writing on social media: “Earl Spencer has apologised to me for his defamatory lies published in his new book, Swan Song, published today.

“But I am pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King’s Trust.”

The earl has made a series of claims in Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, including that King Charles said “we’ll forget her soon enough” after she died, which has prompted a war of words between him and Buckingham Palace.

The book also contains allegations about Morgan, who has rejected the claims.

Speaking earlier on his YouTube show, Piers Morgan Uncensored, Morgan said: “Many allies of his majesty have called into question these facts, ever since the most salacious accusations were serialised by the Daily Mail.

“Many royal commentators and experts have lined up to say that they simply don’t ring true. The king himself issued a furious rebuke that is almost without precedent. But, in essence, this has all been about opinions. Recollections may vary, after all. Well, until now.

“Because I can exclusively reveal on Uncensored that Earl Spencer’s book contains fabricated inaccuracies which will strike to the heart of his credibility. Spencer recounts how he personally called round the tabloid newspaper editors to uninvite them from Princess Diana’s funeral, after they had all been invited. I remember this well, because I was one of them.”

Morgan read an extract from Spencer’s book, which claims the editor “snarled with annoyance before he hung up”, as well as the passage concerning the intrusive photographs.

He told his audience on YouTube that the pictures were published in the Sunday Mirror nearly two years before he became editor at the Daily Mirror.

He said: “Well, this is all pretty extraordinary stuff, isn’t it? And very damning, particularly about me. I come across in the most despicable manner imaginable. There’s just one problem. It’s all bullshit and very, very easy bullshit for me to prove it.

“The photographs which he says that I published were printed by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. I joined the Daily Mirror in October in 1995. In fact, at the time of the gym pictures, I was doing a showbiz column on the Mirror’s arch-rival, the Sun. About as far removed from responsibility for the Mirror scoop as I could possibly have been.”

Morgan, who was the editor of the Mirror from 1995 to 2004, continued: “Earl Spencer was estranged from Diana and living in South Africa at the time of her death. As editor of the Daily Mirror, I had lunch with her at Kensington Palace with Prince William. After that, it wasn’t uncommon for her to call my office or for me to run stories by her … Ironically, by that time in her life I think I was probably talking to her more often than he was.

“My question, though, is this: if Earl Spencer can be so incredibly, defamatorily wrong about such basic facts involving me, well, why should we believe anything else he puts in this book?”

He later added: “In the meantime, Earl Spencer, you’ll be hearing – and your publishers – from my lawyers.”

Bookshops across London were reported to have appeared quiet on the release day of Spencer’s memoir – with the £28 book marked at half its cover price in some stores.

Dozens of copies with red “half price” stickers were stacked in Waterstones flagship Piccadilly store – the largest in Europe. It is also marked as half price on the Waterstones website.

Why you should quit and not look back: ‘Saying yes to everything is saying no to what matters’

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 16:00:02 GMT

In her new book, The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, Lindsay Crouse discusses the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself free

Lindsay Crouse used to define herself as not a quitter.

She went to Harvard University, where she learned to become even more high-achieving and ambitious, then landed an assistant job at the New York Times and worked her way up to become an opinion writer and producer. On the weekends, Crouse ran marathons and did endurance sports, clocking new personal bests throughout her thirties.

“My entire life was really guided by only one question: how can I go harder, and do more?” she says now over Zoom.

Over time, though, that mentality began to backfire. After having two children, Crouse started falling behind, dropping balls and losing her passion for running and writing. Something needed to change.

Like Crouse, many of us are conditioned to persevere. In her new book The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, she reckons with the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself free.

Now Crouse argues quitting is essential for a satisfying, successful life. She herself left her prestigious job to chase unknown risks and rewards. “We need to start viewing quitting as a tool of perseverance, rather than the enemy of it,” she said. “If we find ourselves in a hole, often we dig harder when we should just stop digging.”

Our conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

What is the biggest misconception we have about quitting?

In the moment, not quitting in some ways feels heroic, like you’re martyring yourself to your own capacity or grit. In fact, you’re actually limiting yourself, because you’re not walking away from things that are failing. In the long run, if we want to do our best, we need to get better at quitting. It could be a pivot or a break, but ultimately I think that can help us do better and go further.

Quitting involves entertaining uncertainty and oftentimes risk, but focusing on that means we don’t ask ourselves: are we continuing because we love what we’re doing or because we’re afraid of confronting what might happen if we stop?

What do we stand to gain from quitting?

This is about priorities: if we commit to everything, we commit to nothing. A lot of this book was me talking to myself: I really thought it was so impressive that I was saying yes to everything, like “Wow, look at all you can do!” Writing it, I realised that attitude was a lot more narrow-minded and even timid than I was willing to admit.

Saying yes to everything is saying no to what matters. By quitting things that don’t, we can better commit to what’s meaningful and build our lives around that.

Sometimes, you hit a roadblock when you’re working towards something. How do we know when to quit, and when to push through?

I’m not encouraging people not to engage with struggle or develop resilience. This book is for people who are almost so good at enduring that they don’t realise the costs that come with it. It’s like they’ve confused their ability to persevere with a mandate that they should.

I talk about “quitting intelligence”, which is learning to separate temporary setbacks from fundamental futility: how are we thinking about continuing? Are we rationalising it, feeling desperate to salvage something that we’ve already invested in, veering into self-sabotage?

With longer-term goals, we can think about progress: are we getting closer to what we want over time, or moving further away? Are we working hard productively, or pointlessly? Those two things help us to assess whether it’s time to quit or invest.

If you start working harder or change your approach, and still don’t see the results you want, maybe you’re in the wrong arena and your efforts might be better suited somewhere. If you’re enjoying what you’re doing, that is valuable enough. But if you’re frustrated that it’s not working out, you can just stop and do something else. That sounds obvious, but I think sometimes we tell ourselves we don’t have that choice.

Why do we persevere with things that we know, deep down, we would be better off giving up?

We’ve learned to ignore very instinctive cues. I realised that I’d done the same, writing about a study done on zebrafish at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. At first, when zebrafish encounter a strong current, they will respond with a surge of effort, but if that doesn’t work, they will give up. This is judged by specialised cells in their brains, which scientists call “futility counters”. Zebrafish know to listen to these cues because it factors into their survival, but humans have learned to override them.

A lot of it comes down to the idea of control: where we really want something to happen, we convince ourselves that we have the power to achieve it through hard work, but sometimes we’re denying futility. We equate the idea of being a quitter with being a failure, but often we fail to see that the failure has already happened. We just throw more into it, investing more in a lost cause, and that’s the greatest failure of all.

You interviewed dozens of people about their quitting stories. Did any of them change your thinking?

I interviewed a woman who was going through devastating rounds of IVF. Having a child was central to what she wanted from life, and she sacrificed an entire decade to that cause, putting all these wonderful things on hold for this goal that simply wasn’t happening. Meanwhile, it was making her miserable.

Eventually, she quit IVF and moved on with her life. When I reached out to her a year or two later for fact-checking, she had a baby, having become pregnant naturally at 41 – she didn’t know how. It just confirmed that she never had control in the first place.

after newsletter promotion

That made me think about what isn’t working in my life that I might be refusing to acknowledge. A lot of us just push harder, letting the work itself convince us and stand in for the results or success we’re seeking. We can control how hard we work, but we can’t always control the outcome.

How can we navigate “hope-selling industries” like IVF and dating apps, while protecting our wellbeing?

We need to be mindful, moderate our engagement and create checkpoints for ourselves. The decision scientist Annie Duke calls these “kill criteria”: clear, specific conditions for quitting that we establish before we even start, and before our emotional investment can cloud our judgement.

To some extent, these industries are disincentivised from getting us what we want: they want us to keep coming back, to keep swiping and grinding. That’s not to say don’t use them, but perseverance can become a compulsion, even pathological, and these industries don’t help.

Of course, the flipside is that a lot of people persevere and do end up with a child or a relationship, but that can also make us feel that we’re failing if we don’t. Sometimes we need to realise what actually can work and focus on that instead.

What would you tell someone who talks endlessly about leaving their partner, or quitting their job, but doesn’t act?

Staying is a decision, too. I’ve heard people say “I really want to quit, but I can’t.” I think you have to ask yourself: why can’t you? If you think you can’t quit your job because you need money, have you actually run those numbers? Maybe you have, and you don’t like them. That’s fine, but you need to own that choice to stay.

If you want to leave your relationship, but are afraid of starting over, own that. Maybe you just want to get married. Down the line, tell yourself that was a decision you made, and you knew what you were getting into. Otherwise, you can quit and do your future self a favour – your partner, too. Who wants to be in a relationship without investment?

Being only one foot in is a very passive and kind of cowardly way to live your life. You need to ask yourself: “Am I hoping that this doubt, or deliberation, is just going to abate?” That question helps you reframe the situation – and the answer is no. You have to act: either own it or leave, but don’t think that these problems will just disappear. Maybe you can put up with them, but is that the life you want?

Often we dither over these decisions because we fear making the wrong one. In quitting, do we risk future regret?

In the long course of our lives, we tend to regret inaction a lot more than action. We’re so focused on tomorrow or next week, but we need to think in the long-term: what is the gift that we can give ourselves in five or ten years’ time? It’s often acting now, so that our future selves don’t have to make this choice.

The more that we quit, the better we get at it: we’re less fearful and more able to cope with uncertainty. We have more confidence in ourselves that we’ll make it work. If we don’t develop that muscle, quitting will continue to be understandably scary, and that feeling may keep us stuck in place. Isn’t life all about growth?

What if we’re not in a position to make a big change?

Thinking about what you really want to do and how you want to spend your time can help you move forward more intentionally than just feeling like “I can’t.” For example, if your job isn’t a source of meaning and purpose for you, maybe you can get that somewhere else. Instead of a career change, maybe you need a different work environment.

Otherwise, when we want to solve a problem, often we try to add more when the solution is actually to take something away. Instead of quitting a job or ending a relationship, we can overhaul our lives significantly by eliminating clutter.

That was the case for me. I had so much digital clutter, calendar clutter, physical clutter, and routines that I’d almost slid into, like going to bed with my phone. Eliminating those smaller things helped me build the muscle for making bigger changes.

You quit your job at the New York Times early this year, after 15 years. What part did your book play in that decision?

I realised I was living decisions that I made when I was 20, and they weren’t working for me anymore. I wasn’t happy, and I wasn’t doing the kind of work I wanted to be doing. I wanted to follow my own advice and live in the uncertainty for a bit.

I didn’t write this book to convince myself to quit my job at the Times, but I would still be working there if I hadn’t, for sure. I’ve always been the kind of person to wade slowly in, rather than cannonball. I strongly believe in building an off-ramp, and this book was that for me. I am the kind of cautious person who never quits anything; I wanted to be bolder and take more risks, and I’m at a point in my life where I can.

I’m 42 now. I have a chance to take a swing and bet on myself. If I don’t, I know that’s what I’ll regret when I’m looking back at 60. That made the decision a lot easier.

For me, this book is not about quitting your job or getting a divorce; it’s about questioning the tendency to convince yourself that you can’t or shouldn’t. I felt that was essential for myself, independent of my employment status. It was this idea that I can stop – and so, sometimes, perhaps, I should.

The Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out by Lindsay Crouse is out now

The Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencers

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 15:28:48 GMT

Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy

We’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in a matter of weeks. Prices are rising, troop morale is plummeting, and there is little evidence things will improve.

The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recently threatened to “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doing idiotic stunts on YouTube and getting hit in the face during boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department of War Crimes?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech. In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzinger wrote, “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.” That about sums it up.

The Paul brothers, to be fair, rose to the occasion as best they could. In a speech which channelled Churchill, if Churchill had suffered several major blows to the head, Logan said that touring the Pentagon had been “a cool experience”. Albeit not quite as cool as being deployed to fight and possibly die in an illegal bombing campaign started by president Trump, a convicted felon, on the advice of Benjamin Netanyahu, an accused war criminal. “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight for their country,” Logan said. Which is why you won’t see him doing it; easier to pocket millions fighting on TV.

As well as giving a pep talk to the military, Jake met up with treasury secretary Scott Bessent and the US treasurer to discuss how “to get more young Americans financially empowered.” That must have been an interesting chat considering how, back in 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the YouTuber with unlawfully promoting crypto assets without disclosing that he was being paid to do so; he eventually settled without admitting or denying the charges. (Logan has also faced a lawsuit linked to a dodgy crypto venture, although the case was eventually dismissed). Exactly the sort of person you want the treasury secretary expending energy talking to when US debt recently topped $40tn for the first time ever and a financial crisis seems to be around the corner.

Just how Jake Paul and Bessent hope to financially empower young Americans is unclear. But it is unlikely to be via the traditional method of working hard at school and then going to university. Jake very much shares the Trump administration’s contempt for education. In 2020 he tweeted that he’s “sick of our education system and how it’s teaching kids 0 real life skills for them to secure there [sic.] own future.” He also once described high school as “kids sitting in Geography to learn where Timbuktu is for no reason.” The reason you learn where Timbuktu is, Jake, is so the US can overthrow it after they’re done with Iran and Greenland.

There has always been a strong vein of anti-intellectualism in US politics. “[T]he subordination of men of ideas to men of emotional power or manipulative skill are hardly innovations of the twentieth century,” Richard Hofstadter wrote in his 1963 book Anti-intellectualism in American Life. “[T]hey are inheritances from American Protestantism.” But while this may not be a new impulse, the Trump administration’s embrace of ignorance is doing damage that can’t be easily undone. The US is stuck in a vicious vacuousness cycle: the Trump administration has slashed research funding and disrupted thousands of grants, leading many promising young academics to flee the US. As expertise is eliminated and critical thinking purged from government institutes, chancers like the Paul brothers are elevated.

Still, I suppose we should count our blessings, before even they are affected by Iran-induced inflation. At least the boneheaded Paul brothers are simply having meetings with high-level Trump administration officials. At least they’re not directly involved with military or economic policy. Although, the way things are going it’s only a matter of time. “I’m going to make a prediction that you will be, in the not-too-distant future, running for political office,” Trump told Jake, who has been a vocal Maga supporter, on stage at a rally earlier this year. “You have my complete and total endorsement.” Could another blond buffoon with zero qualifications become president of the US? Tune in to find out in the next season of America: the Empire Implodes

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Great Britain exit Billie Jean King Cup after Czechia triumph in quarter-finals

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:59:06 GMT

Defeats for Kartal and Boulter condemn Britain to loss

Men will play Germany in quarter-finals of Davis Cup

Great Britain’s stay at the Billie Jean King Cup finals lasted only one match as they lost against Czechia in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen. Anne Keothavong’s side were bidding to reach the last four for the fourth time in five years but were considerable underdogs and defeats for Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter sealed their fate.

Led by the Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, the entire Czech team is ranked higher than any of Britain’s players, and it was Noskova who sealed victory with a 6-2, 7-6 (3) win against Boulter. That followed a lengthy struggle between Marie Bouzkova and Kartal lasting a minute short of three hours, which the Czech eventually won 7-6 (2), 4-6, 6-4.

It was a fine effort from Kartal, who was playing her first match in six months after sustaining a stress fracture in her back in Indian Wells in March and she will now hope to finish the season strongly. The Czechs will bid for their seventh title in the competition since 2011, while Britain’s hopes of lifting the trophy for the first time are over for another year.

Keothavong’s team have overperformed in the Billie Jean King Cup of late and did so again by reaching the finals, with an understrength team upsetting Australia in April. Neither Kartal nor Boulter were available for that tie, with the former in the early stages of an injury break that led to her missing the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open.

Kartal found her range immediately against the 26th-ranked Bouzkova, who has had a very good season, but could not convert a 40-0 lead in the third game to make it 3-0 and was edged out in a first-set tie-break. She fought back well in the second set, often dictating the play against Bouzkova, who was preferred to the Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova.

When Kartal broke to lead 2-1 in the deciding set she appeared to be in the ascendancy, but fatigue seemed to catch up with the 24-year-old as Bouzkova reeled off four games in a row. Kartal, now ranked down at 127, hung on grimly, saving three match points and breaking Bouzkova’s serve, but she could not quite get back on level terms.

That left Boulter with the formidable task of trying to beat the world No 6 Noskova, who claimed her first grand slam title at SW19 in July. Boulter struggled with her serve in losing the opening four games but she has a very good record playing for her country and thereafter there was little to choose between the players.

But Noskova served brilliantly in the tie-break to lead the Czechs into the semi-finals for the first time since 2023.

Great Britain’s men, meanwhile, will play Alexander Zverev’s Germany in the quarter-finals of the Davis Cup in November. Britain booked their return to the eight-team finals, held this year in Bologna, over the weekend with a 4-0 victory against Ecuador at London’s Copper Box.

The Davis Cup finals take place at the SuperTennis Arena from 24 to 29 November, with Britain lined up to play either Spain or Austria if they prevail against Germany.

That same month, Panettiere released a memoir titled This Is Me: A Reckoning, in which she detailed her struggled with fame, postpartum depression, addiction and recovery.

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:41:11 GMT

Videos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdict

Ozzy the four-month-old goldendoodle isn’t normally allowed on the sofa. But today he has been granted special privileges because I’ve come round specifically to watch TV with him. We’re not watching Paw Patrol, Scooby-Doo, or even Crufts. We’re watching Sealook, the Netflix kids’ cartoon about a colony of seals that dogs and cats online are supposedly obsessed with. But is this really a thing? And will Ozzy care?

I hit play. A gang of wide-eyed pastel-coloured seals are in a slapstick scrape. There’s no dialogue: they mostly lie around on the ice, and try to annoy each other by doing silly things like making funny noises, throwing snowballs or keeping each other awake. Ozzy seems more interested in chewing his pizzle stick – which I discover, slightly too late, is the dried penis of a bull. Then again, perhaps this is just canine second-screening: Sealook on the telly, bull penis in the mouth.

Ozzy may be playing hard to impress, but he’s in the minority. Search #sealook and there are loads of dogs pawing at the TV and cats batting at the characters. “They do watch television, but not this intently,” says Jessica Blumen from Oregon, who has had nearly 10m views for an Instagram video of her two goldendoodles’ reaction. Benny, nearly one, and five-month-old Myrtle, certainly seem to be converts, judging by their reaction to watching a group of animated seals banging on the ice. “The minute the seals started drumming, Benny sat up and Myrtle had these subtle head tilts.”

It’s even become a sort of doggy mindfulness regime. “Last night Benny was getting a little wild – goldendoodles get zoomies at night – so I turned it on and he immediately settled. Even when an episode ends and flashes up a yellow bar saying ‘fin’, that still keeps his attention.”

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Švepsė, a one-and-a-half-year-old rescue cat in Lithuania, is already a TV fan, enjoying animal documentaries and having previously been fascinated by a Lithuanian strongman competition. But Sealook produced an even stronger reaction. “She became very focused on the screen and tried to catch the characters with her paws. Sometimes, she simply sat there watching very carefully without taking her eyes off the screen,” says owner Erika. “We’re used to her watching animal documentaries, but seeing her try to catch the characters in Sealook was something we hadn’t seen before.”

Rio, a six-month-old golden retriever owned by Melly Roman in Houston, Texas, is another fan. “We have the TV on for background noise and he never normally watches,” she says. “But he started barking when one of the seals came really close to the screen. We tried again later and he sat and watched a couple of episodes.” The clip helped take Rio’s Instagram following from about 115 to nearly 4,000.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

This, I tell Ozzy, is exactly the sort of behaviour that could help boost his own Instagram following of 137. Watching television is a far better party trick than barking at his own reflection or stealing hair scrunchies from his human mum. I’d offer to become his social media manager, but I don’t have any interest in freebies from Bonio.

Still, before I write off Ozzy as a hopeless influencer, what are cats and dogs seeing when they watch Sealook? One possible reason is the colour palette: it’s all white snow, pale-blue ice and brightly coloured seals. Cats and dogs see blues and yellows particularly well, which perhaps makes Sealook about as easy to ignore as a bowl of Whiskas or Pedigree Chum.

Dr David Williams, an associate lecturer in veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Cambridge, thinks movement may be just as important as colour. “Cats and dogs are particularly interested in movement because they’re interested in chasing a mouse or another prey item,” he says. “They’re also crepuscular – most active around dawn and dusk – so movement in low light matters particularly to them.”

Sound may matter too. Dr Emily Blackwell, a companion animal behaviour expert at Bristol Veterinary School, says the seals’ “high-pitched squeaking noises may mimic the sounds of prey species – rodents – and also sound very similar to the squeaky toys that many of our pets have”.

Dr Freya Mowat, an associate professor of veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how dogs watch television, says dogs seem particularly drawn to animal-like movement. “My own research has shown that dogs prefer watching dogs to humans,” she says. “Seals? I don’t know, but they are closer to dogs than people! Cartoons are great content for dogs: high contrast, lots of movement, nice fun music – it’s the whole package.”

Was any of this deliberate? Apparently not, says Leah Yeon, communications lead at The Pinkfong Company, the South Korean co-producer of Sealook. “Seeing cats and now dogs as well becoming so absorbed in Sealook has been a fun and unexpected surprise.”

The show’s simple snowy landscapes, vivid colours and short, repetitive movements were designed for audiences of children, although the team suspects the same ingredients may help explain its appeal to pets. The trend began with cats, then dogs jumped on the bandwagon. “We didn’t set out to make a show for animals,” says Yeon, “but it continues to be fascinating – and very amusing – to see it connect with this new audience.”

Which leaves one final experiment. Williams suggested turning the sound off to see whether Ozzy’s interest changes. Right then, Ozzy. Volume down.

Nothing. I turn the sound back on and, finally, Ozzy looks up. A seal slides across the ice; his ears prick up. Another squeaks and he edges towards the screen. At last! I grab my phone, visions of 4,000 followers dancing before me. But seconds later, Ozzy wanders off in search of a hair scrunchie or bull penis. Sealook, it seems, has yet to earn his seal of approval. Doggy stardom will have to wait.

Sealook is on Netflix

Never mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American people

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:02 GMT

Mark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing ear

At a moment when Europe is focused on persuading Donald Trump to remain committed to Nato, it needs to convince Americans, too. So the presence this evening of the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, in front of a public audience in Des Moines, Iowa, is significant. This is the home town of Trump’s ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker, and the visit brings the debate over Nato’s future directly to a midwestern audience in a red state that operates far from elite foreign-policy circles in Washington. Rutte’s appearance is long overdue.

Russia’s war in Ukraine and uncertainty over the US commitment to European security have forced European leaders to confront their dependence on Washington. While some are pressing for building European capabilities as a means to separate from the US, others see greater European defence spending as essential to keeping the US engaged. Either way, European governments can’t rely solely on meetings with Trump to secure the alliance’s future.

Instead, Europe’s leaders need to look beyond Washington and take a tip from Rutte. Making the public case for Nato, the transatlantic partnership, and shared security across the middle of the country, is essential, not optional. This case should begin with the American people.

For decades, Americans have supported the transatlantic relationship because they understood that Europe’s security is closely connected to their own. Nato and the transatlantic partnership were part of a wider ambition, designed to make the world safe for democracy, not least for the growth and prosperity this created. Public support has been essential to this undertaking.

For many Americans, democracy is now failing to deliver on the promise of prosperity, and in some key areas the contrast with Europe is stark. In the Commonwealth Fund’s 2023 survey, 46% of US adults with lower or average incomes reported skipping or delaying needed healthcare because of cost, compared with 16% in each of the UK, France, Germany and the Netherlands. Populists have been quick to highlight the shortcomings of America’s democracy, and this message has resonated across swaths of the population, particularly rural voters and Americans without a university degree – both central to Trump’s electoral coalition.

When it comes to the American public, there is plenty of room for optimism, but in a political context that is ripe for populists to cultivate antagonism toward spending on foreign causes, there is little room for complacency. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ polling consistently shows that Americans support Nato and the transatlantic partnership. Its recent survey with Ipsos found that 68% of Americans supported maintaining or increasing the US commitment to Nato. Yet only 47% were confident that European allies would come to America’s defence if it were attacked, down from 62% in 2025. Public support for Ukraine has also remained substantial, even as Americans debate the scale and duration of US assistance; a 2024 survey found that 58% supported sending additional arms and military supplies to Ukraine, and the same number supported economic assistance.

European leaders would be wise to invest in a public diplomacy strategy in order to cultivate understanding among Americans outside Washington’s foreign-policy establishment. The secretary general’s decision to travel to Iowa should be seen as a crucial part of Europe’s midwest strategy. Other leading foreign policy organisations have sought to do the same. Over the summer, the Ditchley Foundation used the occasion of America’s 250th to deepen its partnerships across the US, convening roundtables in South Carolina and Illinois.

This outreach is essential to counter the persistent myth that Europeans are free-riding on America’s coattails. Europe’s renewed commitment to defence is significant, with a 20% increase in 2025 compared with 2024 among the EU’s 27 member states. This remains poorly understood in the US. Nato’s Annual 2025 report notes that all of Nato’s 32 members met or exceeded the 2% of GDP expenditure target for that year. Allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP annually by 2035 in defence and related security. The precise figures matter, but so does the broader message: that Europe is investing in the capacity to defend itself and contribute to shared security.

It would also be smart to highlight the opportunities created by this investment for American companies. Defence cooperation supports jobs and growth opportunities. It also boosts transatlantic supply chains and research partnerships. But the ties that bind Europe and America reach deeper than military procurement. The case for the alliance should ultimately be made in terms that people recognise in their own lives: the security of their jobs, the price and availability of energy, the resilience of the technology they rely on and, above all, the prospect of their families living without the threat of a wider war.

The transatlantic partnership cannot be secured through presidential diplomacy alone. European leaders should continue engaging the White House, but they must also make their case to the American public. The long-term future of Nato will depend not only on what presidents decide, but on whether citizens on both sides of the Atlantic continue to see the alliance as essential to their security, democracy and prosperity.

Leslie Vinjamuri is president and CEO of Chicago Council on Global Affairs

How I Shop with Tom Daley: ‘I am obsessed with my knitting machine!’

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:00:02 GMT

Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The retired diver talks scrapbooking, cheap chargers, and trouser fails with the Filter

How I Shop with Laura Jackson

Tom Daley OBE is a retired professional diver who has won five Olympic medals, including gold at Tokyo 2020. Since retiring from competitive diving, he has hosted Channel 4’s Game of Wool: Britain’s Best Knitter, while continuing to share his passion for knitting and crafts through his Made With Love brand and YouTube channel. He is married to US screenwriter Dustin Lance Black, and the pair have two children.

Small treat: vanilla and chocolate soft-serve ice-cream swirl; slightly larger treat: a little getaway we just booked for Halloween with the kids and some friends.

In LA, Trader Joe’s or Ralphs, but in London, it tends to be M&S.

I always make a scrapbook of our year for my husband at Christmas, so we now have 14 scrapbooks of tickets, photos, room keys, memories and things to show the kids when they grow up.

Some ChiaoGoo interchangeable needles.

ChiaoGoo twist lace interchangeable knitting needles

The Selfridges gift section has saved me many times as they always have great ideas!

I love craft stores, the colour and creativity of it all. But there is a shop called Trove 167 (previously Bermondsey 167) in London where I would always buy my gifts from.

I am obsessed with my LK150 knitting machine at the moment. I have made a couple of jumpers using it, and it makes things so much faster, but I am not as good at machine knitting as I am at hand knitting. I also probably use my portable phone charger a lot.

Silver Reed LK150 knitting machine

I don’t tend to regret many things, but I will say it is always the cheap chargers that end up breaking first.

There is something about buying loo roll in person … I just think it should always be delivered, lol, from somewhere like Ralphs (the US version of Tesco) or Amazon.

I usually ask for underwear as a Christmas and birthday gift, so I have a very random collection.

For £20, a reusable water bottle; for £200, a nice massage or spa day.

I often use it as inspiration for things I want to make. I like to think of online shopping now as one big knitting and crochet moodboard.

Yarn! I have an unhealthy obsession with going to yarn shops and feeling it, buying it, and imagining what I could make with it.

I’m a black coffee guy. I make an americano using my concrete AnZa coffee machine.

I tend to splurge on experiences. I like doing things with friends and family, such as going to theme parks or new places.

I don’t spend money on plain T-shirts, especially white ones, because the kids get them mucky so quickly.

When I was in Calgary, I was obsessed with some vintage shops near me, where the prices of items would go down week by week: it was always a gamble whether something would still be there the next week. I found an amazing cropped floral jacket that I wore to death, including to an after party at the Met Gala in 2021, where I ripped my trousers.

Great to see what Tom Cruise’s belly button looks like, but it’s the stuff he is never asked about that interests me

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 13:16:11 GMT

Most stars, and especially women, are endlessly expected to explain the past: the lessons learned and all the regrets. But not Tom – it’s Hollywood’s free pass

There really is no press tour like a Tom Cruise press tour – which is why there have not really been any Tom Cruise press tours for a very long time indeed. We’re now at the stage of this one where even the interviewers have been forced on to the interview circuit to defend their interviews.

Anyway: Cruise. The guy has one child with ex-wife Katie Holmes who dropped his surname as soon as she was legally allowed, and two Scientologist children widely reported to be effectively estranged from their mother, Nicole Kidman. The divorces from Kidman and Holmes were clearly deeply strange and traumatic events for both women, and have remained shrouded in unusually watertight and presumably contractual secrecy. Yet you can currently find Tom Cruise promoting his latest movie not being asked about any of this stuff, or indeed any of his other extensive “stuff” – as always – but instead doing things like giving Travis and Jason Kelce’s podcast a lecture on the benefits of VistaVision. Hate to say it, but a woman could never.

At some level, you have to admire the mad image-industrial complex that labours to keep “the last movie star” from having to talk about the things all the other movie stars are required to lay on the line in order to promote their wares. Only a few weeks ago, Kidman was on the cover of Vogue being required to pick over her two marriages in what was otherwise the most saccharine of interviews.

Meanwhile, the world is obliged on pain of death to regard the 64-year-old Tom Cruise as ageless (and probably deathless). A few years ago, his Top Gun co-star Kelly McGillis – 62 at the time – explained why she had not been approached to return for the sequel, Top Gun Maverick. “I’m old and I’m fat, and I look age-appropriate for what my age is,” she replied with deadly affectlessness, “and that is not what that whole scene is about.”

Cruise, in contrast, has chosen to cover this month’s GQ magazine with his shirt flung open, pulling down the waistband of his jeans – a choice we’d probably have to describe as wholly mesmerising rather than directly appealing. Hand on heart, Tom Cruise feels like someone you’d like to have sex with about as much as you’d like him to explain VistaVision to you. Wait, what am I talking about? Let me adjust: I strongly suspect most women would rather have 87 hours’ worth of defensive questions about image grain and aspect ratio lined up just in case.

Even less enticing is the sheer guffawing prickliness with which Cruise responds to GQ’s question about what it meant to recently turn 64. “It means I’m 64.” Okaaaaay. Does it change anything about the way you think about anything, the interviewer, Zach Baron, wonders with desperate vagueness. “It’s just like, No!” scoffs Cruise. “Zach’s like, Does it change anything? When you’re looking at this, does it, like … Man, I’m just saying: it doesn’t at all. What changes things is I love seeing people do well.”

Even Cruise’s yesteryear PR anecdotes have been written over in the service of making him seem like Hollywood’s apex benefactor. Back in the day, Tom always used to explain how he struggled with reading scripts because he was dyslexic. These days, the story has changed to reflect his unique position in, and contribution to, the cinematic culture. On the Kelces’ podcast, he took the time to explain how he makes writers and directors read their scripts out loud to him: “I don’t read the scripts. I have them read it to me. I have them read it to me because I don’t want my ideas to invade it yet. I want to understand what is their communication. They’ve been working on it. They have things that are just there. So they come to me, and I just sit there, and I’m like, I want you to read it to me.”

As mentioned, perhaps the most meta element of this press tour is that the GQ interviewer now feels he has to get himself out there on the circuit to do interviews about his strange interview. He wasn’t instructed not to ask about Scientology, Baron told the Washington Post, but just decided not to do it because it has been done before. Then again, you sense that even if Baron had asked, he could have been re-hit with an answer like “What changes things is I love seeing people do well”. The good news for those who ordered this word salad is that there are an entire 10 days to go before Digger, the film Cruise is promoting, finally makes landfall. Expect plenty more to be served up by then.

Perhaps most ironically, a report from a Bafta event where Cruise was interviewed this week describes the audience as “otherwise low-key”, until Tom launched into a six-minute monologue about the primacy of human art over AI. “What you put attention on, you give life,” he freestyled. “People wanna see real things.” As he had it: “There is nothing like human.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

And yet, is he anything like human? More and more, the real-life Tom Cruise feels like something sprung from the pages of fiction. He’s a sort of Peter Pan’s shadow who leads a largely disconnected existence from the Cruise of the screen – the only Cruise that makes sense. Strange that for decades now, one of the most obviously bizarre people in public life has still been allowed – required, really – to be routinely hailed as his medium’s one remaining superstar. Perhaps that and his medium’s steady decline are not altogether unconnected.
