The viral Hyrox horror: is the ‘go hard or go home’ attitude to exercise finally over?

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 12:38:31 GMT

When an athlete soiled herself at a hybrid fitness event, it sparked a debate about a culture that pushes people to ignore their body’s signals at real cost

How far would you go to secure an impressive marathon time, or a Hyrox personal best? Maybe you’d turn down a boozy night out in favour of eight hours’ kip the night before? Or perhaps you’d swap sugary treats for protein shakes, and commit to a gruelling training plan in the run-up? It’s not uncommon for athletes to want to give it their all come race day – but few of us would go as far as the Australian Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk, who continued to take part in the hybrid fitness event a little over a week ago, despite having noticeably soiled herself.

Wietrzyk’s immediate response appeared to be one of defiance. “Go hard or go home … a win is a win,” she said in a now-deleted Instagram post, having been allowed to finish and win the event in Beijing. Hyrox organisers initially seemed to back her position, posting a statement (also now deleted) which said: “We ask our athletes to push themselves to the highest levels. At times, they will go beyond what even we thought was possible.”

But as images of faecal matter dripping down Wietrzyk’s legs – while she continued to use communal equipment – circulated online, few appeared to admire her commitment. Rather, some raised concerns that her bowel incontinence posed a health risk to other competitors.

Both parties quickly pivoted to apologies, with Wietrzyk admitting that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there was “more to life than racing”. Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste stated that “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race”, before going on to confirm that, “there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again”.

But could the viral moment mark a turning point in what is considered aspirational or acceptable when it comes to fitness goals? Hybrid training, which combines cardio with strength exercises, has been growing in popularity over recent years, alongside associated competitions such as Hyrox, ATHX and the CrossFit Games. But among the fitness community, attitudes towards the benefits of an unrelentingly competitive mindset may be starting to shift.

“Recently I have noticed individuals showing more consideration for their wellbeing,” explains Harvey Smith, a sport and exercise psychologist whose work focuses on supporting athletes with the psychological demands of performance, training and competition. A number of his clients take part in endurance and hybrid events such as Hyrox, as well as other sports. “There is a growing awareness that chasing extreme performance markers does not always align with long-term physical or mental health, and more people are actively reflecting on that trade-off rather than assuming harder is always better,” he says.

Even so, he acknowledges that competitive culture can be slow to change, and extreme effort is still often celebrated, “so I would say we are in a transition rather than a complete shift”. He believes the incident in Beijing has opened up an important conversation about where the line sits between admirable resilience and a culture that pushes people to ignore their body’s signals at real cost.

“I think it should be obvious that doing Hyrox is not about health, it’s about competition,” says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University and author of books including Exercised: Why Something We Never Evolved to Do is Healthy and Rewarding. “While we have capacities to do extreme things, we never evolved to stand on one line and run as fast as possible to another line 26.2 miles away, or – even more bizarrely – to eight times over run a kilometre and then push sleds, carry weights, do burpees, and so on” – as athletes do as part of Hyrox competitions.

“We now have hundreds of studies which show that you don’t need a lot of physical activity to promote health,” Lieberman adds. “More can bring greater benefits but only up to a point, at which the benefits tail off and possibly reverse.” It is easy to see why even the most devoted gym-goer might question the merits of pushing themselves to the limit – especially if in doing so they have been plagued by injury.

For the sport and performance coach Matteo Massaini, there’s no one size fits all approach. “I think it’s really important for people to challenge themselves and strive to be better – and I think Hyrox has actually really helped with that,” he says. “But extreme competition can also be toxic.”

Massaini has taken part in Hyrox himself, as well as numerous running competitions, and stresses the importance of not prioritising personal achievements over the wellbeing of others – although he can see how it’s easy to get tunnel vision on race day. “The beautiful thing about humanity is that we’re all very different: not everyone needs to have the attitude of ‘go hard or go home’,” he says. “Some people have different goals.”

Likewise, Chloe White, co-owner of small group personal training facility Raw Inc Training, agrees that competitive events can provide “a positive, performance-based goal and shift the focus away from appearance towards what the body can achieve”. She has competed in Hyrox, ATHX, Turf Games and Butterfly Effect events, and has found there is now a “greater awareness of recovery, injury management and longevity, although a ‘more is better’ culture still exists within parts of the industry”.

Is it possible to achieve your fitness dreams without getting caught up in a competitive culture? Smith says that grounding your determination “in process, self-compassion, and realistic support structures” is the key to success – rather than simply fixating on a win or a PB. Meanwhile, he’s seen more coaches, event organisers, and athletes talking openly about sustainable performance and the risks of overtraining. “A more useful question for people to sit with is often: ‘How do you stay determined without the result controlling your sense of self-worth?’”

Swan Song by Charles Spencer review – a furious exercise in score-settling by Diana’s brother

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 11:09:24 GMT

Amid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stage

Charles Spencer’s Swan Song, a memoir of his relationship with his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, is a fascinating document that tells us a little about Diana and a great deal about Charles Spencer – perhaps more than we needed to know. If that sounds snarky, after 400 pages of score settling, chest thumping, wild indiscretion and some truly touching passages about his late sister, the reader is left with a head-spinning story of the world that created Diana and a certain sourness at the manner in which it is told.

Let’s start with the headlines in last week’s Daily Mail, the newspaper to whom Spencer sold serialisation of a book which includes a line describing tabloid journalists as “those who inhabit the murky swamps of malevolence, and who need to suck their victims dry of their souls”. Perhaps he meant a different set of hacks. Anyway the top line in the Mail was that, shortly after Diana’s death, King Charles insulted her in a phone call to Spencer: “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’” Your take on this quote will likely dictate how you receive the book, and here’s mine: I’m willing to believe the king behaved badly, but “hissed” is a red flag, one of those embellishments, like “snarled” or “flounced”, that writers tend to use to make those they’re writing about appear worse. Spencer, always the injured party, has so many axes grinding away in this book that at times it’s impossible to hear what he’s saying.

Before we get to that, the question on everyone’s lips is: why write this book now? Spencer maintains it’s because, as the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death drew near, he kept being asked to contribute to other people’s projects. Rather than allow the narrative to be guided by “some TV producer” from a network “I will never watch” he promptly got on with his own. Likely that’s not the sole reason; elsewhere in the book he writes about how, back in the day, his father was always at risk of running out of cash to run Althorp, the family’s Northamptonshire estate, and one wonders if the present earl is having similar difficulties.

Never mind. For fans of petty grievances, among whom I count myself, the book is an absolute corker of resentment, and in Spencer we have a hero who, decades after the fact, is still harping on about a great many things involving a large cast of characters who he has absolutely not forgiven for any of it. While telling the story of his and Diana’s relationship, there are drive-bys on Peter Carter-Ruck, Princess Michael of Kent, Princess Margaret, his three ex-wives, whom he describes in an amazing parenthetical take down as “all double divorcees”, and members of a police protection squad who, in 1986, let sniffer dogs jump all over his furniture.

If too many words are spent on, for example, the perfidiousness of Martin Bashir, I could read an entire book on the subject of Spencer’s horror at what his stepmother, Raine, did to the interiors at Althorp, including installing “exceptionally ugly double glazing”, “shiny velveteen” upholstery, and “unsightly wall-to-wall carpeting”. (This is before we get to the scene in which Raine, standing at the top of the staircase in search of breakfast, bellows to staff below, “where’s my fucking egg?”)

Interspersed with these delights is a portrait of Diana that is affectionate, sad, and lovely in places. Spencer suffers the pain of the less famous sibling who doesn’t want to give up his own version of their childhood and there’s a stiffness to some passages as Spencer insists it was all less unhappy than the record implies. His portrait of their mother, Frances, feels like a useful corrective to a figure who has been publicly maligned, and who comes across in the book as the parent most responsible for Diana’s gifts: spirited, mildly eccentric, a more interesting character than the plodding males in the Spencer line. (Charles, winningly, allows that this is the case, pointing out that the men in his family have always been outclassed by the women.)

And of course there is the devastating account of the coldness and aggression of the then Prince of Wales. Spencer tells us that Charles’s poor behaviour towards his sister began from the very start of their courtship, during which he commented on her weight, ignored her at parties and told her he didn’t love her, to the extent that, Spencer writes, Diana tried to get out of the engagement. Their father told her it was too late. This all chimes with other accounts of the doomed marriage, albeit in gorier detail, and explains the fury of Spencer’s finest hour, the speech he gave at Diana’s funeral in which he lambasted not only the press but the royals, reclaiming the young princes William and Harry for their mother’s “blood family”.

At his best, in these passages, Spencer acts as a proxy for the rest of us by registering the absolute lunacy of those days after Diana’s death – by which I mean not the public outpouring, but the behaviour of the royal family, who remained deaf to the nation’s needs until they were forced to change course.

“What was Prince Charles actually doing there?” writes Spencer, incredulously, in relation to his former brother-in-law’s prominent role at the funeral, pointing out to some comic effect that no one wants their “ex” at their funeral? Diana’s former husband was there because the young princes were there, walking for two miles behind their mother’s coffin while mourners wailed and shouted out at them, an outcome Spencer had vigorously argued against. Now, he writes flatly, “It all seemed mad to me – the more so as I began to appreciate the extent of the ordeal we had embarked on.”

To be honest, at times in this book, they all seem quite mad. “That’s it ... it’s curtains ... Duch is dead,” Spencer reports his sister Jane as saying to him on the phone when news of Diana’s death was confirmed. Before the funeral, per Spencer’s account, Prince Charles wanted to walk behind the coffin in the middle, centre stage, until brought up short by his father, Prince Philip, who said words to the effect of don’t be so bloody silly, and put Charles Spencer in the centre, with the boys either side and Diana’s ex-husband and ex-father in law on the outside. There was a split second, writes Spencer, when it seemed as if the pall-bearers might buckle under the weight of Diana’s reinforced, lead-lined coffin. All of this is fascinating and Spencer tells it well.

Still, the book suffers from problems of self pity and self regard (I won’t get into the passages about Spencer’s ADHD or the weasily justifications he gives for telling Diana, in her hour of need, that she couldn’t move into a property on the Althorp estate; the main house has 90 rooms). Every few chapters we return to the unfolding play-by-play of how he wrote his speech – the decision he made to substitute the word “power” for the word “strength”; how his oratory gathered, his greatness formed, and look, it was a fantastic speech, but at some point in the book you start to think, alright Alexander Hamilton, give it a rest. Before the funeral, Spencer visits Diana lying in her casket and reads out his speech to her, sensing that his dead sister is “applauding my words, with soft insistence”. Even here, Spencer manages to take centre stage.

After the book’s litany of bitter grievances I came away wondering whether Spencer has been in the ear of his nephew Prince Harry these last few years. Mostly, however, I felt sadness for the insurmountable difficulties his sister faced marrying into that family. The king is peevish all the way through and Spencer is peevish right back at him. You come away feeling the pair thoroughly deserved each other. And in the middle Diana, 30 years dead, frozen in time and – as she ever was – at the mercy of other people’s interpretations.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer is published by Michael Joseph (£28). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘I’m afraid they’ll bomb the cafe where I work, or bomb me’: a day in the life of a 12-year-old boy in Gaza

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 11:00:53 GMT

This week, as the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Ramadan lives in a tent on the beach and works to support his family

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.

The tent is pitched on a platform set in the sloping sand dunes, above a long expanse of golden coastline. Rats have chewed holes in its canvas sides, and tendrils of pale sand blow in through the gaps. Inside, on the torn mattress he shares with his siblings, 12-year-old Ramadan Ghaban blinks the sleep from his eyes. The sun has just risen but it is already hot.

This is a day in the life of a boy in Gaza.

double quotation markI wake up every morning at 6.30am. Sometimes, the heat wakes me up, and sometimes it is the sound of the birds, which are everywhere because we live near the sea.

I wash my face and brush my teeth. We do not have gas, so I gather small pieces of wood and plastic to light the fire so we can boil water for tea.

My name is Ramadan Yaqoub Ghaban. I am 12 years old, from Beit Lahia. I now live in al-Nuwairi, in the coastal area of Nuseirat. I have three sisters and one brother.

Ramadan picks his way over the dunes and between the tents, looking for any wood for a fire to boil the family’s kettle. There are few trees left here, so there’s little to be found, but he finds some scraps of plastic and a piece of driftwood, and crouches to break branches off a thorn bush. With his brother Adi, he builds a small fire to warm the kettle and make tea.

Then he sets off down the beach to work, the wind whipping up sand as he walks.

double quotation markAfter breakfast, I go to work by the sea, at a cafe. The cafe is about 300 metres from our tent, and it takes me only a few minutes to get there.

I usually walk along the beach. On the way, I see fishermen catching fish and crabs and selling what they catch. Sometimes, I stop to watch them bringing the fish out of the sea. Usually I work for 12 hours – from about 7am until the evening. Sometimes, people stay up eating until 10pm, and so I work until late. When I walk home it is dark, and large rats come out of the darkness and brush against my legs.

I move tables, arrange chairs, take tables out and at night bring them back, clean and arrange them, rake the sand around the tables to keep it smooth and collect the trash. Yesterday, some people were grilling food. They were having a barbecue, and the smell of it was everywhere! I was telling myself, “If we were at our home, we might have been having a barbecue.” Then those people went and left a bag of chips behind. I was hungry, so I took it and ate it.

My work is very tiring, but I do it because I have to support my siblings. I see the neighbour’s kids hanging around and playing, living with their father, and he brings them food and drink, but I have to work to get food and drink. Otherwise my younger sisters cry without money to buy food.

Before the war, my father used to work harvesting strawberries in Beit Lahia and gathering recycling, but he doesn’t work any more. He was killed when he was at my aunt and uncle’s house, when he went there to help them evacuate. We heard the Israelis had bombed a nearby house. We wondered, “Which house?” Then a woman came to the school where we were sheltering, saying, “Your father is dead. Your father is dead.” We didn’t believe her, but when we went to the house, it had been destroyed. We rushed to move the rubble and find him, but the Israelis were firing shells, so we couldn’t reach him and we fled.

My father remained under the rubble for four months. After four months, we returned to Beit Lahia, and pulled him out from under the rubble. We buried my father in the cemetery.

At about 1.30pm, a water truck comes, and Ramadan takes a break from his work to dash up the hill and fill the family’s empty bottles. He and his younger sisters take them to the truck and fill about 15 bottles for drinking and washing. When they are all full, he loads them into a trolley made from a plastic crate. Its mismatched wheels spin and wobble on the stick that forms the axel, as he drags it over the sand dunes and back down the hill.

double quotation markWhen the water trucks arrive, I fill as many containers as I can. Sometimes, they arrive at six in the morning, and sometimes in the afternoon.

In our tent, rats have eaten everything, even gnawed the water containers. We don’t have any good ones left – they’re all leaking, so we fill up plastic bottles instead.

Before the war, we had a home. We lived in a house with two bedrooms, a living room, a bathroom and a kitchen. I used to go to school in the morning, sit with my classmates, have breakfast and play during the break. Now we live in tents, and rodents have chewed the whole tent – they’ve torn it all apart. Soon winter will come, and our tents will fly away in the winds – we will have water seeping in while we’re sleeping, or we’ll get flooded. In winter there are strong winds and storms, and all the cafes get shut because the sea rises and gets closer.

The thing I’m most afraid of is that the war will return, or that they’ll bomb the cafe where I work, or bomb me if I’m walking, or they’ll bomb a house, or a hall or something – because we have a hall nearby here where people dance. I’m worried that the war and famine will return, and we won’t find food and water. During the famine we’d go hungry for three or four days. I used to go to the aid point at Zikim to get bread, and I saw people pushing and fighting over a kilo of flour. I saw it with my own eyes, and I saw people being killed. The Israelis would fire bullets right next to us: we’d be lying down, and bullets would come from above. If someone raised their head, they’d die instantly – their heads were torn apart. I hope those days do not return.

double quotation markI finish my work between 7pm and 10pm, and the people at the cafeteria give me 10 shekels [£2.45].

Before the war, 10 shekels could buy a lot of things – but now it buys some cheese and a loaf of bread.

What I like about my work is that it is close to the sea. I like breathing the sea air and swimming when I get the chance. I taught myself how to swim, and if there is a break in between my tasks, I will run into the sea to cool off.

In the future, I want to be a lifeguard to rescue people – so if someone is drowning, I’ll save them. Or I want to be a doctor or a lawyer. My other hope for the future is that the war will end, that we’ll rebuild our homes and the Israelis will withdraw and go back to their borders, and life can be like it used to be. I would not have to work and I could go back to study in classrooms. I have not been to school since the beginning of the war, since the very first day. I really loved reading. Arabic was my favourite subject.

I don’t have much time to play during the day. In the evening, after the customers leave, I go out to see my friends. Sometimes, we used to make kites and fly them, but they started bombing children who flew them. The other day, they bombed three children’s kites, so I stopped making them.

I walk home along the beach. When I return to the tent, I wash, change my clothes, pray, have dinner and go to sleep.

Henry Pollock triples salary after signing ‘multi-year’ deal to stay at Northampton

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 09:14:34 GMT

‘I’m happy. It’s an exciting place to be right now’

Prem champions have moved to tie down huge asset

Henry Pollock has signed a new Northampton contract worth in excess of £400,000 a year, ensuring he will remain available for England beyond the 2027 World Cup.

The 21-year-old has roughly tripled his salary in a “multi-year” deal thought to extend until 2029. Pollock’s future at the club had come into question when his representative, Eddie Hearn, suggested he deserved a seven-figure salary but while the new deal is a long way short of that, he ends up as one of the best paid back-row forwards in England.

The Northampton director of rugby, Phil Dowson, had insisted that a “happy medium” had to be reached for the Saints starlet, who has 13 England caps to his name, having already tied down Tommy Freeman to a new deal at Franklin’s Gardens.

Pollock, who also earns about £150,000 a year as one of the 25 England players with an enhanced contract, last week said he would like to play abroad one day and try his hand at other sports. But for now his future lies with Northampton, with Hearn insisting there were a number of other lucrative offers turned down. “He left a lot of money on the table to stay with Northampton,” Hearn said. “But it wasn’t even a tough decision for him.”

Pollock said: “I’m massively happy to re-sign with Saints, my boyhood club. It’s an exciting place to be right now. We’re in a great spot as a team, but it feels like there’s still so much more growth in us. I’m still young, and we’ve got a young squad with a brilliant group of lads. Some of my best mates are here, and every day everyone pushes each other to improve and be the best players and team we can be. … For where I am in my career, this is exactly where I want to be.”

Dowson, who guided Northampton to their second Prem title in three years last summer, added: “Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game – but just as importantly, he’s a young man of outstanding character. Keeping someone with both his talent and mindset is hugely important for the club.

The truth about UK prisons and organised crime: ‘They’re your good lads. Respectful. Keep their noses clean’

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 09:00:53 GMT

In more than two decades in the Prison Service, Pia Sinha gained a reputation as a fixer. Now, as head of the Prison Reform Trust, she’s sounding the alarm about overcrowding and other problems

Pia Sinha has led the Prison Reform Trust since 2023. In that time, she has seen a Conservative government finally admit to an overcrowding crisis that had tipped over the edge. (It was in October 2023 that the early release scheme was devised; by May 2024, the Tories had also launched Operation Safeguard, using police cells as temporary housing.) She’s watched a change of government, then a change of prime minister, then Andy Burnham instantly assailed by negative headlines as the consequences of that early release scheme unfolded: prisoners had to actually be released early. “We’re a bit concerned about how [Burnham] has handled it,” she says, in the trust’s scruffy, un-corporate offices in central London, “but that’s in the knowledge that he had a bit of a hospital pass.”

To recap on Burnham’s handling: when he came in in July, he paused the scheme for an urgent review; in August he announced a series of exclusions, further crimes for which people couldn’t be released early, including manslaughter and death by dangerous driving. That solved an immediate problem, that the killers of PC Andrew Harper would otherwise have been released, but had the knock-on effect of reducing the numbers expected to be released by about a quarter. The conversation Sinha wants to have is what prison overcrowding looks like, what it does to prisoners and staff – and what it means for society.

Now 53, Sinha arrived in the UK from India with her parents, aged 14. “I think that’s part of the reason I can adapt from one prison to another: I had to learn how to survive and cope, you become very good at reading your environment,” she says, smiling at the implication that the teenagers of north Harrow, circa 1987, were not unlike a prison population. She studied psychology and economics, went on to do a masters in counselling psychology, and was running a pub in north London when she got a job at Holloway, the now defunct women’s prison. When she got her first prison governorship 14 years later, of the open prison Thorn Cross, she was very unusual – not just because she was the first Asian female prison governor, but also for her manner, which is sunny, personable, enquiring and receptive.

Prison governors – the women as well as the men – often construct a quasi-military persona to indicate that their word is final, and it’s easy to assume that is how it has to be done, since someone’s word has to be. That’s not Sinha’s style at all. But she was unusual from the start, since she came into prison work as a counselling psychologist, to support the prisoners themselves.

Traditionally psychologists were forensic: they saw their job as addressing the offending behaviour, with the aim of protecting the public. In 1999, after a spate of self-harm incidents and suicides, the service had started to ask: “How do you get these women out of their crises? How do you get them to not be so suicidal?”

She stayed at Holloway for five years, and it was rewarding work. The forensic and the counselling strands of psychology turned out to be complementary because – who could have foreseen? – it turned out: “You can’t actually do any meaningful work with people unless they are stable.”

A lot of people argue that incarceration per se is unjust to women, since they’re often victims of crimes that are worse than anything they’ve committed, and the stress of it on mothers, unable to care for their children and not necessarily trusting whoever is caring for them, is unbearable. But Sinha isn’t someone who thinks that women don’t belong in prison at all. “I don’t want to slip into describing all women as victims, because that’s often not the case. Women are capable of causing serious harm. Being in prison is an opportunity to look at the harm they’ve caused and get the insight that they need. I’ve seen it work. There are many women who will say that prison was the best thing that happened to them.”

The problem with prisons is that, whatever improvements are made, they’re still part of society and change with it. Nowhere is this more clearly demonstrated than in the women’s estate, where things really did get a lot better at the turn of this century, only to get a lot worse after austerity.

The use of force in the women’s estate has increased dramatically, which seems absolutely extraordinary. And more extraordinary still, as Sinha explains it, this is partly because prisons are often seen as a place of refuge: “Women go through the court process, presenting as really complex, with multiple unmet needs, and they need somewhere they can be safe. Whatever crime they’ve committed, there would need to be somewhere in the community that gives the judiciary some assurance that if they go back home, they won’t be going into more abuse; that their mental health or addictions can be addressed. The default position in many minds is that prison is safer. Prisons have become really good at coping with complexity.”

However, she says, “Women end up in prison and then get hugely triggered by the environment, which creates strong urges to self-harm or commit suicide. Staff are completely overwhelmed by the depth of complexity, so force is often used to try to stop women from harming themselves, which feels crazy.”

What about transgender prisoners? There has been much debate over where they should be held, but Sinha is quite reserved on the issue. “It’s a pressing issue only when it goes wrong, and this is just what happens in prisons. Everything trundles along fine, and then something really horrendous happens and then you have to take a policy position. Prisons are fundamentally all shades of grey. But policy has to be black and white.”

After Holloway, Sinha went to Wandsworth in 2004, during which time governor Ian Mulholland was trying to turn it around, from one of the most degraded prisons in Britain (a huge population, dilapidated, vermin-infested buildings, a febrile, lawless atmosphere) to one of the country’s success stories (though by 2024, per that point about prisons mirroring society, it was a story of yet more failure, with the high-profile escape of Daniel Khalife triggering an inspection that revealed conditions so appalling that the governor, Katie Price, resigned).

After leaving Wandsworth in 2009, Sinha did stints at Wormwood Scrubs, Send and Downview, among others. She arrived at Thorn Cross in Cheshire in 2013, just as the scandal broke that armed robber Michael Wheatley (AKA the Skullcracker) had absconded from a different open prison and immediately raided a building society. “Then there was another high-profile abscond,” she remembers. You can hear her 27 years in the service when she uses the jargon: “abscond” as a noun; “ROTL” for release on temporary licence. “The public didn’t realise, really, that open prisons existed, and that even quite notorious criminals might be ending their sentence in one.” This was where she got her reputation as a fixer, someone who could turn a crisis around, and that’s how she arrived at Liverpool prison.

This was 2017, and what was happening at Liverpool was “symptomatic of what was happening in prisons up and down the country,” she says. “It just got hit first.” It was a crumbling Victorian local prison, that was falling apart. “The estate contract had just been privatised, and grossly underfunded. They weren’t getting to any of the repair jobs, so it was literally breaking. The overcrowding wasn’t quite at the scale and magnitude of the crisis now, but every space mattered. And people were being put in cells that were disgusting. Every window broken. No plumbing, no heating, mould. Dickensian. It became a bit of a joke to staff. A prisoner would come in through reception, and officers would say: ‘Do you want a cell with lights or do you want a cell with windows? Do you want a cell that’s got mould or do you want a cell that has electricity?’ As a joke.” She is still audibly enraged.

“It was full of rats and cockroaches. Honestly, it made me cry when I went there. The inspector had written about a prisoner sitting with this vacant look, in a dark room without electricity, with the smell of mould, a broken window – mentally unwell. And the nail in the coffin was that when the inspector asked senior leaders, ‘How are you presiding over this? What do you think of the state of it?’ they said: ‘It’s going quite well.’”

The story of how Sinha remade Liverpool prison – getting prisoners involved in the refurbishment, fixing the electricity so that everyone could have a kettle, building partnerships with charities, universities, businesses, everyone she could find outside the jail – is a painstaking one, but it all started because the crisis was so bad that the head of the Prison Service, Michael Spurr, let Sinha cut capacity. Not every problem in a prison is down to overcrowding, but there’s almost nothing you can fix until you’ve fixed that.

Certain activities, such as 45 minutes’ exercise a day, are mandated, but an overcrowded prison is understaffed by definition, so it could take the prison officers the full day just to get everyone into the yard, one wing at a time, which means prisoners spend the other 23 hours locked in a cell. It wrecks morale, Sinha says, because “whether you go in as a prison officer or a psychologist, if you’re public spirited, you want to do a good job. But if really all you’re doing is banging people up, you start thinking: ‘I don’t want this job. This is shit.’”

When the right people leave the service and the wrong people stay, you get a lot of corruption. The range and scale of crimes committed by staff last year was staggering: one prison governor was convicted of having a relationship with an inmate; one prison health worker smuggled in drugs with a value of £1m to a single jail. You also get areas and corridors where prison officers won’t go. In Liverpool, Sinha asked an academic to see if there were any no-go areas, and she said: “Not yet, but there’s a risk, especially on the fives.” She meant the fifth floor of each wing, the reason being that overstretched officers don’t have time to go up five flights of stairs. “Nobody wants that. Prisoners don’t want their jails to be like that. In the end, you want a peaceful life as a human being, no matter where you are.

“The real underbelly of it,” Sinha continues, “is that if you lose control of the prison it falls into the hands of really sophisticated organised criminals, running quite successful, profitable businesses.” Phones and drugs are dropped in by drone; there’s a large captive market of bored, impulsive people (some of these conditions are modern, some timeless). And the prisoners running these empires? “They’re your good lads. They’re respectful. They keep their noses clean. They’re not really in trouble, and they are in plain sight. I don’t want to mince my words. This situation is very dangerous. When prisoners are controlling the prison as opposed to the staff, who protects the vast majority of prisoners? There are vulnerable prisoners whose only source of security is another prisoner. Staff are scared as well. I’m not saying this is everywhere, but it is a lot of places.”

Regularly, now, HMIP (his majesty’s inspectorate of prisons) warns of serious failings, “and HMIP is good – it’s independent,” Sinha says. But it can’t magic away the reality, “which is that standards are irrelevant if there are too many prisoners and not enough staff. The whole legitimacy of the inspectorate pivots on their standards being attainable.”

In this era, “the noise in the political system is all that prisoners need to be punished. When you’re saying, ‘Prisons should be decent’, you’re screaming into the void,” Sinha says. But she can’t stop making the case for reform, because the situation as it stands is absurd. It’s not just that overcrowded prisons can’t rehabilitate prisoners. It’s not even solely a humanitarian case, that conditions in many prisons aren’t defensible. It’s simply a fact that some prisons are in such chaos that they’ve become temples and academies of further crime. “So what’s the outcome for future victims?” Sinha asks. “You might be able to satisfy current victims with harsh policies, but what happens to the victims of the future?”

My son has left home – and I feel full of complicated joy

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 06:00:37 GMT

I took him to university this weekend, and it reminded me of the exhilaration of suddenly having your own space, absolutely separate from your mother

When kids are small, and their expectations of an event diverge from yours in some important way, you feel terrible about it. You might be taking them to a play, and they thought that meant they’d be allowed to play, but actually it meant they had to sit still while strangers shouted things. You experience their disappointment as much as your own physical pain.

Then when they’re “adults”, your expectations diverge again. They thought you’d drop them at university and immediately leave, while you thought you’d unpack, and meet their flatmates, explore the city, and spin round a supermarket, then have a Nando’s, and maybe read a bedtime story, get chatting to the other parents and maybe all do karaoke? Well, then it’s time to manage your own disappointment, and the only thing to be said for that is that it’s way less bad than managing theirs.

When I went to university, my mum’s boyfriend drove me and there wasn’t room for her in the car, so it was a beautifully symmetrical event: I wanted him to leave and he wanted to leave. Then when she came to see me, I would count down the hours until she had to leave, and I used to love it when other people’s mums came to see them, because often they were nice, but, also, the schadenfreude was intense.

Mothers out of context are appalling. I don’t think there’s a feeling I’ve ever had that I remember with more clarity. Tugging on that memory unspooled the whole Technicolor exhilaration of suddenly having your own context, that your mother is absolutely not in. So there was more joy in being rejected by my son after dropping him off than you’d think, plus I went to KFC with his out-of-context dad on the way home and they gave us some free chicken selects. Don’t know why, maybe because we looked so complicatedly overjoyed.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 05:00:35 GMT

The issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solution

There is always something oddly unreal about party conference season. In theory, everyone is getting away from Westminster to better reflect on the state of the nation. In practice, the whole circus just briefly relocates to the coast, to live off warm white wine and gossip for three days, before coming back with a streaming cold. But this year, reality seems more elusive than usual.

Everyone knows hard choices loom, but everyone is frightened to make them. Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock, whose future will be vigorously debated on the fringes and in private conversation this autumn, but less so on the stage.

George Osborne’s shameless 2011 bid for pensioner votes – under which the state pension rises, come rain or shine, by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth for working people, or 2.5% – has already cost around three times as much as the Treasury originally expected.

The Office for Budget Responsibility reckons that by 2030 it will be swallowing more than £15bn a year – almost enough to fund the cause over which chancellor John Healey was recently willing to resign, namely raising defence spending to 3% of GDP in time to prevent a Russian attack on Nato. But even if you’re willing to roll the dice on another war, there’s no shortage of alternative proposals for spending the money.

The British Chambers of Commerce wants it diverted into tackling youth unemployment via cuts to national insurance, while the rightwing thinktank Centre for Social Justice argues for spending it on boosting the life chances of working-class boys. But perhaps more fittingly, it could pay for Andy Burnham’s dream of free social care for the very age group that is liable to lose out from breaking the lock. Would pensioners rather have a 3.9% rise next year – though it could be higher, if inflation really rockets this autumn – or relief from the fear of having to sell family homes to fund nursing care? Because right now, it’s difficult to see how they can have both. Yet the failure to be honest about these tradeoffs is bending British politics out of shape.

It’s making fools of MPs, who will readily say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable but have to keep pretending otherwise in public, even as they’re being asked to nod through painful cuts to disability benefits. It’s sending young and painfully squeezed people a message that nobody cares about them, fuelling intergenerational resentment. And it’s encouraging a phoney debate about tax and spend, in which parties of the left pretend they can find serious money from unicorn taxes – the magical kind that raise billions but somehow without hitting anyone likely to vote for them, or driving the highly mobile rich to Monaco – while parties of the right pretend they can make huge welfare savings they somehow missed during 14 years in power.

Breaking the triple lock is becoming enough of a no-brainer to attract genuine cross-party consensus, stumped only by the cross-party conviction that the public will hate them for it.

That fear is not unfounded. According to YouGov, two-thirds of Britons – and 70% of over-65s – want to keep the lock. Labour remains terrified of repeating Rachel Reeves’ 2024 gambit, when she tried to take winter fuel allowance away from better-off pensioners in a hurry, but couldn’t bring herself to make the political case for doing so, and was eventually forced into retreat.

For the Tories, going after pensioners would be suicidal, and the same goes for the Liberal Democrats, so long as they’re trying to hold on to the formerly true-blue shire seats they captured two years ago. Only the Greens seem to be keeping their options open, and they’re not going to win the next election. Fear of a pensioner backlash is distorting everything, like a dam in a river that forces the water to find other ways around it, eroding the banks until they eventually collapse.

Nobody is arguing that pensioner poverty has ceased to be a problem. (If anything, retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers did, which means this conversation may get harder the longer it’s deferred.) And even for those who aren’t on the breadline, the prospect of losing money at an age when you can no longer try to earn your way out of trouble is genuinely frightening.

But there are better ways of helping older people who genuinely need it than a triple lock that benefits both rich and poor, and working-age poverty is real too. Choosing to shield pensioners from the harsh economic realities of the last few years has hit some of their children and grandchildren unfairly hard: while pensioner benefits rose in real terms by £900 between 2010-11 and 2024-25, benefits for children and working-age people fell by £1,400, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank. Yet anyone daring to make that case at the next election for breaking the lock can expect to be mercilessly shelled by rivals, including those who deep down agree with them.

What is focusing minds now is the realisation that for the first time, next spring, the state pension may rise high enough to attract tax (though ministers say anyone poor enough to rely solely on it would be exempt). The stealth option would be to keep the triple lock nominally in place, but tax away the increase for wealthier pensioners – essentially giving with one hand and taking with the other, a bit like the Tories did over child benefit for higher-rate taxpayers. It avoids an outright confrontation, but plenty of pensioners will notice the money being clawed back and resent it nonetheless.

Better, surely, to break the lock as part of a new and much broader deal on generational fairness, which protects vulnerable elderly people but recognises that the young are also struggling – while lifting the burden of social care and settling arguments around pension tax relief into the bargain.

Smart spending in an era of shrinking resources ought to mean working out how to use the same money differently to meet new challenges, not just clinging to the past because you can’t face talking about the future. But for now, it seems, that’s just a little too much reality to bear.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

A tale of two trap houses: being cuckooed ruined my friend’s life – but did it then help save him?

The Guardian Tue, 22 Sep 2026 04:00:34 GMT

Drug gangs have moved off Britain’s streets and into vulnerable people’s homes. Addicts like my friend are easy targets, but the reality can be more complicated than it seems

Duncan is a good friend of mine. He looks like a Dickensian rock’n’roller: tall and skinny, long hair, retro clothes. He’s read the Flashman novels three times. We met in secondary school in west London in the early 1980s. We got drunk, smoked Rothmans and banana skin spliffs and played Dungeons & Dragons. At 14, we got into punk together and spent our teens playing music and seeing live bands. As we moved into our 20s, I trained as a journalist and Duncan, a talented songwriter and guitarist, carried on with music.

At the age of 23 he got involved in heroin. He found the lifestyle immediately seductive, his partner at the time, Lucy, told me. He would often befriend his dealers. “I remember more than once waiting in his car as he’d gone up some tower block to score, thinking where on earth is he?” Lucy said. “He’d be hanging out chatting. There were some genuinely fascinating characters with incredible stories to tell.”

We kept in touch. By the 2000s, after a few near fatal overdoses, it became obvious he had a long-term drug problem. But at the end of the decade, when Duncan was in his late 30s, his life changed when his then-partner gave birth to a boy. He was a natural father, becoming a full-time dad when his partner returned to work after maternity leave. Love and dedication to his son reduced Duncan’s drug use, but did not entirely dislodge it.

In 2013, he swapped the west London council flat he had been subletting for a nicer, ground floor studio apartment in a council estate in north-east London, near where his partner and young son now lived. By this time, Duncan was what drug experts call a “functioning” heroin user, managing his addiction with methadone while living a relatively stable life. He was working as a painter and decorator, played in a band that toured the US, and remained a dedicated dad. He got a job as a teaching assistant, helping some of the most troubled kids in the borough, which he loved.

His friends regularly spent time at his flat, which he had turned into his own, homely space. He had repainted his bedroom-lounge, and filled it with his collection of trinkets, retro furniture, artwork, vinyl records and a huge plant. His mother visited, his son regularly stayed the night and I crashed on the couch a few times.

By 2015, even while house prices were rocketing in trendy areas a few streets away, Duncan’s estate became neglected and scary at night. Families moved out and were replaced by single tenants leaving prison and care. Eventually, the estate was officially condemned by the council, which planned to decant tenants into a new estate being built a mile away. Duncan had watched as a group of noisy local kids had grown up into a gang of aggressive teenage drug dealers. They were made up of about a dozen boys and young men from the estate and the surrounding area, most aged around 15 to 17, and some as young as 12.

Coming home in the evening, Duncan would find the gang, dressed in black joggers and puffer jackets, hanging around the stairwell selling crack and heroin. “Sometimes, something, or somebody, would get thrown against my window,” said Duncan. “A couple of times I heard someone who got a really bad kicking from them, whimpering outside and I phoned an ambulance. They were horrible cunts.”

Within a year, Duncan’s home would be doubling up as the gang’s drug dealing base.

Over the past 30 years, the British “trap house”, slang for a place used as a drug dealing base, has evolved. Rather than derelict crack houses, drug gangs now prefer to operate from a hidden countrywide network of vulnerable people’s homes that they have taken over in a process known as “cuckooing”.

The origins of this shift go back to the 1990s, when a new wave of professionalised drug dealing crews spread out across the country. Their growth was fuelled by two products that were transforming Britain’s drug trade: crack and mobile phones. Blackberries and Nokias had enabled buyers and sellers to arrange transactions in less visible locations, and dealers now started to expand their operations, using a system of young runners who would call in orders and deliver the drugs.

In Brighton, a gang called the Londoners moved their drug sales teams off the streets and into the homes of local people, where they could more easily operate away from the prying eyes of police and rival gangs. When 10 of the Londoners were jailed in 2000, along with a man whose home they had taken over, a fresh gang from south London arrived to fill the gap. “I was buying crack and heroin from 15- and 16-year-old south London boys on BMXs in 2001,” Pete, a former Brighton street drug user told me in 2018. “I thought, fuck, you’re young. They would come down on the train and set up flats with heroin users.”

Over the 2000s and 2010s, wave after wave of gangs fanned out from Britain’s drug supply hubs – London, Liverpool and Birmingham – to set up shop in smaller towns and cities across the country. They took over the homes of drug users and young women who had been groomed by older male gang members. As early as 2008 Suffolk constabulary reported that more than a third of Class A drug dealers arrested in Suffolk were under 21, and the majority were from London. (Before this period, most crack and heroin dealers in towns and smaller cities were “user-dealers”, addicted heroin users in their 30s or older, who were not as “professionalised” as the big city drug gangs.) Gangs often used sex workers, who targeted male tenants and moved in, bringing the young dealers with them. Community safety teams, who rescued 80 tenants in London in 2005, were the first to call the tactic “cuckooing”.

In 2015, the National Crime Agency published an intelligence assessment that belatedly acknowledged “cuckooing” was part of “an emerging criminal business model”, whereby young people were being sent by drug gangs to sell out of town, which they dubbed “county lines”. By 2018, children who were described as “missing” in their local papers could now sometimes be found on Snapchat waving wads of notes, boasting to their classmates about their out-of-town moneymaking adventures “going country”. Rap lyrics, particularly drill music – where victims of cuckooing were denigrated as “fiends”, “cats” or “nitties” – soundtracked and glamourised the rise of the British trap house.

The reality was far more bleak: children hanging out in dingy flats with ageing drug injectors, earning far less than they had hoped and living in daily fear of being jumped by police, or worse, rival gangs. The whole system was reliant on grooming and exploitation. Over the years, reporting on Britain’s drug trade, I’ve spoken to several young drug dealers and cuckooed tenants about what it was like for them. One boy from Liverpool sold drugs from cuckooed homes in Devon, staying in a middle-aged crack user’s flat when he was 14. There was mould, “a plant growing out the wall” and the place was so dirty he ended up cleaning it himself. He smoked weed “to take the smell of crack away”. Another teenager from London, from a strict religious Nigerian family, worked 15-hour days from cuckooed flats in the east of England for three years. He told his parents he was on football trips or staying with friends; in reality he was holed up with drug users and armed with a machete.

A former sex worker and crack user I spoke to, whose home in Southend was cuckooed, actually felt sorry for the young dealers camped out in her flat. “They used to lie on my settee and sleep with the phone by their head, working 22 hours a day. They were putting on an act, trying to pretend they were the big boys, but they were young kids getting exploited.”

Cuckooing can involve sexual and financial grooming, the targeting of disabled and mentally ill people, people in private rented properties in affluent neighbourhoods, and even relatives and carers of gang members. In one case, said Insp Andrew Cameron of Operation Pantera, which was aimed at tackling the problem in London, a nephew cuckooed his aunt’s house for a south London drug gang. In another, a care worker cuckooed the home of a patient, who was tortured with cigarette burns and beaten by drug dealers. One particularly grim case involved William Algar, a 53-year-old jazz trumpeter from Barnes, south-west London, who had mental health and drug problems. In 2019, his home was cuckooed by a gang of drug dealers. He fell out with one of them over money, and the dealer threatened to kill his cat. After Algar’s sister reported him missing, police found his severed head and torso in the flat, and the rest of his body in a park. He had been stabbed to death with a zombie knife and dismembered in his own bath.

Jack Spicer, a lecturer in criminology at the University of Bath and author of Cuckoo Land, has interviewed many victims of cuckooing. What makes the practice so insidious, he says, is that for many victims there is nowhere to run. Yet Spicer also notes that in some cases, cuckooing can be a more complex scenario than is commonly understood: “From the perspective of an outsider looking in, cuckooing can take on a seductively simplistic appearance: the ‘evil’ drug dealer duping the vulnerable user of drugs, the naive local resident opening their door to the dangerous outsider. At best these tell only a partial story.”

That helps explain why Duncan, a musician, artist and father, ended up opening his doors to drug gangs – not once but twice – and why his two experiences turned out to be so different. The first brought him only misery; the second, in his telling at least, brought him a strange kind of friendship.

Life started unravelling for Duncan in 2016. His girlfriend left him and his close friend, the band’s singer, died of cancer. He was fired from his teaching job after his drug treatment service informed the school that he was in rehab. Losing his job made him particularly bitter. His drug use increased. He stopped returning his friends’ calls and saw less of his son.

Before, he had no reason to interact with the estate’s teenage gang. He bought his drugs – methadone, with a bit of heroin and crack on the side as a treat – from a trusted seller back west. But in January 2017, during a cold snap, Duncan offered shelter in his flat to two heroin users who had been sleeping rough in a tent in a nearby snow-covered graveyard. Patrick, a beggar from Bristol, took the kitchen floor and Josef, an unemployed Polish stonemason, took the living room sofa. “The estate was feeling more and more threatening during that time,” said Duncan. “I felt safer with those two around.” But his two lodgers bought drugs from the gang on Duncan’s estate, and he became a regular buyer, too.

Around this time, Chloe, a school teacher and friend of Duncan’s, began to worry about him. The two of them had been in a relationship for a period, and after they split, they remained friends. To her, he was “the loveliest person in the world – caring, kind and creative”. When they were together, she never saw him taking heroin, but she knew he did. So when he stopped returning her calls, she went round to check on him. The door was answered by a man she recognised as Patrick, the train station beggar, who nervously told her Duncan was out. When she later saw Duncan in the street, he ran off. “I was thinking, what is going on here?” she recalled.

One day, in the summer of 2017, one of the boys from the estate gang knocked and asked if his pregnant girlfriend could use Duncan’s toilet. From then on, said Duncan, the gang’s presence in the flat “escalated”. First it was repeated visits to charge phones or use the toilet. Then, as autumn approached and the weather got worse, the gang made Duncan an offer: £30 worth of crack and heroin a day for the use of his flat as a drug dealing base. He found himself agreeing.

“They had something to offer,” said Duncan, who had developed a debilitating leg wound from years injecting in his groin. “I’d wrecked my health and couldn’t work much so I needed the freebies. Heroin makes you quite fearless. It makes you feel as though you can cope with anything, but it also imbues a certain amount of recklessness. The strangest situations start to seem normal very quickly.”

The gang – a mix of Asian, black and white teenagers – was in and out of his home from about 10.30 in the morning, when one of the senior members would drop off the drugs stash, until late at night. A trio of slightly older gang members, aged about 16 and 17, made him feel particularly uneasy. The younger dealers would all be paid at his flat by a senior gang member in the afternoon. Usually there were only one or two of them there at once, but sometimes his home was packed. They used the flat as a base for dealing crack and heroin, to relax, prepare drugs for sale and to stash their zombie knives.

Duncan said some of the younger dealers were respectful, and that “three or four of the little soldiers were alright to chat to”. He would shoot up while the young gang members were in his flat, trying to find a vein in his groin or his leg. “All that stuff frightened those kids and probably disgusted them, so it kept them at a distance,” he told me. One of the gang would use the bathroom after dropping off the stash in the morning, always leaving the toilet seat covered in carefully laid out layers of tissue.

Without work, and with a constant supply of free crack and heroin, Duncan’s life became dominated by getting high and waiting to get high. And as time passed, the cuckooing turned nastier. “Some of the younger ones were fascinated with knives, they liked to pretend to stab me. They thought it was funny,” he recalled. “Sometimes they poked me with the tips. They didn’t mean it, I don’t think. I got lots of small cuts, it wasn’t too bad. One time they were playing and one of them stabbed me quite deep in the leg. I don’t know why.”

One of the gang’s associates forced Duncan to register a car in his name that was then used to sell drugs. The car accrued a string of fines and was written off in an accident. The debts fell on Duncan.

After a string of complaints from other residents, in early 2018 the police warned Duncan that if he continued to let the gang use his flat he could lose his tenancy. By this time, he was too scared to stop them. According to internal local authority case notes, one housing officer messaged colleagues in February 2018 to say that council staff were themselves scared to visit Duncan’s flat: “Attended flat and went in for short while only … didn’t feel it was very safe. Duncan said he is desperate to move out as soon as possible as drug gang is using his flat whenever they want.” (The council later launched an investigation into its management of Duncan’s tenancy.)

In April, the police emailed the council to say that it was no longer safe for Duncan to stay in the flat because he was being cuckooed. “We are getting inundated with complaints from neighbours. He needs moving urgently in my opinion,” one email reported. “I’ll try and keep an eye on the address although it’s difficult to visit Duncan as he doesn’t like police being seen walking into his property, which I can totally understand. The gang in question seem to have eyes everywhere on that estate.”

That month, Duncan was talking to a housing officer at his front door about how he wanted to move off the estate because he was scared of the gang. Some of the gang were listening from the stairwell and wrongly presumed Duncan was talking to a police officer. They put the word out that they would kill Duncan. Later that week he was cycling near his home when someone jumped out of a car and shouted: “You fucking grass we’re going to kill you.” “I knew I had to get out of that flat,” said Duncan.

A few days later, a place in an emergency homeless hostel was found for him in the east of the borough. Duncan packed what possessions he could into one of his key worker’s cars and left the place he’d made home for six years. His flat, which contained the rest of his belongings, was secured with heavy duty steel panels.

The relief of escaping the gang did not last long. In the dingy, crowded hostel, Duncan’s mental health was already deteriorating, when one day he received a call from the council. They told him that, owing to a communication error, they had accidentally sent all the possessions he had left in his flat for incineration. This was not just furniture, but smaller things of great sentimental value, such as his son’s childhood drawings, his own artwork, treasured LPs and keepsakes. Duncan was heartbroken. He told his housing officer it was one of the worst things that had ever happened to him.

Duncan’s friends had no idea where he had fled to. “This cuckooing thing had obliterated his life, but he totally disengaged with us all during that period,” said Billie, a fellow punk musician who’d known Duncan since the early 1990s. It took her six months to trace him to the hostel. After hearing snippets of information about his perilous health, she left him messages there, but heard nothing. “That was the first time since I’ve known him where I thought: ‘Oh my God, the wheels have completely come off.’ I really think we could have actually lost him then,” she told me.

After 10 months in the hostel, in 2019 he was eventually rehoused in a decent one-bedroom flat in a low-rise estate in a quieter, more suburban part of the borough. But he found it hard to start anew. Debt collectors were chasing him for fines and damage to the cars the gang rented out in his name, and because of the threats to his life, he was scared to go to the part of the borough where his son lived, and where his drug treatment service was.

Worried about him, in March 2019, a friend and I drove to his flat to see how he was. Inside, it was a mess. A bowl filled with stinking, mouldy fruit sat on the table. Duncan seemed to be living on a diet of Shreddies and milk with jam mixed in. He was convinced he had parasites under his skin, in his hair, and in his blood, a feeling that can be triggered by long-term crack use. We took him to hospital for some check-ups, particularly on the large injecting wound on his leg, for which he started to receive treatment.

In between Covid lockdowns he was able to move more freely around the borough, after most of the teenage gang that cuckooed him were arrested. We met a couple of times as he started taking action against the council, with the help of a lawyer, for destroying his possessions. After several months of legal wrangling, he was awarded a good chunk of money, which he mainly spent on an array of beautiful guitars and drugs. He drifted away from his friends again.

Then, in November 2024, I got a call from Duncan. He told me he felt really lonely and he wanted to meet up. He explained that over the past three years, he’d built a close bond with someone, but that person had just been sent to prison. Anyone I know, I asked? No, he replied, it was a drug dealer who had been using his house as a base for his business for the previous three years. I couldn’t believe it. But this time, as Duncan explained over a fry-up in a local cafe, wasn’t like the last one.

Compared with the teenagers on Duncan’s old estate, the second gang, which I’ll call the T-Line, was a more professional outfit. It ran a sizeable chunk of the heroin and crack trade in this part of north-east London. It was led by an experienced dealer in his early 40s. A confident, charming east Londoner, Tony was a well-known figure in the borough’s drug trade. Duncan had bought drugs from him while he was living in the homeless hostel. “He’s a personable kind of bloke,” Duncan told me. “He’s ingratiating. He liked sharing recipes and he liked my artwork. We just clicked, I guess.”

The first time Tony had visited him at home, he noticed portraits Duncan had painted of his own family. Tony said he liked them, and paid Duncan to paint a picture of his own two young sons. There was another thing Tony liked about Duncan’s flat: it would make an ideal trap house. The estate was low key, plus Duncan was one of his calmer, more reliable customers. He could be counted upon to keep quiet. The few times Tony’s crew had been round Duncan’s flat, he had seemed unfazed.

Tony suggested a deal: free daily crack and heroin in return for the flat being used as the gang’s secret weighing and stash house. So in 2021, for the second time in the space of three years, Duncan opened his home to a drug dealing gang. And when Tony asked him if he wanted to help prepare the drugs for sale, in return for more crack. Duncan knew that, legally speaking, doing so would change him from a passive victim to a willing offender. If he was caught he could be kicked out of his council flat and sent to prison. Even so, he said yes.

Duncan’s coffee table was repurposed as a drug processing station. Every day Tony, who now had keys to the flat, arrived at about 11.30am on his scooter with kilo bricks of heroin and crack, usually leaving around midnight. They worked long days together at the flat. It was Duncan’s job to weigh out and line up hundreds of 0.1 gram “shots” of each drug, ready to be wrapped into bags for street sale. Duncan estimates he helped cut and weigh about 5,000 “shots” of heroin and crack every week. Surrounded by enough narcotics to get the whole neighbourhood high, Duncan would have a regular puff on his crack pipe, part of his daily drug wage. “It was therapeutic for me,” he said. “I’d do 100 shots and have a pipe and do another 100 and so on.” As Duncan sorted out the drugs, Tony would be shouting via speakerphone, bossing his underlings.

Members of Tony’s crew came and went throughout the day. The longer the T-Line was camped out at his flat, the more Duncan found himself involved in its day-to-day business. “I did quite a lot of stuff for him like you would do with a friend,” said Duncan. “I tested his gear for him, I opened bank accounts he could use.”

Tony’s world was full of risk and violence, yet amid this dark backdrop, grew a friendship “built through a kind of domesticity”, according to Duncan. Tony brought a packed lunch, usually Jamaican food made by his sister or mother, which he put in the fridge. Sometimes while Tony coordinated drug deals over the phone, and after Duncan had finished dividing up the crack and smack, Duncan painted pictures for Tony.

“I used to tidy the house for him,” recalled Duncan. “I felt privileged to be accepted, and proud he was friends with me. He would make me look after myself. On my own, I couldn’t be bothered, but he got me together.” Even though he provided Duncan with a constant supply of class A drugs, Duncan said Tony “tried to discourage me from using drugs so much”, and “encouraged me to eat better – he was always feeding me his mum’s food”.

As they weighed and bagged drug deals, with Duncan sat at the coffee table and Tony at the small dining table, they talked about everything from conspiracy theories and the causes of poverty in Britain’s black community to their hopes for the future, and their pasts. Tony liked to get involved in every conversation. “He would never shut up, so I went out of the room to make calls.”

Tony told Duncan he grew up in poverty with a “wasteman” dad and had been selling drugs since he was a teenager. His chief motivation was to give his children, who he said were both in private school and the only two black kids in their class, a life different from his own. “He told me he was always going to go a bit further, take more risks, than the police chasing him because he was doing it for his kids, and the cops didn’t have as much to lose as he did.”

But Tony had a plan. By Christmas 2024, he said, he would call time on his drug dealing career. He had prepared the ground by setting up a catering truck and a semi-legitimate transport business. Come the following year, he would start anew.

The problem was that in 2023, things had started to unravel for the T-Line. A rival drug crew started ramming T-Line scooter riders off the road. They responded by squirting their attackers with ammonia. The beef was halted only after Tony contacted a criminal associate who warned the rival gang that there would be lethal consequences unless they backed down. Then Kane, Tony’s lieutenant who distributed the T-Line’s drugs to street dealers, was arrested for running a drug network in Norwich. Tony took on more responsibility, including doing more of the “road work”, moving drugs around the neighbourhood himself by scooter.

“It made him more exposed,” said Duncan. “He was getting more abrasive, more anxious, shouting at people more on the phone. He was very stressed. I told him not to bring bad energy into my place. He said he would try to keep calm, but he couldn’t.” When Duncan discovered that Tony had been hiding bricks of crack and heroin in his flat, he started stealing bits for himself, reasoning it was in his house after all. When Tony found out, they had fierce rows. “I said, if you don’t like it, don’t come back. But he would come back because it was the perfect house.”

Within the space of a few months in mid-2024, both of them came within inches of death. Duncan collapsed at his flat. He had contracted septicaemia after his injection wound became infected, and doctors told him he was lucky to survive. Not long after, Tony confronted a gang of teenagers trying to steal his scooter and was stabbed four times. Lying in the street, bleeding heavily, Tony managed to call a friend, who came to the scene, lifted him into a car and took him to casualty. “When I saw him a few weeks later we hugged. I was really happy to see him,” said Duncan.

Tony was getting increasingly nervous about being caught. He had been in prison three times for dealing. He was getting too old for jail, he told Duncan. He “didn’t have the energy for it” and dreaded being separated from his boys. His retirement date was coming closer.

One day in November 2024, Tony didn’t turn up at his usual time. Later that day Duncan got a phone call from one of the gang to say he’d been arrested after a police helicopter pursuit. Duncan was gutted for him. He was also thinking that, if the police had been keeping Tony under surveillance, his flat would be next. Yet as the days went by, alone at home, it wasn’t fear that he felt, but an intense loneliness.

Before Tony’s arrest, Duncan had ended his “love affair” with crack. It no longer agreed with his body, he felt. He also cut down from two grams of heroin a day to half a gram. “For the first time, it felt like it was holding me back,” he said.

Today, a year and a half later, it seems like Duncan has never been better. He’s eating well and looking after his health. He’s ditched his sometimes curmudgeonly attitude, he has his addiction under control, and he’s seeing his family and friends more than he has done for a decade.

Duncan believes his friendship with Tony helped him turn his life around. “The most obvious way he helped me was by bringing food from home,” he said. “Good home-cooked food. So my diet improved and I got a taste for Caribbean food. Music too. We listened to a lot of music and he turned me on to stuff I’d not heard before. Having a guest come to my home made me look after the place and myself more, and the work, although pretty tedious, was something to try to be good at, so that was positive too. I felt part of something, and part of a team.”

It’s hard to comprehend how Duncan, who had helpful, open-minded friends with money in their bank accounts, would be aided most by someone most people considered his biggest threat. But, in Duncan’s telling, this is exactly what happened. Tony “helped me to pull my socks up, so to speak”, he said. Behind his day job as a drug dealer, according to Duncan, Tony was essentially a businessman, a family man, a nice guy. “Well, it’s an odd person who only has one side to their character, wouldn’t you say?” said Duncan.

There are indeed nice drug dealers, I’ve met many myself. I’ve met some nasty ones too. People do not like to see themselves as being exploited, and Duncan denies he was manipulated. He said the two of them had a genuine friendship, and that if he had wanted Tony to stop using his home, he would have complied. But some of Duncan’s friends have a different take.

Chloe, the teacher, met Tony by accident one day in 2024. After hearing that Duncan had been in hospital and having not seen him in two years, she called round to his flat to check he was OK. As they chatted over tea, the front door opened and Tony let himself in. Chloe was surprised, and so was Tony. She was scared, not because of Tony himself, but because she knew it was drug business. “Duncan really likes Tony,” said Chloe, “but if you’re storing your illegal drugs in someone else’s house, if you’re asking them to do something in return for a thing they cannot resist. There’s a power imbalance; you are definitely the boss”.

Cuckooing is now a specific criminal offence, after the Crime and Policing Act took effect this year. But experts say it will not be stopped so simply. A rise in “deep poverty”, tracked in the Joseph Rowntree Foundation’s 2026 report, has led to more people living highly precarious, marginalised lives in deprived areas. These people are easy targets for cuckooing.

Drug gangs are increasingly targeting people’s homes in cities such as London, Bristol and Leeds. Operation Pantera recorded 1,539 cases of cuckooing in the capital between May 2025 and April 2026. Two years earlier, cuckooing had been flagged by the Met in just 380 investigations. In Leeds, cuckooing is now a major cause of vulnerable people being evicted from their homes.

Tony was sentenced to three years in prison in early 2025, but he and Duncan still chat on the phone, mainly about local gossip. Now and then Duncan buys things online on Tony’s behalf, which a friend of Tony’s will pick up and deliver to him. Sometimes Tony sounds downbeat, says Duncan, but he also talks about his kids, and plans for a future outside the drug business. During a day release in August, Tony paid Duncan a brief visit. “He’d obviously been working out inside, he was huge,” said Duncan. “He told me I looked really skinny and to put on some weight. It was really lovely to see him, he was smiling and we hugged.”

Tony is due to be released in a year or so. I asked Duncan what he would do if Tony wanted to use his home again as a drug dealing base. “I’d say no. I’ve got other things to do in my life now,” he replied. “I couldn’t give him the time he’d need off me.”

Their friendship was partly a matter of timing. “What [Tony] gave me at that time was a purpose,” Duncan said. “There seemed to be more regard for me as an artist and musician within his community than I’d ever felt before and my experience and knowledge of drugs was valued too. It was flattering to be respected like that and to be accepted into that world. And it was exciting.”

Like many of his friends, Billie the guitarist is delighted that Duncan is doing so well. She thinks that his turnaround was more to do with his wound finally healing in 2024 than his friendship with a drug dealer. And she’s scared. “He’s very positive about this person, and they probably saw it as a mutually beneficial relationship, but to me this was complete parasiticism. Hearing that he’s going to come out soon actually worries me a lot. I want to just keep on telling him, think about your son.”

I asked Duncan if he and Tony would still be friends when Tony gets out of prison. He said yes, but only to a point. “As close as we were, there was always a distance he kept between us,” said Duncan. “He never acknowledged his real name, he never told me it or allowed me to call him it. He kept up this pretence that we never actually knew each other well, a bit like people having an affair.”

All names have been changed
