Guest Essay

By Sharon Waxman

Ms. Waxman is a contributing Opinion writer. She wrote from Los Angeles.

Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, and his ragtag rebel alliance of unions, concerned celebrities and fellow Democratic state attorneys general were never going to win.

We had to endure months of back-and-forth posturing and some glee over the idea that Paramount Skydance might compromise in a serious way — or even fail — to complete its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery before an Oct. 1 late-fee deadline. And then it all ended with a friendly entente, a bunch of warmed-over deal points, a performative editorial oversight board and a paternalistic assurance that Paramount loves California after all and has no plans to leave.

It was the threat to leave California that won it in the end. Gov. Gavin Newsom and Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, took seriously the Paramount Skydance chief executive David Ellison’s threat to leave the state for Nashville. (Reports emerged as recently as last week that the company was looking for space there.) The potential fallout — the permanent loss of up to 60,000 jobs and $21.2 billion in economic output — was just too much to contemplate.

So Mr. Bonta cut a not very good deal, and with it an enervated Hollywood is — for now — spared the worst.

Few people in the film industry not named David Zaslav ever wanted a Paramount-Warner Bros. merger. Combining the two legacy studios and their streamers will reduce competition and, thanks in part to the huge debt load taken on to pay for it, require layoffs.

It’s also part of a larger shift away from the old Hollywood order. Other tech giants — Netflix, Amazon and Apple Studios among them — wield significant clout. But this particular combination, especially because it will include HBO and CNN, provides ready-made cultural (and thus political) power. Mr. Ellison is backed by his tech titan father, the Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, one the world’s richest men. In the end, the combined entity will be 49.5 percent owned by foreign investors, including Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the Qatar Investment Authority and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.

These terms, combined with the Ellisons’ friendliness with the Trump administration, have made the traditionally liberal industry players anxious that they will lose influence.

To be fair to Mr. Bonta, Paramount’s threat to leave California was seen as serious, not a bluff, by politicians and union leaders in the state. Every time Mr. Bonta notched a win in his 12-state lawsuit accusing Paramount of breaching antitrust laws, the company countered with a legal maneuver, such as demanding a $1.9 billion bond from the states and the Writers Guild to cover its potential liability.

None of that ever got to court, because the threat of leaving California panicked Mr. Newsom and Ms. Bass. Their apparent lack of support for continuing the fight seems to have forced Mr. Bonta’s hand.

In the end, Mr. Bonta secured nothing structural: He did not force the sale of CNN; no restrictions exist on operating the companies’ movie studios separately, though they need to operate both studio lots; there are no guaranteed protections from job losses.

Mr. Bonta couldn’t shut the merger down, but he did secure some wins: Paramount promised to spend $1.5 billion in U. S.-based production over the next five years. Mr. Ellison committed to releasing 30 films per year for the next two years and 32 per year for the following three years. But he had already more or less agreed to that. What happens after that five-year window closes is unclear.

Paramount’s board of directors will also establish an independent oversight board for CNN and CBS News. It’s not clear how this will work yet, or what “oversight” actually means.

Some critics have been quick to call the agreement worthless. To say this was an underwhelming end to all the Sturm und Drang — the opinion essays, the protests outside the Paramount lot, the rallies with Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, the dire warnings by politicians such as Senator Elizabeth Warren — is a vast understatement.

There’s no sense of triumph or even defeat in Hollywood, merely numb exhaustion. Big changes are coming for the century-old entertainment industry, which until now was never seriously threatened with red-state relocation.

Less than 48 hours before the deal was announced, members of the Hollywood A-list gathered to celebrate the opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which looked like a “Star Wars” spacecraft that had docked near Downtown L. A. George Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, were joined by Oprah Winfrey, Nicolas Cage, Eva Longoria, Samuel L. Jackson, Christopher Nolan, Steven Spielberg, and others.

It was a reminder of the film industry at its monocultural zenith: one that could create a shared set of powerful experiences imbued with simple moral purpose. “Star Wars” was about the struggles of the mystical Jedi masters who sought to protect their republic against the Galactic Empire, which was ruled by fear.

Things are not always so clear in real life. In between posing near Luke Skywalker’s landspeeder, all attendees could talk about was the Paramount-Bonta negotiations. When I ran into Mr. Newsom at the party, he told me he’d had an update less than two hours beforehand. Moguls privately shared their views that the deal was basically done and Hollywood would be better off with a resolution rather than prolonging a pointless and expensive battle.

They may as well bow to the inevitable.

Sharon Waxman is the founder, chief executive and editor in chief of The Wrap.

Trump Officials Eject 750,000 From Obamacare Markets, Claiming Fraud

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Vice President JD Vance said the measure would save the government $2.2 billion.

By Margot Sanger-KatzSarah Kliff and Christopher Rowland

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration has ejected more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces, Vice President JD Vance announced on Tuesday, claiming that many were receiving premium subsidies they did not qualify for and that some were not real people.

“We’re actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them,” Mr. Vance said at a news conference, using a different name for the health law. He estimated that removing the targeted enrollees would save the government $2.2 billion.

The announcement was the latest initiative by an anti-fraud task force Mr. Vance leads that has often turned its efforts toward federal health programs. In recent months, the task force has been involved in withholding billions in Medicaid funding from Minnesota and California, contending that the states had not adequately combated fraud.

Obamacare enrollment has already declined significantly this year, as the cost of the plans has risen, a potential political risk for Republicans heading into midterm elections in which voters are worried about affordability and the cost of living.

Congressional Democrats immediately criticized the Trump administration’s announcement on Tuesday as an unjustified move to dismantle Obamacare.

“Using the false pretext of fighting fraud to strip Americans of their healthcare is as cynical as it is cruel,” Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, posted on social media.

The dropped enrollees account for about 4 percent of the 19 million Americans who receive coverage through the marketplaces created by the Affordable Care Act. Many live close to the poverty line.

Under the law, people who earn more than four times the poverty limit — around $64,000 for a single person — are ineligible for subsidies to help them afford premiums. But people who earn less than the federal poverty limit — around $16,000 a year — are also ineligible. The lawmakers who wrote Obamacare had intended that such people would obtain health insurance through an expansion of Medicaid, before the Supreme Court made Medicaid coverage for this low-income group optional for states.

The officials speaking at the news conference on Tuesday offered few details about how they determined which accounts were fraudulent or ineligible.

Mr. Vance said the 750,000 who would lose coverage were a mix of people who did not meet the eligibility requirements or did not exist.

Officials said they planned to investigate an additional 440,000 enrollees who may also fall into one of those categories.

“They had something about their story that was a little bit different than what we expected from the 100 percent fraud story,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said of the Obamacare enrollees the administration would allow to remain enrolled. “We’re giving them another chance.”

In statements, two large insurance industry groups, America’s Health Insurance Plans and the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, said they welcomed efforts to reduce fraud in the marketplaces.

There is evidence that ineligible low-income people have enrolled in coverage in recent years, either because they overestimated their expected income or because a broker coached them to do so to obtain coverage. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that there were around 2.3 million such people in 2025.

There is also evidence that some insurance brokers, who earn commissions for each enrollment, illegally signed people up for coverage without their knowledge, though the number of such people is estimated to be substantially lower. During the Biden administration, health officials decertified around 200 brokers after learning they were engaged in such behavior — in many cases switching people from the plan they chose to another plan to harvest commissions. The Trump administration recertified those brokers last year, but has since removed more brokers from the program.

“We absolutely found that there was a fair amount of unauthorized activity,” said Ellen Montz, who oversaw the Obamacare marketplaces for the Biden administration. She described an uptick in fraudulent enrollments that started in 2024, and said that in response, the Biden administration cracked down on brokers and began requiring more documents during online enrollment.

At the news conference, Dr. Oz focused on fraudulent broker rings and announced a six-month moratorium on new brokers selling Obamacare policies. He highlighted the case of two Florida brokers who had been found guilty of bribing homeless people to enroll in Obamacare plans, so they could earn commissions. Both were sentenced in February to 20 years of jail time.

Cynthia Cox, the director of a program on the Affordable Care Act at KFF, a health research group, said that the administration’s action appeared to fall outside the normal process for verifying eligibility. “There is widespread agreement that unauthorized enrollments should be canceled,” she said. “The question is whether these were all indeed unauthorized enrollments and whether this was the appropriate process for determining whether an enrollee was legitimate or not.”

Ms. Cox and Ms. Montz both noted that problems with the data of enrollees did not necessarily constitute fraud.

“I would absolutely foresee that totally legitimate enrollments are going to get cut off here,” Ms. Montz said.

Enrollment in coverage sold in the Affordable Care Act marketplaces had already fallen by several million this year, after Congress allowed after Congress declined to extend temporary funding that had made coverage less expensive. . Prices rose substantially, and many low-income Americans lost access to free coverage. Early filings from insurers suggest that prices will increase substantially again next year. The sign-up period will begin days before the midterm congressional election.

Though there is little current data on the uninsured rate now, estimates from the C. B. O. and other analysts suggest that most of the lower-income people who have lost Obamacare coverage will remain uninsured.

The Paragon Health Institute, a right-leaning research group with close ties to the administration, has published reports estimating that more than a quarter of Obamacare enrollees were improperly signed up. The research noted disproportionate sign-ups among low-income enrollees, enrollments with missing data, and a subset of enrollees who never made medical claims. That research helped inform changes in how people sign up for coverage that were passed into law last year as part of the large Republican tax bill. But those changes do not kick in until after the election.

The administration also tried to add new requirements to the enrollment process through regulation, but the changes have been stopped by a court.

Margot Sanger-Katz is a reporter covering health care policy and public health for the Upshot section of The Times.

Sarah Kliff is an investigative health care reporter for The Times.

A. I.: Let’s Not Have Another Failure of Imagination

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Thomas L. Friedman

By Thomas L. Friedman

Opinion Columnist

“Looks like by April, you know, in theory, when it gets a little warmer, it miraculously goes away.”

That’s what President Trump said about the Covid-19 outbreak on Feb. 10, 2020, about a month before it forced our country and the world into a lengthy lockdown.

Why do I recall that today? Because when I think back on the biggest disaster stories I have covered — including 9/11 and Covid-19 — I am struck that they have one big thing in common: a failure of imagination. Sure, government experts prepared for these events in theory, but in practice how many of them imagined that suicidal terrorists would fly commercial airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon? And how many imagined that a respiratory virus that emerged in Wuhan, China, would kill millions of people and drag down the world economy for years? So today, when it comes to the possibility that artificial intelligence, which is falling into the hands of rogue actors and is beginning to manifest a will of its own, could become incredibly destabilizing, my imagination is fully engaged.

Here is what my imagination is telling me. It is telling me that the big A. I. companies in America and China are not being candid with us about how little even they understand the power and reach of the models they have developed, like sorcerers, in their labs. It is telling me that the Trump administration, headed by a man who so often governs by social media post, is uniquely unsuited to the kind of comprehensive, sustained, coordinated governance that keeping A. I. safe demands. And it is telling me that there is so much at stake — economically, militarily and technologically — and so little trust between Washington and Beijing that it would take a miracle for the United States and China to agree on the kind of deep collaboration needed to defuse the most nightmarish threats posed by A. I.

It is still not too late, though, for radical rethinking before something very bad happens that forces all the key players to do things they never imagined, things they will have to do in the middle of a full-blown A. I.-driven crisis. I’d rather be remembered as the boy who cried wolf when the wolf never came than as someone who got eaten by it.

So here goes: “Wolf, wolf, wolf, wolf.”

I will stand down when I see the United States and China start to address the immediate threat by teaming up to defend critical infrastructure — water systems, power grids, the internet — in their own countries and around the world.

But I will breathe a sigh of relief only when I see Washington and Beijing put their heads together with their respective A. I. companies to draw up a long-term plan for how they can continue to compete on A. I. technologies, while simultaneously agreeing on internal A. I. guardrails to prevent increasingly capable A. I. systems from, on their own, creating catastrophic cybersecurity, biological, nuclear or financial risks. This a geopolitical, geoeconomic and technological challenge no generation of American and Chinese statesmen has ever before faced. They dodge it at their, and our, peril.

I sincerely hope a strategy along these lines is what comes out of Thursday’s summit in Washington between Trump and President Xi Jinping. A. I.’s potential to deliver transformational breakthroughs in energy, biology, new materials and drug discovery is unprecedented. But so too are its risks.

We need a way to get A. I.’s best and cushion against its worst — and we do not have that today.

Until there is a U. S.-China agreement to ensure that the A. I. agents that the world’s two A. I. superpowers are developing will operate only in ways that are consonant with human flourishing, and be kept that way, I am in the slow-this-thing-down-until-we-are-sure-we-can-control-it camp. I’m in it for the same reason that the Stanford political theorist Francis Fukuyama argued in the Substack publication Persuasion on Monday: “A. I. is a tool that can be used for good or bad purposes — and at the moment we have few mechanisms for regulating the bad uses other than the good intentions of the people creating the technology.”

The last time we trusted the good intentions of the tech bros of Silicon Valley, when they told us to “move fast and break things” — regulations be damned — we unleashed social networks that helped fracture our society. I do not trust for one second that these people will put the national interest ahead of their own on A. I.

Anyone who tells you we can’t afford regulation now because it might slow down innovation is missing three things. First, those who contend that regulation is, by definition, innovation-destroying and market-destroying are “just ignorant of history,” Eric Beinhocker, the executive director of the Institute for New Economic Thinking at the University of Oxford’s Martin School, told me. “Good regulations create trust, and trust grows markets. How do you think the airline industry or the pharmaceutical industry grew so big, so fast? Because government regulations created trust among consumers that the planes they fly and the medicines they take are safe.”

Would the pharma industry be what it is today if people didn’t trust that the drugs they buy at the drugstore, without a second thought, have gone through a regulatory process? Because we have not yet had an A. I. catastrophe, people are going along with the hands-off approach. But when one happens, the pitchforks will be out for the “no-regulations” gurus, like Trump’s A. I. whisperer David Sacks — and for good reason.

Any company that creates an A. I. agent that does something bad in the world “should be held liable for it,” Beinhocker added. That is precisely what we did not do with the lords of the social networks, and we have paid a huge price for it. I was happy to see Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tell CNBC on Monday that the Trump administration won’t give A. I. leaders a “liability shield.” That may be the best way to slow them down in the near term. I hope China does the same.

Second, A. I. is not just a technology but also, as the computer scientist Craig Mundie has been saying, “a new species.” And like a new species, it is already exhibiting evolutionary properties.

“We’ve unleashed Darwin in silicon,” Beinhocker explained. The latest A. I. models have demonstrated a capacity for “self-improvement, self-replication and self-preservation. When you put those three things together, and their evolution happens at silicon speed, not human speed, you’ve got something extremely powerful, potentially dangerous and impossible to control.”

This becomes even more true as we begin to give our A. I. systems bodies in the form of robots, drones and vehicles. We must ensure that there is always a human in the loop — that they are never fully autonomous — until we can guarantee these systems will always operate in line with human well-being, Beinhocker added.

Third, our president now runs the country the way he is said to have run the Trump Organization, which had to deal with multiple bankruptcies: There is virtually no regular policy process, interagency collaboration is weak, and on most days everyone in the administration just sits around waiting to see what the president posts on social media — often based on the last person he spoke to or something he heard on Fox News — and then tries to frame policies around it. (Thank goodness that at least Bessent, sources tell me, has done a deep dive into A. I. issues and has been talking to the Chinese. But whether he can herd the cats in this administration on this issue remains to be seen.)

My Times colleagues recently reported that sources close to Trump made clear that his dismissal of fears that A. I. could lead to mass extinction as a “hoax” is driven not by any technological assessment. It is said to be driven, they reported, by his fear that “if the artificial intelligence boom fueling the American economy slows down, the market could crash and recession could quickly follow.”

That kind of thinking is begging for trouble. Trump should be thinking about another president. Dwight D. Eisenhower famously said, “Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.” What he meant was that no fixed plan can survive all the unanticipated stuff that happens once a war or crisis starts to unfold. But if you’ve gone through a rigorous planning process — familiarized yourself with the depth of the problem and the kinds of things that could go haywire and built trust within your team — you greatly improve your ability to adapt on the fly.

That is precisely what was missing in the run-up to Trump’s war with Iran, and we are paying a huge price for that today. Imagine what could happen if A. I. agents — a thousand times cleverer and more dangerous than Tehran or Trump — go off the rails.

Supreme Court Declines to Intervene in Custody Fight Over Surrogacy and Abortion

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

A surrogate refused to have an abortion after the fetus was diagnosed with a serious heart problem. She asked the justices to block a court order giving custody to the biological parents.

By Ann E. Marimow and J. David Goodman

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court. J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The New York Times.

Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday refused to intervene in a high-profile custody battle that has spanned three states and involved difficult questions surrounding surrogacy and abortion.

The case drew national attention when a surrogate from Alaska refused to have an abortion after the fetus she was carrying was diagnosed with a serious heart problem. She eventually traveled to Texas and gave birth to the child over the initial objections of the biological parents.

The surrogate had asked the Supreme Court to block a court ruling giving custody to the biological parents, a couple from California.

Justice Kagan, who oversees emergency filings from California, acted on her own on Tuesday without referring the matter to her Supreme Court colleagues. The justice denied the request without explanation, as is often the case when the court responds to such filings.

The couple, Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, had struggled to have a baby and entered into a surrogacy arrangement with McKenna West, a nurse. Their legal dispute began in April after the fetus was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome at around 20 weeks of pregnancy.

The rare and life-threatening congenital heart condition requires open-heart surgery soon after birth, followed by two additional childhood heart surgeries.

The couple asked Ms. West to terminate the pregnancy, citing a provision of their contract with her that left decisions dealing with abortion to them. Ms. West refused. She later moved to Texas, where the baby boy was born on Aug. 12. He received open-heart surgery and has been in a pediatric intensive care unit at a hospital in Dallas, where Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed have also been living to be with him.

Ms. West is represented by the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative Christian legal organization whose lawyers appear frequently before the Supreme Court. The Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, also intervened in state court to ensure the child received medical treatments. He later dropped out of the case.

In June, a California court recognized Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed as the boy’s parents. A judge in Texas extended a temporary order barring Ms. West from presenting herself as a parent to the baby.

After a subsequent court hearing in Texas, a judge directed the hospital in Dallas to provide lifesaving care and prohibited the baby’s removal from Texas. On Sept. 2, the court also dismissed Ms. West from the proceeding.

In their emergency request, Ms. West’s lawyers told the Supreme Court that she had been denied “control over the medically fragile child.” Without intervention from the justices, they said, “she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.”

The case should have been resolved in Alaska, her lawyers said, adding that the California courts had stripped Ms. West of her rights to “protect the baby’s life.”

In response, lawyers for the couple said on Friday that they have ensured that “their child receives the lifesaving care he needs — and they are committed to doing so for the rest of his life.”

An order from the Supreme Court blocking state court decisions would allow Ms. West to be involved in the child’s medical care and “serve only to cause chaos and confusion,” according to the heavily redacted filing.

Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed are “providing the precise medical care for their child” that Ms. West desires, the lawyers said, adding that “a right to life is not at issue here.”

The relationship between the couple and the surrogate got off to a smooth start. Ms. West stayed with them when she met with fertility doctors in California. Ms. Gilkar said in state court proceedings in Texas that she had sat by Ms. West’s side during the procedure transferring the embryo — biologically Ms. Gilkar’s and Mr. Ahmed’s — so that Ms. West could carry it to term.

But now they are at odds over even what to call the child. Ms. Gilkar and Mr. Ahmed named him Rumi, which their lawyer said had been put on his birth certificate. Ms. West’s lawyers used a different name, Gabriel, chosen by Ms. West, until they were told by the Texas judge to stop.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.

F. B. I. Shut Down Inquiry Into Top Ally of Senator Susan Collins

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The inquiry was closed last year because senior bureau officials questioned the veracity of a campaign donor’s account, according to current and former officials.

By Glenn ThrushAlan Feuer and Devlin Barrett

The F. B. I. in 2025 shut down an inquiry into allegations that a political adviser to Senator Susan Collins had participated in a scheme to funnel illegal campaign contributions from a defense contractor seeking lucrative federal contracts, current and former officials said.

The bureau began investigating the matter under the Biden administration, after Martin Kao, the chief executive of Navatek, a military contractor in Hawaii, said he had discussed circumventing campaign finance laws with a political adviser to Ms. Collins, Republican of Maine. Mr. Kao is now serving an 87-month prison sentence for wire fraud, money laundering and bank fraud, some of which related to a separate scheme to defraud the government of pandemic aid money.

The inquiry was closed under the Trump administration last year because senior bureau officials questioned the veracity of Mr. Kao’s account, which he began offering around the time he pleaded guilty in 2022.

Current and former officials familiar with the investigation, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a sensitive inquiry, said agents did not uncover much evidence to corroborate Mr. Kao’s claims against the senator and her advisers including Scott Reed, a fund-raiser for Ms. Collins. But they acknowledged that it was possible more could have surfaced if the investigation had developed further.

The disclosure of the inquiry and its closing came in the final weeks of a midterm election in which Ms. Collins is in a tight race that could help decide control of the Senate. It prompted accusations that the F. B. I.’s decision to shut down the investigation last year was influenced by political considerations — safeguarding a critical seat that could decide which party controls the Senate.

Annie Clark, Ms. Collins’s deputy chief of staff, described the allegations against the senator and her advisers as “categorically false.” In a lengthy social media post on Tuesday morning, she said that her campaign “cooperated fully with the F. B. I. throughout the investigation, producing all of the documents it requested and serving as fact witnesses in official settings.”

“As Martin Kao was awaiting sentencing, he began making outlandish charges about the Collins office, deflecting blame from himself and placing it on Senator Collins,” she wrote, adding: “The FBI and the Court obviously did not believe Kao.”

In an email to ProPublica, which earlier reported the nature of the investigation, Ms. Clark added that the campaign ultimately returned the money. The committee sent the donations to a group that was rebuilding a school in Frenchville, Maine, that burned down in 2021, according to a person with knowledge of the move.

In President Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has scuttled the main unit responsible for investigating public corruption, while dropping investigations against Republicans and Trump allies, including Eric Adams, the former mayor of New York.

Kash Patel, the F. B. I. director, also fired many agents in a public corruption unit at the Washington field office that had handled the Kao inquiry who had gone on to work for the special counsel Jack Smith, including one of the agents who had investigated Mr. Kao.

Ms. Collins, a moderate, is not close to Mr. Trump and has often sought to distance herself from some of his policies.

Mr. Kao told investigators that executives with his company had met in 2019 with Mr. Reed, who asked them for a large donation even though federal law prohibits direct contributions from federal contractors, according to ProPublica’s account, which was later confirmed by two former officials.

Mr. Kao said he was willing to do so provided Ms. Collins’s team could ensure the company received millions in naval contracts in Maine. As a workaround, Mr. Kao created a shell company and sent a $150,000 check to a super PAC associated with Ms. Collins, ProPublica reported.

Shortly afterward, Navatek received an $8 million contract for a boat hull research project. Ms. Collins visited the company’s offices in Maine to celebrate the deal, posting a photograph of herself on Facebook holding a model boat and standing next to Mr. Kao.

Ms. Collins, 73, faces what is arguably the toughest re-election campaign of her three-decade career as a Republican representing a blue state.

Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, the former speaker of Maine’s State Senate, seized on the disclosure of the F. B. I. investigation to accuse Ms. Collins of corruption and to cast Mr. Trump as her political wingman.

“Susan Collins delivered millions in taxpayer dollars for a corrupt donor bankrolling her campaign, and then Donald Trump helped her cover it up,” he said in a fund-raising email sent on Tuesday.

Ben Williamson, a spokesman for the bureau, said it had investigated claims against Ms. Collins and “found nothing” indicating that the senator or her campaign had done anything illegal. “Any suggestion otherwise is totally false.”

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Hispanic Voters, Abandoning Trump, Are Transforming the Midterm Map

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

Texas and even Florida are the places to watch in November if a polling pattern holds.

By Nate Cohn

President Trump’s enormous gains among Hispanic voters in the last election propelled him to victory in the national popular vote and prompted talk of a political realignment. Two years later, that talk is over.

In an average of high-quality national polls over the last month, Democrats led Republicans among Hispanic likely voters by 35 percentage points, 64-29, on the generic congressional ballot, which asks voters which party they will support for Congress.

That would mark an extraordinary reversal since 2024, when the same pollsters found Kamala Harris leading Mr. Trump by an average of only seven points among Hispanic voters in their final surveys.

A shift toward Democrats on anything like this scale could remake the electoral map — threatening longtime Republican incumbents, new Republican gerrymanders and the party’s crown jewel, Texas — and represent a final unraveling of his winning 2024 coalition.

If one applied the demographic trends from recent Times/Siena national polls to districts across the country, Democratic gains among Hispanic voters would imperil Republicans in more than a dozen districts that Mr. Trump won by double digits but where Republicans depend on support from Hispanic voters. Texas and Florida would become ground zero for a possible Democratic tsunami, with the party’s chance at a large congressional majority potentially hinging on whether it could break through Republican gerrymanders in those states.

Democrats could contend for many House districts with significant Hispanic populations that President Trump won by double digits. These estimates are based on demographic shifts from the latest Times/Siena national poll, not specific candidate polling.

Source: 2024 presidential election results; 2026 estimates based on a New York Times/Siena national poll conducted Sept. 8 to 13.

It’s important to caution that it’s challenging to precisely measure shifts among smaller groups like Hispanic voters. High-quality national polls have largely anticipated major swings among Hispanic voters in recent cycles, but they have not been perfect. With the polls showing Democrats gaining so much, even a modestly larger or smaller shift could be the difference between victory and defeat for Republicans in heavily Hispanic districts.

Nonetheless, the national, state and district polls leave no doubt that many Republicans in these districts are in jeopardy. The reason is simple: Mr. Trump.

His approval rating among Hispanic voters has fallen to the 20s, including just 26 percent in the most recent New York Times/Siena poll. Just two years after concerns about rising prices propelled him to victory, only 8 percent of Hispanic voters approved of his handling of the cost of living in the last Times/Siena poll, while 18 percent approved on the economy. His approval rating on immigration, at 26 percent, was not much better.

The polls have shown signs of growing Democratic strength among Hispanic voters all cycle, but it’s only over the last few weeks that the state and district-level polling has begun to confirm and reveal the extent of Democratic gains.

James Talarico has led every recent survey of the Texas Senate race, with polls showing him ahead among Hispanic voters by at least 20 points. Although his lead is often mostly dismissed as a reflection of the profound flaws of his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, the polls also show the Democrat Gina Hinojosa to be surprisingly competitive in the race for governor against the incumbent, Greg Abbott, who leads by an average of three points in recent polls.

Perhaps even more striking than a poll result was a recent advertisement from María Elvira Salazar, who represents Florida’s 27th District, a heavily Cuban area in Miami-Dade County that voted for Mr. Trump by 15 points. She filmed a television ad in which she spoke directly to the camera — and to Mr. Trump — about how “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

Early in the cycle, few analysts expected a competitive race for Texas governor or for a South Florida House seat. In both states, Republicans felt so secure in their success among Hispanic voters that they redrew their state’s congressional maps to try to gain as many as nine combined Republican seats. These aggressive gerrymanders were drawn in part on the assumption that the Republicans would retain at least some of Mr. Trump’s gains among Hispanic voters.

With Democrats surging back among Hispanic voters, many of the districts that Republicans hoped to flip might remain in the Democratic camp. At the same time, Republican-held seats that the party thought it might be able to take for granted could be in jeopardy.

In Texas, Democrats would be expected to lead on the generic congressional ballot in five Texas congressional districts where Mr. Trump won by at least 10 points in 2024 and to stay close in a sixth, based on the trends in Times/Siena national polling. In a sign that the G. O. P. itself doesn’t consider the races safe, Republican groups are spending in all six of these seats — which include four of the five districts Republicans thought they could flip with their new gerrymander.

Republicans in Florida might also be jeopardized by a Democratic surge among Hispanic voters, though it is worth cautioning that Democrats in Florida have underperformed national trends for a decade. Even so, gains among Hispanic voters ought to be sufficient for Democrats to be competitive in the state’s heavily Hispanic Republican-held districts in South Florida, including Ms. Salazar’s district. It could also help Democrats retain the districts with more modest but still substantial Hispanic populations that Republicans targeted in redistricting.

One important complication is financial: Florida and Texas are two of the nation’s most expensive states for ad campaigns. Republicans have a substantial financial advantage, and Florida and Texas might be exactly where it pays off, by allowing the party to defend congressional districts in expensive media markets that will be difficult for Democrats to match.

Either way, Democratic gains among Hispanic voters put Texas and Florida center stage. The Democratic Party’s chances of having a truly exceptional midterm election — one that yields a large congressional majority and control of the Senate — could depend on whether Democratic gains among Hispanic voters translate into breakthroughs in Texas and Florida.

If Democrats fall short, the surge of support among Hispanic voters will boost the party’s popular vote while doing relatively little to give Democrats the seats needed to control Congress. But if the breakthrough happens, it could essentially cancel out the G. O. P.’s gerrymanders in both states and give Democrats a long-awaited victory in Texas.

Rachel Buigas-Lopez contributed graphics.

Nate Cohn is The Times’s chief political analyst. He covers elections, public opinion, demographics and polling.

What to Know About the Search for the Next Leader of the U. N.

The New York Times September 22, 2026

U. N. General Assembly

Advertisement

Supported by

António Guterres is stepping down in December after two terms as secretary general. No front-runner to succeed him has emerged so far.

By Farnaz Fassihi

Farnaz Fassihi has covered the U. N. and the annual General Assembly of world leaders for 11 years through four U. S. administrations.

As the United Nations searches for its next leader, diplomats say there are key qualities they would like to see in the next secretary general. They seek someone who proactively puts the U. N. at the center of resolving global conflicts and enforces cost-cutting and reform.

The topic of who will succeed António Guterres when he steps down in December is expected to be hotly debated this week behind closed doors in diplomatic meetings during the annual U. N. General Assembly in New York. The conversations “will drive a lot of the candidates’ fortunes and separate contenders from pretenders,” said Daniel Forti, the head of U. N. affairs at the International Crisis Group.

Here’s what else you need to know:

The U. N. Security Council selects the secretary general in a monthslong process that begins with an informal, nonbinding and closed “straw poll,” or informal ballots. The 15 members of the Council vote for the candidates.

They say whether candidates are “encouraged” or “discouraged,” or “no opinion is expressed.”

The last straw poll was conducted on Sept. 18, and although the results are meant to be confidential, they have leaked to the news media.

Once the Council agrees on a single nominee, it will pass a resolution and recommend the person to the General Assembly, which will take up a procedural vote. The nominee has to have nine votes in favor and no vetoes by the Security Council’s five permanent members — the United States, France, Britain, Russia and China — to get the job.

Eight candidates were whittled to seven after Michelle Bachelet dropped out of the race on Friday because of low polling numbers.

Ms. Bachelet, 75, the former two-time president of Chile, had also served as the U. N. high commissioner for human rights and as the executive director of U. N. Women, an organization focused on women’s rights. She had one encouraged vote, 11 discouraged votes and three votes of no opinion.

So far, no clear front-runner has emerged, according to diplomats and leaked results of three secret straw polls held by the Security Council. Mr. Forti said more contenders were likely to join the race or drop out ahead of the Council’s final recommendation.

In previous selections of the secretary general, by this time at least one or two front-runners had emerged, diplomats say. The results of the straw polls have been so inconclusive that, for the first time, Mr. Forti said, diplomats and U. N. officials are openly wondering what will happen if the Council does not settle on a candidate.

Mr. Guterres, 77, a former prime minister of Portugal who also led the U. N.’s refugee agency, has held the post of secretary general since 2017 and served two terms. He has indicated that he is not interested in remaining in an interim role and plans to be in his native Portugal come the beginning of next year, said his spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric.

A successor to Mr. Guterres has to be chosen before Dec. 31, after which the person would take the helm of the U. N. on Jan. 1, 2027.

Diplomats and a senior U. N. official said that Russia had indicated it would veto one candidate, Rafael Grossi, the leader of the U. N.’s atomic watchdog, because it was not pleased with how he had handled the standoff between Russia and Ukraine over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant.

The United States had also indicated it would block Ms. Bachelet over her positions on abortion. It also opposes Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the U. N., for calling Israel’s conduct in Gaza a genocide.

The U. N. typically rotates the office of the secretary general from one of its five recognized regions. And because the past three leaders have been from Africa, Asia and Western Europe, it is expected that the new secretary general will originate from Latin America or the Caribbean.

A female secretary general would also be a first in the organization’s 81-year history.

Rebeca Grynspan, 70. The economist and former vice president of Costa Rica currently leads the U. N. Conference on Trade and Development. She stepped away from her duties to avoid a conflict of interest while she campaigns for the top U. N. job. Ms. Grynspan gained a narrow edge in the most recent straw poll, with nine encouraged votes, five discouraged votes and one no-opinion ballot.

Ms. Rodrigues-Birkett, 53. Guyana’s former foreign minister has served as the South American country’s ambassador to the United Nations since 2020. As a former member of the Security Council, she has U. N. leadership experience. She received eight encouraged votes and six discouraged votes, and one person voted no opinion.

Olara Otunnu, 75. The Ugandan politician and diplomat served as an under secretary general at the U. N. in the administration of Secretary General Kofi Annan. Mr. Otunnu is the oldest candidate in the race. He served as Uganda’s ambassador to the U. N. in the 1980s and was his country’s foreign minister from 1985 to 1986. He received five encouraged votes, seven discouraged votes and three ballots with no opinion.

Mr. Grossi, 65. An Argentine career diplomat, he leads the International Atomic Energy Agency, the U. N.’s atomic watchdog. For the past six years, Mr. Grossi has played a prominent role in two notable nuclear crises: the standoff with Iran over its nuclear program and the threats to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine after the Russian full-scale invasion. He had five encouraged votes, eight votes of discouraged and two votes signaling no opinion.

Macky Sall, 64. A prominent politician from Senegal, he served as the country’s president from 2012 to 2024. He was also its prime minister and president of the National Assembly. He had five encouraged votes, nine discouraged and one no-opinion vote.

María Fernanda Espinosa, 62. She was the foreign minister and defense minister of Ecuador. She also has a range of experience with the U. N., serving as Ecuador’s ambassador to the body and president of the General Assembly. She is the executive director of GWL Voices, a nonprofit organization that works on gender equality, and has been an adviser to the U. N. on climate change, biodiversity and the rights of Indigenous people. She had three encouraged votes, six discouraged votes and six votes of no opinion.

Ivonne Baki, 75. An Ecuadorean politician and diplomat, she was the minister of industries and productivity and the president of Parliament. She was her country’s first female ambassador to the United States and was ambassador to France and Qatar. She had zero encouraged votes, 10 discouraged ones and five votes of no opinion.

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.

The Israeli prime minister falsely accused Mayor Zohran Mamdani of supporting Hamas after CNN interview clips showed Mr. Mamdani again calling Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal.

By Liam Stack

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel released a video broadside against Mayor Zohran Mamdani, one of his most high-profile critics in the United States, hours after CNN published clips of a new interview in which the mayor again called the prime minister a war criminal.

Mr. Mamdani has called on the federal government to arrest Mr. Netanyahu, who is expected to arrive in New York later this week to address the United Nations General Assembly. In the video posted on Tuesday, the prime minister falsely accused the mayor of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against Jewish New Yorkers.

Addressing the mayor directly, the prime minister said he was coming to the U. N. “to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers” and “to tell the truth about you.”

Mr. Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor and an outspoken supporter of Palestinian rights, has condemned Hamas as a terrorist organization and described the attack it led against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, as “a horrific war crime.”

And while New York has seen an increase in antisemitic hate crimes since the Oct. 7 attacks and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza, as well as widespread pro-Palestinian demonstrations, there have been no riots targeting Jewish New Yorkers in the city since Mr. Mamdani was elected mayor in November or during his time serving in the State Assembly.

Mr. Netanyahu is the subject of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, which has accused him of war crimes in Gaza; he vigorously denies the charges. After Mr. Mamdani’s previous comments calling Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal outraged many pro-Israel Jewish leaders, the mayor’s office convened a meeting at which prominent rabbis urged the mayor to tone down his rhetoric on Israel and its leaders.

Asked about Mr. Netanyahu’s remarks at an unrelated news conference on Tuesday morning, Mr. Mamdani said, “We all know that what the prime minister has said in that video is not true.”

On Monday night, CNN released clips from an interview with Mr. Mamdani, which it said would be aired in full on Tuesday afternoon.

In one part of the interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour, Mr. Mamdani was asked directly about his opinion of Mr. Netanyahu, and he said he owed it to New Yorkers to share his honest views.

“When it comes to Benjamin Netanyahu,” the mayor said, “I have described him as I believe him to be: a war criminal and an architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people.”

Mr. Mamdani has described Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza as genocide, a claim that has upset many pro-Israel Jewish leaders. A United Nations commission and international and Israeli human rights groups have also said that Israel’s actions amounted to genocide.

During the campaign, Mr. Mamdani pledged to have the Police Department execute the International Criminal Court warrant against Mr. Netanyahu if he were to come to New York. He repeated his desire to do so in an interview with The New York Times in July. But days later, the mayor released a video saying the city’s Law Department had told him the city did not have the authority to arrest the prime minister, and challenged the federal government to do so.

Mr. Netanyahu, who is in the midst of a pivotal electoral campaign in Israel, has frequently condemned the mayor, calling him a danger to Jewish New Yorkers. On the second day of Mr. Mamdani’s term, the Israeli government accused him of antisemitism, citing his decision to cancel two executive orders signed by his predecessor, which had barred city agencies from boycotting Israel and defined some criticism of Israel as antisemitic.

While Mr. Mamdani’s stance on Israel has caused deep unease among many Jews in New York, which has the largest Jewish population outside Israel, many others have supported the mayor, especially his fellow progressives. On Monday, Mr. Mamdani attended a meal marking the end of the Yom Kippur fast at the home of Ruth Messinger, a political ally who has served as Manhattan borough president and as the president and chief executive of the American Jewish World Service.

Liam Stack is a Times reporter who covers the culture and politics of the New York City region.

Fact-Checking Trump’s Speech at the United Nations

The New York Times September 22, 2026

U. N. General Assembly

Advertisement

Supported by

Fact Check

President Trump’s remarks about oil reserves, the drug trade and his peace efforts contained falsehoods and exaggerations.

By Linda Qiu

Reporting from Washington

President Trump praised his own domestic and foreign policy accomplishments in a speech Tuesday morning before the United Nations General Assembly, repeatedly making remarks rife with falsehoods and exaggerations.

Here’s a fact-check.

What Was Said

“When you add the United States and Venezuela together, we have more than 60 percent of the oil in the world.”

This is exaggerated. Mr. Trump, heralding a deal he struck with Venezuela that allowed the United States to take control of a significant portion of its oil, overstated the scale of that agreement.

Mr. Trump has said that Venezuela will give the United States more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves based on geological and engineering data. Venezuela has about 303 billion barrels in proven oil reserves, while the United States has about 46 billion barrels, according to the Energy Information Administration. Together, that is about 22 percent of the nearly 1.6 trillion barrels of global reserves.

Currently, the United States produces about 23.6 million barrels daily and Venezuela about 1 million a day. Together, that is about 23 percent of the 106 million barrels produced worldwide.

What Was Said

“A few weeks later, we ended the war in Gaza, saving untold thousands of lives.”

This is exaggerated. Mr. Trump helped broker a cease-fire in the Israel-Hamas war in October 2025. While much of the large-scale fighting has stopped, Israel still conducts military operations and strikes regularly in Gaza and the death toll continues to climb. The Gaza health ministry has reported that Israel’s military has killed more than 1,000 Palestinians since October, including both Hamas officials and civilians.

Elements of Mr. Trump’s peace plan remain stalled. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in August rejected a 15-point plan backed by the Trump administration for disarming Hamas. Later that month, one of Mr. Trump’s own officials on his Board of Peace accused the Israeli government of jeopardizing the cease-fire, noting that ongoing strikes in Gaza undermined the plan.

What Was Said

“The United States has carried out dozens of strikes on cartel drug boats, destroying 97 percent of the drugs coming into the ocean and sea. You’ve seen it; they disappear very quickly, and we’re down 90 percent. They’re down 97 percent.”

This lacks evidence. For months, Mr. Trump has claimed a decimation of maritime drug trafficking as an achievement of unauthorized boat strikes in the waters off Central and South America that began last September. But that claim is unsupported, unlikely and disputed by his own administration.

The White House previously cited a record amount of drugs seized in July 2025 and a low amount seized in December by one branch of Customs and Border Protection as evidence of Mr. Trump’s claims. But the bulk of the drugs seized was marijuana (Venezuela is a transit hub for cocaine) and it is unclear where those seizures took place. Moreover, C. B. P. is not the only agency that seizes drugs.

Criminologists who focus on the region have said that the strikes most likely disrupted some drug routes but the campaign had not halted trafficking altogether. Rather, traffickers have been forced to find new routes. The Washington Post also reported in July that an internal assessment from the Drug Enforcement Administration “found the strikes had failed to affect the supply or price of cocaine in the United States and had led traffickers to diversify beyond go-fast boats and to avoid international waters.”

Other Claims

The president repeated a number of claims that The New York Times has previously fact-checked:

He falsely claimed to have ushered in $21 trillion in foreign investments. (This is almost double the White House’s own tally, which includes broad pledges and previously announced investments.)

He falsely claimed to have signed the largest tax cuts in American history. (The tax cuts signed into law last summer rank sixth.)

He claimed that there are “more Americans working today by far than ever before.” (This is a meaningless statistic, given population growth. The unemployment rate in August was currently a low 4.1 percent, which is slightly higher than in January 2025, when he took office.)

He misleadingly said that “we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before.” (The Iran war has drained the United States’ arsenal of munitions.)

He overstated credit for settling eight wars. (It is an exaggeration to call some of the conflicts “wars,” and some countries dispute Mr. Trump’s role in others.)

Linda Qiu is a Times reporter who specializes in fact-checking statements made by politicians and public figures. She has been reporting and fact-checking public figures for nearly a decade.

The U. N. Brings Everyone to Town. That’s Good (and Bad) for New Yorkers.

The New York Times September 22, 2026

U. N. General Assembly

Advertisement

Supported by

Big names flood New York City each year for the United Nations General Assembly. But that also means traffic (oh, the traffic!), closed streets and a little more chaos than usual.

By Victor Mather and Davaughnia Wilson

Davaughnia Wilson reported from the turbulent streets of Manhattan’s East Side. Victor Mather reported from the relative serenity of The New York Times building in Times Square.

It takes a lot to faze New Yorkers. This week is doing its darnedest.

Leaders from all over the world have descended on New York City for the weeklong United Nations General Assembly. The hot topics will include Ukraine and Russia, Israel and Gaza, and President Trump and Greenland.

But outside the General Assembly building on the East Side of Manhattan, New Yorkers’ thoughts are more on the horror-show traffic.

Yes, the annual chaos ushered in by the General Assembly has arrived.

Black cars and S. U. V. s are everywhere. And they always seem to drive in packs with two or three of their buddies. Bodyguards and security officials from various agencies are ever present. Traffic cops yell at drivers or passers-by who violate the rules.

If you make the mistake of bringing your car into the area, know that First Avenue is closed from 41st to 48th Streets. Numerous side streets in the 40s are also off limits. It’s not the day to drive to your bridge game in Tudor City.

On the other hand, a lot of notable people have come to the neighborhood. Hey, is that a head of state grabbing a bacon, egg and cheese? (I guess you never know, but it’s probably their assistant.)

“When the world visits New York City,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference last week, “our streets are inevitably impacted.”

Things weren’t easy for pedestrians either, and more than one stood forlornly on the sidewalk contemplating the seemingly impossible task of getting to their destination only a block or two away.

Meanwhile, inside the U. N., delegates and dignitaries heard a lot of long speeches and went to a lot of long meetings. So, who really drew the short straw?

Kidding. It’s the New Yorkers outside. Just ask them.

Some were angry less about traffic and more about geopolitical issues. About a dozen were peacefully protesting on Tuesday. One held a sign saying, “Stop the genocide and ecocide in West Papua.” Dave Robinson, 65, was protesting Mr. Trump. He was holding up a sign that read, “Sorry, world. We hate him too.”

A store owner on Second Avenue between 43rd and 44th declined to give her name but said the blocked roads were deterring customers from coming into her business. And she found it “kind of annoying,” she said, to show proof of residency to get into her apartment above.

A contrarian dry cleaner said that he was actually happy about the General Assembly because it had brought in business from suit-wearing attendees. Still, delivery trucks have had to park a few blocks away.

Sometimes it’s just a matter of which side of the street you are on. You can walk Second Avenue on its west side more or less freely.

The east side is trickier. Navigating between 42nd and 43rd is almost impossible. (Unless you tell officers you want to go to the bagel shop, then they might let you past. Don’t say we told you.) Bicycles are in the same pickle. And forget about getting to First Avenue.

New York City has declared a gridlock alert for all five days of this workweek. But then it will be over, and the city should return to normal, at least until the three gridlock alert days in November and 12 more in December.

And by normal, of course, we mean, streets choked with traffic, subways packed to bursting, buses that never turn up, and every other person having an attitude. So, New York.

Victor Mather, who has been a reporter and editor at The Times for 25 years, covers sports and breaking news.

Davaughnia Wilson is a news assistant at The Times who helps to cover the New York City region.

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Less than a year ago, Gov. Greg Abbott welcomed data centers. Now he is confronting concerns about the projects even among fellow Republicans.

By Scott Dance

Reporting from Washington

Texas is effectively halting development of new data centers as Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican running for re-election, confronts growing opposition to the projects and concern over their environmental impacts.

Mr. Abbott on Monday ordered state environmental regulators to pause their review of data center permit applications until audits can be performed to evaluate how the projects affect the power grid and water supplies.

The action expanded scrutiny of data centers planned in the state, including on a growing number of projects designed to run on their own sources of power, separate from the grid. Dozens of new gas-fired power plants have been proposed to support data center projects across Texas, Appalachia and the Mountain West, a boom that could cause air pollution to surge in those regions.

Texas had previously welcomed the data center industry and was forecast to drive much of the growth in the nation’s computing capacity over the coming years. But Mr. Abbott’s shift underscores rising concerns in the communities living near the hulking facilities.

“Simply put, Texans must come first,” Mr. Abbott said in a statement. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water,” and complete the audits, which he ordered in August as pressure against data centers began to mount, even within his own party.

Cameron Poursoltan, the Texas director of energy policy for the Data Center Coalition, an industry group, said the industry would work with the state “so that our industry’s growth in Texas remains responsible, transparent, and responsive to the communities where our members operate.”

Mr. Poursoltan said coalition members whose projects are in the process of connecting to Texas’ power grid, known as the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, were complying with the state’s demand for audits of effects on the grid.

Less than a year ago, Mr. Abbott had called Texas an “epicenter of A. I. development.” As artificial intelligence increases demand for high-powered computing, the state is forecast to host up to half of the new data center capacity expected to develop in the United States from 2027 through 2030, according to Jefferies, an investment bank.

But as a political backlash has grown, Mr. Abbott has joined officials in other states in trying to slow the projects. In August, he called for a pause on data centers that were seeking approval to draw power from the electric grid. That did not affect projects building their own power plants and would not request connection to the grid, nor did it affect data centers that would use less than 75 megawatts of power.

This week, he expanded that pause. In a Monday letter to the leader of the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, a state agency, Mr. Abbott said the broader halt on data center projects was needed to “ensure Texans’ natural resources and way of life are protected.” The commission is responsible for reviewing air and water permits for data centers and other industrial facilities.

Representatives for Mr. Abbott declined to answer questions about how the governor’s directive would affect projects developing their own power sources.

In the letter, Mr. Abbott said data center projects must pay for any needed electrical infrastructure projects, report their electricity and water usage, and result in lower electricity bills for residents. Mr. Abbott also said he would work with Texas lawmakers to eliminate state financial incentives for data center development.

Scott Dance is a Times reporter who covers how climate change and extreme weather are transforming society.

An Army of Paid Creators Is Carpeting the Web With Political Content

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Unlike celebrity influencers with large followings, these creators produce a blizzard of videos for a fraction of the cost of traditional online campaigns and, in the process, shift public conversation.

By Ken Bensinger and Stuart A. Thompson

Judging from his TikTok feed, Drew was struggling to get by as a young man living near Dallas. Grocery bills were skyrocketing, he said, and he was looking for thrift stores to help keep costs down.

In reality, according to his LinkedIn profile, Drew was a man from Utah named Alex Forrester, who said he was now in Florida. “All of it was paid for,” he said in a video posted in late June, which was later deleted. “I don’t even live in Texas,” adding an expletive.

Mr. Forrester, who did not respond to requests for comment, is one of more than 100 content creators identified by The New York Times who in recent months have been paid as much as $30 per post by a progressive group to create videos about affordability for social media.

Similar campaigns this year have paid ordinary people to promote a Republican candidate for Los Angeles mayor, to oppose a regulatory bill pushed by the crypto industry and to call for tighter regulation of artificial intelligence. Early this month, an unidentified nonprofit group offered up to $1,500 for videos on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram that support “mail voting working correctly.”

The accounts posting these messages aren’t run by celebrity influencers with massive engagement, legions of fans and lucrative product endorsement deals. Most have only a smattering of followers and, often, the people behind them aren’t even based in the United States.

Functioning more like birdshot than a single bullet, these high-volume social media campaigns represent the new vanguard of modern political influence, saturating the internet with a topic until it is all but unavoidable. That can help game social media network algorithms so that they treat coordinated content as organic, spreading the message even wider. Built from dozens or hundreds of posts from accounts you’ve never heard of, they amount to an echo chamber on a budget.

“This is digital astroturfing, plain and simple,” said Samuel Woolley, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh who studies how new technologies can be used to manipulate public opinion on the web. “The more people see an idea online, the more inured to it they become and the more commonplace and acceptable it becomes.”

In the political sphere, social media strategies centered around big payments to marquee influencers are still prevalent, with some large accounts taking in $25,000 or more for a single video.

But increasingly, efforts are shifting to content made by smaller freelancers who churn out on-camera videos, slide shows and other material targeting specific audiences.

Some posts, known as user generated content, or U. G. C., feature an individual content creator speaking directly to the camera. Others, referred to in the industry as clipping, consist of short clips taken from longer videos overlaid with text or commentary driving a particular point home.

Such content is rarely marked as paid advertising and, in most cases, laws don’t require any such disclosures for political topics.

One recent campaign, called “Protect What’s Human,” offered $300 or more for posts on Instagram and TikTok that called for “real rules on A. I.” But the job listing made no mention of who funded the effort or any requirement to disclose that it was not organic content. The only obligation was that creators verify that they “have a personal perspective or experience related to how A. I. may affect my work, profession, family, or community.”

“Protect What’s Human” was advertised on a site called People First, one of a growing number of specialized online marketplaces where content creators can look for paid opportunities. Some focus mostly on political advocacy, while others largely feature commercial gigs with a smaller number of political jobs mixed in.

A recent clipping campaign listed on the social commerce platform Whop offered $3 per 1,000 views for short-form videos praising Pierre Poilievre, the conservative leader of Canada’s opposition party. For inspiration, it provided a video of Mr. Poilievre blaming the country’s prime minister for high food prices. Another campaign offered $2 per 1,000 views to promote Maria Syrengela, a member of Greece’s parliament.

A different opportunity on the same marketplace offered even less — $1.50 per 1,000 views — to “join a community of volunteers” working to elect Mike Minogue, the Republican nominee for Massachusetts governor, by cutting videos of the candidate “into compelling 15-60 second clips” posted on social media. The maximum payout for any pro-Minogue post was $150, according to the listing, a tiny fraction of what a big-name social media star would typically charge and an even tinier fraction of the $12.7 million Mr. Minogue has spent so far on television advertising, according to data from tracking firm AdImpact.

“People are sick of paying the insane pricing that typically comes with influencer marketing,” said Drew Levin, a co-founder of SideShift, a popular U. G. C. marketplace, on a podcast last year. “Why spend $1,000 on one video, when you can spend $1,000 on 30 videos?”

Early this year, Project Bullhorn, a Democratic-aligned venture that has said it wants to combat right-wing dominance on social media, turned to SideShift to seek out “U. G. C. creators to speak on the rising crisis of affordability around the United States ahead of the 2026 midterms,” according to a job posting on the site. Initially, it offered $30 per video, but the affordability crisis apparently hit Project Bullhorn as well: That rate recently dropped to $25, the job listing showed.

The Times identified more than 100 social media accounts that took part in Project Bullhorn’s campaign by analyzing the activity of thousands of content creators who signed up with SideShift.

The videos they produced featured creators talking about the high cost of food, fuel and housing around the country; few disclosed they were paid for their posts.

Only a third of the affordability campaign creators appeared to live in the states about which they had posted, according to a Times analysis of participants who had shared their locations.

One man who claimed to be “born and raised” in Texas was actually from Leicestershire, England, according to his profile on SideShift. A woman hired by the campaign to post about affordability in the United States actually lived in Ontario, Canada.

Project Bullhorn declined a request for comment. But a person familiar with the campaign who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the group’s activities said that participating creators are supposed to live in the states that they talk about, or have a close connection to those places, and should be speaking about their own experiences.

Starting in May, creators were offered $1.50 per 1,000 views of videos that combine flattering clips of Ron DeSantis, the Republican governor of Florida, with scripted captions like “DeSantis not holding back 🔥” and “This DeSantis clip has me 😮” on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram.

A detailed set of instructions laid out guidelines for what to do — and what not to do. The golden rule? “Can’t make Ron look bad.”

Mr. DeSantis is term-limited as governor and not currently running for any other office. The job listing does not say who paid for the campaign, but the digital marketing agency Clipping Culture, which posted the ad, stated on its website that the campaign generated more than 6 million views from 1,441 videos.

A review found that a number of those videos appeared to have been made by accounts based overseas. A video featuring Joe Rogan appearing to react to a clip of Mr. DeSantis that included one of the suggested captions was posted by an account that was created in April and is based in Pakistan. Mr. DeSantis’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

dragoni7372

Because clipping campaigns rarely feature the face or voice of the account holder and they tend to pay less per post than U. G. C. content, they often attract creators in other countries, many of whom operate multiple accounts.

A recent report in The Atlantic, for example, found a pro-Republican clipping campaign called Elephant Clipping that paid $3 for every 1,000 views. The instructions stated that “the goal is to showcase how modern conservative figures approach issues such the economy, foreign policy, public safety, education and community development.”

A Times review of accounts posting the suggested content included ones from Nigeria and India; one based in Pakistan used the name Trump in its handle and was created in July.

During his unsuccessful run for Los Angeles mayor this spring, Spencer Pratt, a Republican, paid two clipping firms a total of more than $55,000 to promote his campaign; one of the firms, Cliphaus, boasts on its website that its efforts generated over 50 million views.

“Spencer went from celebrity to serious candidate in the public conversation,” the Cliphaus site says. A Times review found accounts supporting Mr. Pratt based in India, Turkey, and the Philippines. Cliphaus, which is based in Los Angeles, brags of having a “network of 50,000+ independent creators.”

In a statement, ClipHaus co-founder Peter Sint said the firm “operates a global creator network, so creators and publishers participating on the platform may be based in different countries.” He added that “clients can choose specific geographies to target (i. e., U. S.-based accounts only). When it comes to most clients, this is the case.”

Jafari Jackson, a content creator based in Arizona, said he has participated in several campaigns he found on DrumBeat, another marketplace specializing in paid advocacy work. One, he said, pushed the idea that “extreme heat is a climate problem, not a political one,” while another called for content opposing the Save Our Bacon Act, legislation that would roll back state level animal welfare protections.

In recent weeks, DrumBeat hosted a campaign opposing President Trump’s efforts to restrict voting by mail that was sponsored by an unnamed nonprofit that “works to advance policies that support former U. S. service members and their families” and paid $5 per 1,000 views. Another, opposing the Clarity Act, a bill in Congress that would create business-friendly rules for cryptocurrencies, paid $250 per post and suggested scripted talking points including “if a financial system can be used to move money, it needs rules that help investigators stop trafficking and fraud.” (Last week the Senate blocked the bill.)

Mr. Jackson said that he doesn’t bother applying to the vast majority of paid campaigns advertised on DrumBeat, because he “wouldn’t make a video about something I didn’t believe in.”

But he said other creators might find it hard to turn down such opportunities. “While I do think that people should be 100 percent honest in these things,” he said, “it’s hard not to acknowledge the role money plays.”

Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

Ken Bensinger covers media and politics for The Times.

Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.
