Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on 2028: ‘Life Doesn’t Wait for You to Be Ready’

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Times Exclusive

In a wide-ranging interview, the New York congresswoman offered her most detailed insight yet into how she is thinking about a possible presidential run.

Times Exclusive

In a wide-ranging interview, the New York congresswoman offered her most detailed insight yet into how she is thinking about a possible presidential run.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York has several choices ahead of 2028: Keep her House seat, run for the Senate or seek the White House. Credit... Gordon Welters for The New York Times

Supported by

By Shane Goldmacher

Shane Goldmacher is a national political correspondent.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said she will weigh the decision of whether to run for president after the midterm elections. The decision is clearly already weighing on her.

In an interview with The New York Times, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez revealed the electoral equations she is crunching and the mental “math” she is calculating as she approaches the biggest crossroads of her political career.

Her gender. Her ethnicity. Her electability. Her eggs. Her movement. Her moment.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said. “And you don’t — and just in life in general — life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, 36, the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, is now in her eighth year representing parts of the Bronx and Queens. She could simply keep winning re-election. But in 2028, she has two other choices: run for the White House, or seek the seat now held by Senator Chuck Schumer of New York.

“Every element of this is something that’s within consideration,” she said.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez weighed aloud the pros and cons of running for president with unusual candor, sounding less strategic than searching, as if the right answer were somewhere nearby.

At times, she played the part of political pundit handicapping her own potential presidential candidacy from afar. At others, she voiced the unvarnished concerns of a woman who just opened up on Instagram (“Bloat check!”) about fertility treatments preparing for a possible future pregnancy.

“I think about it personally,” she said of a White House run. “I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life.”

“Pretty candidly, I think about my identity,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez went on. “I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez arrived in Congress as a left-wing outsider and remains one of the party’s most progressive voices. Some party strategists are urging Democrats to move to the middle. But Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was heartened by “the ascendance for the first time” of progressives like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan who toppled big-money candidates in this year’s Senate primaries.

“I have a tremendous amount of fear over the corruption of our political system,” she said.

She spoke by phone last week as she recovered in her Washington apartment from Covid. She had called to discuss an upcoming swing through upstate New York and a cash transfer to help Democrats in her home state.

She wound up describing much more.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez knows that broaching the roles of race and gender in politics can be unpopular, even unappealing. “I often hesitate to even talk about it,” she said, “because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint.”

She is talking about it anyway.

“If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh,” she said of running for president as a woman. “It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?”

She described the gender gap as a fact of American electoral politics: Roughly 27 percent of Congress is female, she said, and 0 percent of past presidents.

It’s not just that a five-second video of her adjusting her hair in the Bronx this year drew more than 25 million views on X and a tsunami of sexualized replies (“that’s the most kind of, like, brazen and obvious forms of it,” she said). It’s how “female politicians are discussed, approached, covered” overall.

“What is very odd about our political culture is that for some reason when you raise it, people just freak out,” she said. “They get so defensive at the mere suggestion that gender could play a role.”

She made plain that this was a problem “independent of ideology.”

“I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left,” she said.

The losses of the only two women ever to secure the Democratic presidential nomination, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, loom large. “It may or may not be related, but I absolutely empathize with the heartbreak that people feel around that and, frankly, how those women were treated,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said.

She said she had discussed the issue with Ms. Harris, who is also considering a 2028 run, but she declined to describe their private conversations.

“This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said with a laugh. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.”

Few politicians can command public attention like Ms. Ocasio-Cortez. Her egg-freezing set off a national conversation about fertility. Her offhand remark on ABC News that “Woke one was crazy” spawned a thousand takes on her thinking and her party’s evolution.

No matter the size of her megaphone, it is also true that no House member has ascended directly to the presidency in modern history. (Few see any applicable lessons in the election of James A. Garfield in 1880.) Even if she is one of the House’s most prolific fund-raisers, a potential attempted leap to the White House would be essentially unprecedented.

The Senate seat in New York could be an alluring alternative.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who won her seat by toppling a powerful Democratic House leader in a 2018 primary, did not rule out the possibility of challenging Mr. Schumer — even if he helps Democrats win a Senate majority in the midterms.

“That would honestly be the best possible problem we could have as a country,” she said of the idea that a Democratic Senate majority could further complicate her 2028 choices. She added, “We’re working hard to have that problem, and I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.”

Mr. Schumer, 75, has not announced his own 2028 plans.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez made this much clear: She is not waiting on anyone other than herself, whether that pits her as a primary challenger to a potential Senate majority leader or to a former vice president.

“I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference,” she said.

Back in May, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez went viral for an answer she gave at a forum with David Axelrod, the onetime adviser to former President Barack Obama, in which she said her ambitions were not a “title or a seat.”

“My ambition is way bigger than that,” she said. “My ambition is to change this country. Presidents come and go, Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go, but single-payer health care is forever, a living wage is forever, workers’ rights are forever, women’s rights, all of that.”

Mr. Axelrod said in an interview that he believed Ms. Ocasio-Cortez when she spoke about her motivations.

“She is very honest in her communications. It’s what makes her disarming,” he said. “Her bottom line is producing something for the people she’s fighting for, so I think this decision is partly seen through that prism.”

In her interview with The Times, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez repeated variations of that line about her lack of interest in “my title.” But she also expressed a keen awareness of the realities that House members must seek re-election every two years and that losing would mean being out of office entirely.

“It’s very all or nothing,” she said. “If I were to run in this cycle, and not win, I would be done.”

“And I am not opposed to that,” she added. But it was also a consideration. “That, in and of itself, does not exclude the decision,” she finally said. “But it has to make it worth it.”

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, her mentor and ally, is 85. Many on the left see Ms. Ocasio-Cortez as his natural successor. The two politicians’ “Fighting Oligarchy” tour in 2025 drew huge crowds.

“These rallies were bigger than the sum of their parts,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said. “When Bernie was on his own, or when I’m on my own, it’s different because we have overlapping but also complementary coalitions.”

In other words, she is thinking about the political coalition of Mr. Sanders, the runner-up in the last two open Democratic presidential primaries — and how it might intersect with her own.

Mr. Sanders had advantages that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez does not. His 2016 run made him a national figure on the left before the right took to attacking him. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has been a boogeywoman for Republicans almost since her arrival on the scene in 2018, and she would be the Democratic Party’s most progressive standard-bearer in decades, if not ever.

In a recent New York Times/Siena University poll, her favorable rating among Republicans was less than 1 percent — with 75 percent rating her unfavorably.

Overall, just 30 percent of likely voters nationally viewed her favorably, with 41 percent holding an unfavorable opinion.

Her democratic socialist ally, Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, had a higher favorable rating, 38 percent, and a lower unfavorable rating, 33 percent. (Born in Uganda, Mr. Mamdani is not eligible to serve as president.)

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez hailed Mr. Mamdani, 34, as “an incredible political talent.”

“There are also major differences between an executive position for a municipal seat and a legislative position,” she said, which regularly sets up “conflict with your peers.”

“Of course, obviously, there are…” she paused. “I don’t know why it’s controversial to say that there are headwinds in identity and gender.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is not just a good fund-raiser. She has raised $32 million from January 2025 to July 2026 — more than double the sum that any other House incumbent raised in their re-election account other than Speaker Mike Johnson or Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader.

She is prideful of her almost exclusive dependence on small donors.

“I have a tremendous amount of fear over the corruption of our political system,” she said. “There’s very few people who are financially independent from special interests that are able to advocate directly for the needs of working people.”

In the end, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez landed on the most familiar of lines to describe the driving force behind her 2028 decision.

“Where can I do the most good?”

I spoke with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez last week for a story about her plans to campaign in upstate New York. But during the call I found her unusually open about how much she is weighing a potential presidential run. She has said previously that she would decide after the midterm elections. In the interview, she offered some of the most detail to date about why she might run for the White House — and why she might not.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

An A. I. Image of Trump Kissing a Woman Was Fake. It Spread Anyway.

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Advances in artificial intelligence and the myriad ways content is shared online have made establishing authenticity even more difficult for users of social media.

paulinefulham

@paulinefulham

@rufus_matte

SprinterPress

@SprinterPress

SaltyGoat17

@SaltyGoat17

David Pakman Show

@davidpakmanshow

By Steven Lee MyersTiffany Hsu and Stuart A. Thompson

Steven Lee Myers, Tiffany Hsu and Stuart A. Thompson write about ways information is manipulated and spread online.

The first known instance of the fabricated image appeared online the afternoon of Sept. 14.

It was small, too blurry to make out much detail. Yet it seemed to show President Trump on a golf course locked in a kiss with a woman.

The woman can be seen only from behind, but resembles his personal assistant, Natalie Harp, whose role in Mr. Trump’s White House has become fodder for political attacks from Democrats. And from there, imaginations ran amok.

The image was posted on Threads, the social media platform, by a user who described himself as “the Rebel Scum Trump is warning you about.” From there it caromed to Facebook and Instagram, all platforms owned by Meta, and to X, the platform controlled by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk. A higher-quality version appeared as a thumbnail for the YouTube show of Keith Edwards, a Democratic political strategist and online influencer.

Disinformation researchers and digital forensics experts who scrambled to verify the image ultimately agreed that it was a fake generated by artificial intelligence, but that took many hours. Despite numerous red flags, the image racked up tens of millions of views and comments by users, who either believed or acted as if it were genuine.

The viral image exemplified how difficult it has become to trace fabrications to their origins, given the advances in technology and the variety of ways images can be altered as they are shared — perhaps intentionally. The diffusion of such a dubious image also served as a stark warning, ahead of the midterm elections on Nov. 3, that audiences online are highly susceptible to narratives that seem to affirm their own beliefs.

“They’re not even hiding it anymore,” a teaser on Mr. Edwards’ show claimed, promoting an unsubstantiated and vulgar commentary about Ms. Harp’s sudden prominence in Mr. Trump’s political orbit.

The White House promptly denounced the image as a fake. The half dozen researchers and experts who spoke with The New York Times concurred, though the consensus was not conclusive on the exact source and the origin.

The White House accused Democrats of being behind it; there is no evidence of exactly who created the image.

Whatever the case, Mr. Trump found himself the target of a practice he and his aides have embraced: posting manipulated, even fantastical images generated by A. I., including ones denigrating his political opponents and people protesting administration policies.

A reconstruction of the image’s spread by The Times shows how A. I.-generated images are quickly outpacing efforts to detect them, as social media is increasingly inundated with A. I. slop.

In this case, the image was made as if paparazzi had furtively captured Mr. Trump in an unguarded, intimate moment. That gave a sense of authenticity compared to the obviously artificial, cartoonish images that A. I. tools often create.

“It is a well-crafted little viral image, I have to admit,” said Darren L. Linvill, a co-founder of the Media Forensics Hub at Clemson University, which tracks how disinformation and propaganda spread online. “Fuzzy. Peeping through the trees. Spying on young love. It seems genuine.”

The post on Threads, which according to the account’s biography belongs to Martin L. Dart, “is what made this go viral,” Mr. Linvill said. Mr. Dart did not respond to messages on the platform.

As the image spread, many treated it as a smoking gun, saying it illustrated the Republican Party’s hypocrisy when it comes to personal conduct by its leader.

More discerning users immediately viewed the image with skepticism.

Some turned to A. I. tools to enhance the image, making it crisper and easier to study. That version contained telltale signs of A. I. — the woman appears to have six fingers — but it was difficult for experts to say whether those details were in the original or added by the enhancement.

Some A. I. detectors seemed to confirm the image was real, even though the tools frequently make mistakes. Other detectors found the opposite.

X added a community note to some posts suggesting it was likely to be a fake, but numerous other posts with the image remain online without a note. X did not respond to a request for comment.

Snopes and Lead Stories, two online fact-checking sites, also questioned the uncertain provenance of the image. No photo agency or photographer had claimed credit for it. Mr. Edwards, the podcaster, did not respond to questions about his post of the image, but a representative of his show told Snopes that they had found it online.

According to PeakMetrics, an analytics company, four distinct versions of the image surfaced online. All seemed to derive from one original, based on the position of the couple near a golf cart, framed by a white flagstick and trees along the fairway.

Mr. Trump had spent the previous weekend at his golf course in Ireland on an official visit, causing some users to think the image was from his trip. But the treeless landscape at that course differed significantly from the one in the image.

There were other clues casting doubt on the image: Mr. Trump is almost always photographed wearing a hat while he golfs, but was not wearing one in this image. Also, Ms. Harp, the aide, is not known to golf, though she has accompanied him on his frequent outings on the links. Some users pointed out that Mr. Trump in real life now appears far heavier than he does in the image.

The blurring in many of the images that spread made it more difficult to detect the role of A. I., according to the experts and researchers. Hany Farid, a professor at Dartmouth College and a founder of GetReal, a company that detects fakes, suggested that might have been the point.

He said the company’s analysis found that while the original was apparently A. I. generated, the reproduction of it as a thumbnail had the effect of erasing the digital fingerprints that identified it as an inauthentic image. Many companies add hidden watermarks to A. I.-generated images to help researchers identify fakes.

One low-resolution version of the image had no watermark, Mr. Farid said. Another sharper, higher-quality version looked like an authentic photo but did have embedded watermarks from either Google or OpenAI. Yet another version had a weak but different watermark.

Within a couple days, the fact-checks and official denials largely put the matter to rest, and the internet moved on, though the images remain online.

Mr. Farid, one of the world’s foremost digital forensics experts, said the speed of the image’s spread was startling. “It went from zero to millions really fast.”

His team’s attempts to retrace the image’s online trail was “pretty messy,” he said.

“We were really struggling to figure out what was going on,” he went on. “You can usually draw a little tree, like ‘this one is derived from that, and this one from that.’ We just couldn’t do it in this case.”

Steven Lee Myers covers misinformation and disinformation from San Francisco. Since joining The Times in 1989, he has reported from around the world, including Moscow, Baghdad, Beijing and Seoul.

Tiffany Hsu reports on the information ecosystem, including foreign influence, political speech and disinformation

Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.

Republicans in Tight Senate Races Call for End to Iran War

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Mike Rogers of Michigan distanced themselves from President Trump amid concern that high diesel prices could hurt the party in November.

By John Yoon

Two Republicans in tight Senate races have called for an end to the war in Iran, the latest sign that some candidates feel compelled to distance themselves from President Trump as they face voters angry about surging prices tied to the conflict.

Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, running for the open Senate seat in her state against Josh Turek, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, who faces Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, in Michigan, both separated themselves from the president on Monday after months of defending his authority to attack Tehran.

Persistently high fuel prices driven by the U. S.-Israeli war in Iran, launched in February, have caused frustration especially in rural areas and red states where trucks and farms rely on diesel, which reached $6.50 per gallon on Sunday, according to AAA.

The candidates’ remarks underscore mounting concern among some Republicans that the fallout from the conflict could prevent the party from retaining control of Congress. Democrats seized on the lawmakers’ turnabouts, noting that Ms. Hinson and Mr. Rogers had defended Mr. Trump and arguing that their proposals to tame fuel prices echoed Democratic platforms.

In a social media post, Ms. Hinson said that she supported the suspension of gas taxes, a pause in diesel exports and “a successful and immediate end” to the war. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” she said.

Mr. Rogers proposed similar measures in a campaign ad released later on Monday. “The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly,” Mr. Rogers, standing in a grocery store, says in the video. “When it does, energy costs will plummet.”

The candidates’ appeals put them directly at odds with Mr. Trump, who has dismissed concerns about the rising gas prices. The national average for a gallon of regular gasoline is $4.47, up 20 cents from last week, according to AAA Gas Prices. Mr. Trump said in a speech in North Carolina last week that the soaring costs were “a very inexpensive price to pay” for the war. He has said for several months that the war would end soon, easing prices.

But voters have grown increasingly weary of the conflict. More than three-quarters of independent voters said that they disapproved of Mr. Trump’s handling of the war, along with other issues like the economy, immigration and the cost of living, according to a poll from The New York Times and Siena University released last week.

Top Republicans have proposed to ban diesel exports to ease fuel prices before. Senator Charles E. Grassley of Iowa called on Mr. Trump to institute an embargo over the weekend, while Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, indicated last week that he was open to exploring the option. Another Republican, Vivek Ramaswamy, the nominee for governor in Ohio, said on social media on Monday that he supported a gas tax suspension.

Republicans have sought to distance themselves from the president in other ways. Mr. Rogers said last month that he supported a one-year moratorium on data center construction despite Mr. Trump’s vocal support for the A. I. industry.

Ms. Hinson has similarly downplayed her ties to Mr. Trump and the administration as a whole, skipping an appearance onstage at the president’s midterm convention in Dallas this month and opting not to attend a rally on Friday headlined by Vice President JD Vance in Council Bluffs, Iowa. Her campaign cited previously scheduled events as the reason.

Senator John Curtis, a Republican from Utah, on Tuesday called on the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate Donald Trump Jr. over whether he used his family relationship for financial benefit. Mr. Curtis also demanded the same scrutiny for Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joseph R. Biden.

On Monday, Democrats criticized the reversals. Dr. El-Sayed assailed Mr. Rogers as inconsistent, saying in a statement that “for Mike, we will see which way the wind is blowing next week.”

Mr. Turek, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Iowa, responded to Ms. Hinson on social media, needling her for changing her mind.

“Glad you’re finally following my lead after waffling on the proposals I put forward last week to address the rising costs of the war in Iran,” Mr. Turek said.

He added that Ms. Hinson, as a sitting House member, had repeatedly voted against resolutions calling on Mr. Trump to halt military operations or to seek explicit congressional approval to continue them, including one last week.

In that vote, other House Republicans facing competitive re-election bids crossed the aisle to curb Mr. Trump’s war powers in Iran. In all, seven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the measure, and two were Ms. Hinson’s Iowa colleagues — Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks.

John Yoon is a Times reporter based in Seoul who covers breaking and trending news.

GLP-1 Prescriptions for People With No Medical Need Are Climbing

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A new study identified more than 1 million people taking weight-loss drugs without any apparent medical reason to do so.

By Dani Blum

A large new study confirms what many people have long suspected: A sizable number of people taking drugs like Ozempic have no medical reason to do so.

The study, an analysis of the medical records of more than 92 million U. S. adults, identified more than 1.1 million who were taking GLP-1 medications, without any record of an issue that would make them eligible, like obesity or diabetes. While the researchers didn’t examine why people took these medications, doctors said many people are probably using them simply to shed some pounds or in the hope they might deliver other, buzzy potential benefits.

“You see it all over the place. You have people describing publicly their experience with these medications, some good, some bad,” Dr. Babak Orandi, an obesity medicine specialist and transplant surgeon at N. Y. U. Langone Health, and the lead author of the study, published Tuesday in the journal Obesity.

The positive anecdotes, he said, “may open up people’s curiosity to say, ‘Hey, maybe that could work for me.’”

Technically, GLP-1s have only been approved for a few conditions, including obesity and diabetes. The Food and Drug Administration has also approved some GLP-1s to prevent heart attacks and other cardiovascular issues and to treat sleep apnea, both in people with obesity, and to treat kidney disease in those with type 2 diabetes.

Age of Ozempic: The “fat activist” Virginia Sole-Smith is inspiring and infuriating her followers, and calling out the bias and discrimination faced by people in bigger bodies, especially from doctors and research scientists.

Adolescent Boys: For the longest time, researchers focused on diagnosing and treating girls with eating disorders, but that is changing. Two experts share why increasingly boys have these disorders too.

A Bigger Concern: TikTok shut down the “legging legs” hashtag, but experts said they’re more worried about other content surfaced by social media algorithms.

Palliative Psychiatry: Treatment wasn’t helping her anorexia, so doctors allowed her to stop — no matter the consequences. But is a “palliative” approach to mental illness really ethical?

But the drugs have become a cultural phenomenon, with the public discourse about them and the aggressive marketing of the medications generating far broader interest.

“It’s the first time that I can recall that the general public knows so much” about a drug, said Dr. Nils Krüger, a researcher at Harvard Medical School who has studied GLP-1s.

These “off-label” prescriptions, as doctors call them, became far more common as the study went on, jumping 15-fold between 2021 and 2025. And researchers say those findings are almost certainly an undercount, since they may not capture people who are accessing the drugs through telehealth platforms or taking compounded versions.

Shedding some weight is perhaps the most obvious reason people without obesity or diabetes might turn to the drugs. More than one in three of those taking a GLP-1 drug off label had a normal body mass index. Patients taking the drugs off label were also much more likely to have had a documented eating disorder than those who were not taking one of these medications. While the number of patients with eating disorders was still a small fraction of patients, doctors said it was still cause for concern.

Beyond weight loss, there are a host of other reasons people may be seeking out these drugs, outside experts said. For example, the study found that patients taking a GLP-1 drug off label were more likely to have high blood pressure or high cholesterol.

People might think, “‘Oh, it’s being used for vanity purposes,’” Dr. Orandi said. But he said that he has talked with patients who are interested in whether the drugs might help for other issues that aren’t included on their labels.

Scientists are in the early stages of studying the drugs for other possible uses, including improving fertility, curbing cravings for alcohol and alleviating brain fog. While researchers need far more data to determine if the drugs work for these purposes, doctors said they are already seeing patients try them, in the hope that they will.

Dr. Andrew Kraftson, a clinical professor at the University of Michigan Medical School who treats patients with obesity, noted that the new study also highlight how many doctors seem to be prescribing these drugs to patients who do not appear to qualify for them.

Busy primary care doctors whose patients request the drugs may think, “Well, what can it hurt,” he said.

“But still,” Dr. Kraftson added, “we totally are not giving comprehensive care in these situations,” Dr. Kraftson expressed concern that some doctors may not fully be assessing whether a patient could benefit from the medication, and whether any potential benefits outweigh the possible risks.

There is little data on how the drugs might affect people without obesity or diabetes, because they were largely excluded from major clinical trials.

These medications might pose unique risks to people who are not overweight, Dr. Krüger said. Those risks include malnutrition, as well as muscle mass loss, side effects of the drug that can affect anyone but that could be especially concerning in people with lower starting B. M. I. s.

“We don’t know how this will play out,” Dr. Krüger said. “It’s like this big Ozempic experiment.”

Dani Blum is a health reporter for The Times.

Hayden Panettiere Died From Toxic Effects of Fentanyl and Other Drugs

Hayden Panettiere (1989-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Panettiere, who starred in “Heroes” and “Nashville,” died last month at the age of 36. Her death was ruled accidental.

By Derrick Bryson Taylor

Hayden Panettiere’s death was caused by the toxic effects of fentanyl and other drugs, the Greenville County Coroner’s Office said in a statement on Tuesday.

The authorities added that alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine were also found in her system. The manner of death was ruled an accident, the statement said, and an autopsy showed no signs of trauma that would have contributed to the death.

According to the Cleveland Clinic, alprazolam, known as Xanax, is used to treat anxiety; methocarbamol, known as Robaxin, is a muscle relaxant; and quetiapine, known as Seroquel, is an antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and depression.

On Aug. 16, paramedics arrived at an apartment building in Greenville, S. C., where emergency responders administered advanced cardiac life support and resuscitation efforts. Ms. Panettiere, an actress best known for her roles on “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was pronounced dead at 36.

Ms. Panettiere was with Brian Hickerson, her on-and-off boyfriend, at the time of her death. According to her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” which she published this year, she met Mr. Hickerson in 2018 in Los Angeles. The two dated sporadically for several years.

Court records show that in 2021, Mr. Hickerson pleaded no contest to two felony counts of injuring Ms. Panettiere.

Derrick Bryson Taylor is a Times reporter covering breaking news in culture and the arts.

Veterans Package Stalls After House’s Swift Departure

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A veterans benefits bill that Republicans had hoped to pass ahead of the midterm elections is falling apart amid a battle over its cost.

By Olivia Diaz

Reporting from the Capitol

When House Republican leaders last week called off their final day of voting before the midterm elections and sent members home, they left behind a multibillion-dollar veterans benefits package they had once hoped would be a popular win to campaign on.

The sweeping bill, the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, would devote critical resources to veterans benefits and programs — the kind of measure that lawmakers typically relish taking back to their districts to promote in their bids for re-election.

Instead, the legislation is stalled and on the brink of collapse, mired in a funding dispute that has divided the two parties, splintered Republicans and driven a bitter wedge between powerful veterans groups that normally band together when benefits are at stake.

The impasse grew so intense that last Tuesday, Democrats won enough support from Republicans to go around House leadership and force action on a piece of the bill — a long-shot maneuver to salvage a measure that supporters worry is now doomed anyway.

The centerpiece of the bill is a provision that would allow service members who retired from the military because of a combat-related disability to receive their full retirement pay, rather than having it reduced dollar for dollar by their disability benefits, as current law requires. It is known as the Maj. Richard Star Act, named for a combat-injured Army veteran who advocated the policy change after he was forced to medically retire because of cancer that he developed from toxic exposure during deployments to the Middle East.

Republicans demanded that the cost of such a change — an estimated $9.4 billion over a decade — be covered by cuts elsewhere, and settled on paring back disability compensation for future veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus. But Democrats resisted the trade-off and dropped their support for the entire package, which also would include funding for dozens of other veterans programs, from suicide prevention to lactation rooms at V. A. hospitals. So did some Republicans, who blasted an approach that they said pitted veterans against one another.

“It is wrong and unseemly to take benefits away from a certain number of vets for a different group of vets,” said Representative Jeff Van Drew, Republican of New Jersey. “And I’ll tell you what: The veterans don’t like it.”

The proposed cuts, which lawmakers have estimated would save as much as $57 billion over a decade, created deep rifts in the veteran community. The American Legion and some other veterans groups urged Congress to back the package, in the interest of enacting the long-stalled Richard Star measure. But two other major veterans advocacy organizations — Disabled American Veterans and Veterans of Foreign Wars — said they could not support a bill that would slash tinnitus and sleep apnea benefits and have lobbied lawmakers to fix the bill or drop their support.

“I would love to see my full retirement pay, but I would feel terrible,” said Naomi Mathis, a deputy legislative director at D. A. V. who served in the Air Force before medically retiring in 2007. “I couldn’t even lay my head on the pillow and say that this is OK.”

The fierce divide among veterans and lawmakers came to a head in July, when House leaders tried to bring up the veterans package but were forced to pull it from the floor when it became clear they did not have the votes to pass it.

“Thank you, VFW, for screwing over current and future veterans and their spouses!” Representative Daniel Crenshaw, a Texas Republican and Navy SEAL veteran, wrote on social media at the time.

Other Republicans who opposed the cuts took matters into their own hands by going around Speaker Mike Johnson and signing on to an effort by Democrats to force a version of the Richard Star Act to the floor on its own.

Last Tuesday, that effort — a so-called discharge petition that can fast-track legislation to a floor vote if a majority of House members demand it — got the 218 signatures it needed to succeed. Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina provided the final signature, becoming the fifth Republican to do so.

“Washington has no business nickel-and-diming veterans who were willing to put their lives on the line for ours,” Ms. Mace said in a statement, adding, “Combat-injured veterans have waited long enough.”

It was the latest in a series of instances over the past two years in which Republicans have steered around Mr. Johnson to demand action on legislation he has been unable or unwilling to bring up.

“For months, one man decided whether this bill got a vote,” said Representative Mark Takano, the California Democrat who started the petition. “That is over. The House will have to vote, whether Speaker Johnson likes it or not.”

Mr. Johnson abruptly scrapped the House’s final day of voting last week after Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that would have required a vote by Thursday had the House remained in session.

Action on the Richard Star measure will not happen until after Congress returns following the midterm elections to what could be a radically different political landscape, leaving the fate of the entire package deeply uncertain.

That has left proponents of the broader bill embittered.

Representative Don Bacon, Republican of Nebraska and an Air Force veteran, said he was frustrated that the package had been stymied, suggesting that sleep apnea and tinnitus benefits had been manipulated by some of those who served. After retiring from the military, he said he remembered fellow veterans encouraging him to apply for relief for those conditions even though he did not experience them.

“The whole thing bothered me,” Mr. Bacon said. “I know that not everybody falls into that category, but there was surely some exploitation of these rules.”

The earliest House members could vote on any veterans bill would be upon their return on Nov. 9, two days before Veterans Day. Representative Mike Bost, Republican of Illinois and the chairman of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee, said the broader measure could still have a shot.

“I look forward to working with Speaker Johnson and our entire House Republican team to deliver on the promise we have made to these families when the House is back in session in November,” he said in a statement.

Even so, it could face steep obstacles in the Senate. Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, said he would not support cutting any benefits.

“The cost of caring for these veterans is part of the cost of war — past wars and the current,” Mr. Blumenthal said.

Olivia Diaz is a congressional reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Connections Coach

The machinists union shows how workers are negotiating for a say in the ways artificial intelligence is used in their workplaces.

Tim Suitter, president of the union that represents ship builders at Bath Iron Works, knows workers must be prepared for the arrival of artificial intelligence. Credit... Ryan David Brown for The New York Times

Supported by

By Rebecca Davis O’Brien

Rebecca O’Brien, who covers labor for The Times, was determined to write a story about A. I. without using the word “guardrails.”

Tim Suitter knows change is coming to Bath Iron Works, creeping up the adjacent Kennebec River in Maine like a foreboding fog.

Mr. Suitter, the president of the union that represents more than 4,400 workers who build battleships for the U. S. Navy at the shipyard, knows the workers must be prepared for the arrival of artificial intelligence.

“It’s going to be here,” said Mr. Suitter, 50, who has worked at the shipyard for nearly 30 years. “You have to wrap your head around it.”

Last month, when Local S6 of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers negotiated a new five-year contract with the defense company that runs the shipyard, the union insisted on updating longstanding language about technology. Now the union must be informed at the “conceptual stage,” rather than at implementation, of “any proposed addition or modified technology, equipment or process,” including A. I. and robotics.

“It was the union trying to force the company’s hand about being more transparent when it comes to A. I.,” Mr. Suitter said. “The sooner we can be part of that conversation and represent the members’ side of it, the better off we are.”

Unions are confronting A. I. as an existential danger to workers, not only because of the possibility of massive job losses but also because of its hand in the widening gap between wages and corporate profits. In April, Liz Schuler, the president of the AFL-CIO, called A. I. “the single biggest threat to working people of our lifetime.”

The threat has galvanized a labor movement that has been on its back foot for years. In terms of public opinion, unions are popular. A. I. is not. And yet union membership is at a low ebb — about 6 percent of American private-sector workers are represented by a union — and unions have been hobbled by state laws and a weakened National Labor Relations Board.

Putting A. I. at the top of the bargaining agenda is part of a strategy to overcome that disadvantage, using negotiations to establish boundaries and, labor leaders hope, direct A. I. from the ground up. As workers and employers try to make sense of the A. I. economy, these contracts could help shape policy.

“There is power, there is leverage right now,” said Moira Bulloch, a spokeswoman for the Communications Workers of America, which represents journalists, flight attendants and call center workers. A. I. policy is being set “contract by contract, employer by employer.”

The machinists union, which represents about 600,000 workers in the United States and Canada in industries like defense, aerospace, railroads and aviation, has been particularly proactive. Recognizing that A. I. portends promises as well as threats, the machinists have crafted model contract language and pushed for early, open conversations with companies that employ their members.

“Unions can set the pace,” said David Sullivan, the general vice president for the union’s eastern territory, who encouraged Local S6 to put in the new language.

About a year and a half ago, Joseph Bonomo, a labor lawyer at Pitta, a law firm in New York, realized that while companies were incessantly talking about A. I. on earnings calls, the unions he represented were not. He set out to change that, starting at the bargaining table.

“A. I. is the hill to die on,” Mr. Bonomo tells union clients. “Because if you don’t have a job at the end of that contract, what good was the contract?”

Mr. Bonomo is working with the machinists’ air transport division as an adviser. Richie Johnsen, who runs the division, said he was fine with A. I. being used as a tool to improve corporate profits that can transfer to his members: “But it shouldn’t be replacing people.”

“We have to put in language into our contracts that addresses that,” he added. “Because that’s the only way that happens.” The machinists represent workers at nearly every U. S. airline. The union is in negotiations with United Airlines and Alaska Airlines, and will begin negotiations with Southwest before the end of the year and with American early next year, Mr. Johnsen said.

When Mr. Bonomo spoke to Mr. Johnsen’s team in June, he began by talking about language. “Define the Function, Not the Marketing Label,” read one of his slides. Corporate speak about A. I. can be euphemistic, vague and mind-numbing.

“Employers may not necessarily say, ‘Hey, there’s a new A. I. system,’” Mr. Bonomo said. “They’re going to label it, characterize it as a scheduling tool, a safety platform, a productivity system, a camera upgrade, some routing software.”

He challenged the machinists to interrogate the jargon. What does the system do? Does it collect data? Make predictions? Is it influencing discipline, staffing, scheduling, pay rates? Did the vendor consult with the union before writing the code?

Unions are particularly concerned that A. I. is going to be used to monitor and discipline workers. Mr. Bonomo urges his clients to press for contract provisions that guarantee human review of reports generated by an algorithm.

“I want to be able to say, at the top: ‘If we come back with a contract for ratification and it doesn’t have this, they’re not going to approve it,’” he said. “‘There’s going be a rat outside tomorrow morning, and there’s going be a line of 1,000 people saying that you’re trying to eliminate jobs.’”

Mr. Bonomo also encouraged the machinists and other unions to leverage A. I. to their advantage. Unions could build their own large language models to harness decades of institutional knowledge and records. They could use A. I. to organize more shops.

“Unions have to be in that driver’s seat,” he said.

Like most Americans, the workers at Bath Iron Works primarily encounter artificial intelligence today in slop on social media, or web searches that spit out paragraphs instead of links. They may regard A. I. with distrust but fail to recognize that it’s already in use all around them.

This disconnect has made Devin Ragnar, who at 33 is one of the younger machinists at the shipyard, particularly nervous. Mr. Ragnar handles communications for Local S6 and has been pushing his colleagues, and the union, to be more aware of the reach of A. I. and more proactive about confronting it.

Last year, Huntington Ingalls Industries, a competitor to the shipyard, announced a partnership with Hyundai Heavy Industry that yielded a pilot program to bring A. I.-guided welding equipment to shipyards in Mississippi and Virginia.

“In construction, you hear a lot of ‘You can’t automate this!’,” Mr. Ragnar said. They think a robot can’t do the work, can’t climb a ship. But, he said “it’s very real — it’s happening.”

Mr. Ragnar served on the bargaining committee for the new contract at Bath Iron Works and pushed his fellow members to include language on A. I. He and Mr. Suitter said the company had seemed surprised by the request, as if they hadn’t put a lot of thought into the matter.

Recently, Bath Iron Works introduced a programmable arm that could weld — a co-bot, or collaborative robot, in modern parlance. “They didn’t exactly follow our contract language,” Mr. Ragnar said. The union filed a grievance, and is now working with the company to resolve it.

“A big part of our response was — imagine if this was a much more drastic, broad-reaching change?

In the past, the company might have just said, “Hey, we bought this $10 million machine,” according to Mr. Sullivan. In the future, the union would have warning. Mr. Ragnar said that since the contract was ratified, the company was coming to union leaders with questions about technology.

In response to questions, the company, General Dynamics Bath Iron Works, said it was “committed to being transparent with all its employees about future A. I. and new technology initiatives.”

Mr. Ragnar said he did everything he could to avoid using A. I. “If we let A. I. do menial tasks for us, we are letting these machines think for us,” he said. If welders surrendered some of their work to a co-bot, their skills would erode.

“It’s one of the best things about being human — creating, thinking, and problem solving,” he said.

Mr. Sullivan is more optimistic about the constructive use of A. I. in shipbuilding. If an A. I.-guided machine can weld a seam in 15 seconds — a fraction of the time it takes a human, without the risk of injuries — it could mean more ships under construction, and, in turn, more jobs, with a healthier work force.

“Maybe the new technology would be great,” Mr. Sullivan said. “It’s the unknown.”

Rebecca Davis O’Brien covers labor and the work force for The Times.

Mathematics Isn’t Just a Game to Let A. I. Solve. History Shows Why.

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

In our field of applied mathematics, the long, human process of trial and error — not just the solutions themselves — is often what has led to progress.

By Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend

Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend are professors of mathematics at Cornell University who will be writing occasionally for The Times about the future of research.

This year, artificial intelligence models have been mowing down open problems in mathematics, one after another, with brutal efficiency. The carnage escalated in early September, when OpenAI unleashed 10,000 agents on the Navier-Stokes problem, cracking it in just 88 hours. Just yesterday, the company announced that the same internal model had now “resolved more than 100 longstanding problems across most areas of mathematics” — results that OpenAI was waiting to release until it had figured out “the best way to inform the community of the rapid progress to prepare and adapt the field.”

Some mathematicians, however, are now drawing a line: To “adapt the field,” they believe, could hollow it out. This month, 27 Fields medalists — winners of mathematics’ highest honor — have signed a joint declaration stating that solving famous open problems is not, in itself, the goal. Such problems are “landmarks and lighthouses,” they write, whose deeper purpose is to guide mathematicians toward conceptual understanding and insight.

Terence Tao, one of the signers and among the most celebrated mathematicians alive, has put the concern more gravely. He has described what’s happening as “strip-mining” mathematics. Good problems, he argues, are like nonrenewable resources. Some of them — the smaller, easier ones — can help train the next generation of mathematicians. Young researchers try their hand on them, learning what they will need to push the field forward. If A. I. strips away the big problems and their satellites, it could destroy the entire mathematical ecosystem. Tao has suggested that some questions may even need to be fenced off from automated solvers, as if they were national parks for math problems.

Among A. I. enthusiasts, the declaration was met online with a great deal of eye-rolling. Aren’t mathematical problems supposed to be solved? If A. I. can solve them faster and better than we can, isn’t that progress? From the outside, mathematicians’ insistence on human understanding looked like guild protection — an attempt to save something for themselves now that machines are starting to beat them at their own game.

What this skeptical reaction misses is a distinction within mathematical culture. The Fields medalists are, by and large, “pure” mathematicians, scholars who look inward at mathematics itself, seeking beauty, coherence and a deeper understanding of its conceptual structures and abstractions.

By contrast, “applied” mathematicians — like the two of us — tend to look outward, drawing inspiration from problems in the real world and using mathematics to help solve them. And the long history of that pursuit, we believe, shows how costly it could be to cede our understanding of mathematics to machines.

For centuries, science and technology have advanced through a gradual but remarkably successful process: Observe patterns in nature, uncover the principles beneath them, express those principles mathematically and then use them to predict what happens next. Isaac Newton showed what that process could achieve. With a handful of mathematical laws, he explained both the fall of an apple and the motion of the planets. Three hundred years later, those same laws helped guide astronauts to the moon and bring them safely home.

Again and again, it was a slow back-and-forth between equations and applications that pushed math and engineering forward in tandem. Take the story of wireless communication. In the 1800s, Michael Faraday discovered empirical laws about magnets and electrical currents; James Clerk Maxwell then translated them into mathematics and predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves. Follow that understanding forward and eventually you get radio, television, wireless communication and cell phones.

That long process of trial and error, and the human understanding it led to, drove every revolution in physics that followed. Relativity eventually made GPS possible. Quantum mechanics led to lasers, transistors and much of modern electronics. With understanding came prediction, and with prediction came power.

By the middle of the 20th century, scientists and engineers were confronting problems of staggering size — too many variables, too many interactions, too many calculations for any human being to keep up with. World War II brought the issue to a head. Calculating artillery trajectories, breaking codes, predicting shock waves from explosions and designing atomic weapons demanded mathematics applied on a gigantic, unprecedented scale. People needed help.

Modern computers arrived just in time. At first there was nothing philosophically threatening about them. They were glorified adding machines: fast, indefatigable servants that obediently ground through calculations too arduous for any human to manage.

After the war, computers spread into civilian life, helping businesses with bookkeeping, databases, airline schedules and countless other chores. Along the way, their role began to broaden. Once almost anything could be represented as numbers, computers became handlers of data, giving us the everyday miracles we now take for granted: digital photographs of our children, the songs in our pockets, the messages we send around the world.

Before we knew it, computers were transforming medicine as well.

Consider magnetic resonance imaging, or M. R. I. These scans reveal the body’s soft tissue in extraordinary detail, something X-rays can’t do, and they do it without exposing patients to harmful radiation. Doctors use them to diagnose everything from brain tumors and multiple sclerosis to ligament injuries and cancer.

But M. R. I. has its drawbacks. A typical scan lasts 30 to 60 minutes, sometimes more. Move too much, shift a foot or take a deep breath, and the technician might have to start the scan all over again. Children who can’t keep still often need sedation to get through it.

M. R. I. scanning is slow because it collects an immense amount of data. Unlike an X-ray, which snaps a picture in a single flash, an M. R. I. machine works gradually. It builds up an image one piece at a time.

But what if the M. R. I. didn’t have to collect all that data to get a usable scan? What if a fraction of the data were enough to construct the whole image, as if filling in the blanks?

That’s the leap behind a mathematical breakthrough known as “compressed sensing.” The key insight is that an M. R. I. image contains much less information than its enormous number of pixels might suggest. Neighboring parts of the image tend to resemble one another, and many of its details are mathematically redundant. That means you don’t necessarily have to measure everything. With the right mathematics, a surprisingly small number of measurements can be enough to reconstruct the whole image.

But where did this breakthrough come from? For decades, mathematicians, scientists and engineers had been wrestling with a basic fact about the real world: Its signals and images are full of structure. They’re not random jumbles of numbers; they’re intricately patterned. A photograph of a landscape, a piece of music, the sound of a voice — each harbors mathematical regularities that allow it to be summarized economically. The trick is to find the right building blocks. Expressed in those terms, a natural data set that seems to require millions of numbers can sometimes boil down to just a handful of ingredients.

As people learned to exploit this feature of natural images and signals — a feature known as “sparsity” — the mathematics around it kept mutating and migrating. Fourier analysis showed how complicated signals and images could be built from simple waves. Wavelets gave a new way to pick out the most important building blocks. Work in statistics and optimization showed how to identify the most informative components among a host of possibilities.

And cross-fertilization from an unexpected source helped too. In the 1970s, geophysicists were trying to make sense of seismic waves traveling through the earth, either generated by earthquakes or deliberately deployed in the search for oil and gas. Like radiologists peering inside a human body with M. R. I., these earth scientists were trying to reconstruct something hidden but important — in their case, structures deep underground.

By the early 2000s, these once-separate streams of thought were ready to come together. Compressed sensing was their offspring. The breakthrough came when mathematicians, including Emmanuel Candès, Terence Tao (yes, the same Terry Tao) and David Donoho, proved rigorously that, under the right conditions, compressed sensing could reconstruct an image accurately from shockingly few measurements. These mathematical guarantees turned doubt into action, and soon, Donoho and his collaborators Michael Lustig and John Pauly translated the theory into a procedure that doctors could use.

The benefits were dramatic. In pediatric imaging, a scan that once took eight minutes and required sedation could now be done in just over a minute while the child was awake.

This, to an applied mathematician, is why human understanding matters. It lets us take a brilliant idea developed in one setting and confidently wield it as a tool in another. This is mathematics doing what the public rightly expects of it: making a difference in the real world.

Now, for the sake of argument, imagine that an A. I. model could bypass all of this hard-won understanding and skip straight to a much faster way of doing M. R. I. scans, without shedding any light on how it got there. That would be a wonderful advance, medically speaking.

But the history we’ve just told gives us reason to hesitate before declaring human understanding dispensable. We wouldn’t know what we might be missing — what new ideas, unexpected connections or applications might have emerged from our understanding of why the method worked.

Seen in that light, Terence Tao’s strip-mining concern looks less like mathematicians trying to save problems for themselves and more like a worry about what humanity as a whole might lose. Understanding has always been a mathematician’s private pleasure, yes. But again and again, it has also given humanity gifts that it never knew to ask for.

Steven Strogatz is the Susan and Barton Winokur Distinguished Professor for the Public Understanding of Science and Mathematics at Cornell University. Alex Townsend is an associate professor of mathematics at Cornell. Their book “Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World” will be published in November.

The Other Victims of China’s Church Crackdown

The New York Times September 22, 2026

Cherie Geng is trying to free her husband, a pastor, who was among dozens of church members detained by the Chinese police. At the same time, she must rebuild her life in exile.

Cherie Geng is trying to free her husband, a pastor, who was among dozens of church members detained by the Chinese police. At the same time, she must rebuild her life in exile.

Cherie Geng in her front yard. Credit...

Supported by

By Vivian Wang

Photographs by Lauren DeCicca

On the 308th day after the Chinese police took her husband, Cherie Geng was making dumplings. The smell of a finished batch wafted from the kitchen as she mixed flour and water at her dining table. Her 6-year-old son was busy trading Pokemon figurines with a friend, so Cherie pushed a plate toward the friend’s mom, who had come to drop him off for the play date.

“This is pretty good — the dough is soft,” the other mom said. “Last time I made dough, it was so hard I felt like I was choking.”

“I’m not great at it either,” Cherie said. “Normally it’s my husband who likes making dumplings.” He had been a one-man assembly line, sifting flour, mixing filling and folding wrappers. “If we were feeding two or three people, he’d say, ‘You don’t need to do anything.’”

Now, though, Cherie had to do everything. Her husband, a pastor at one of China’s biggest underground churches, was seized last October by officers who roused him from bed at 2 a. m. Afterward, Cherie, fearing arrest herself, had fled with their son to Thailand. Since then, she had been in charge of not just cooking, but also renting a home, sorting out visas, finding schools and earning an income. She’d had to figure out where she could find authentic Chinese beef noodles, where to buy Chinese picture books. Having just learned to drive in Beijing, she now had to drive on the other side of the road.

All this while trying to get her husband out of jail. She spent hours learning the intricacies of Chinese law and trying to craft attention-grabbing social media posts. Most days, it felt like all she could do was explain to her son where his father was.

The Chinese government’s crackdown on Zion Church was its biggest roundup of Christians in nearly a decade, as the authorities have increasingly tried to shut down religious groups that do not declare loyalty to the ruling Communist Party. In May, President Trump personally asked China’s leader, Xi Jinping, to free the lead pastor, Ezra Jin; Jin was soon released and now lives in the United States.

But eight church members remain in detention, including Cherie’s husband, Gao Yingjia. China has signaled that it may sentence them to more than 10 years in prison, and their families are desperately trying to keep attention on their cases.

At the same time, they must contend with how the arrests have rippled through their own lives. Most of the relatives who remain free had little public role at the church, and little preparation for what befell them. When Cherie once asked her husband whether they should make a plan in case he was arrested, he replied that they should just place their faith in God.

Now, Cherie, 46, had little choice. It wasn’t easy. She was on her own in a part of Thailand she had never been to before, unsure when she might see her home or her husband again. Even here, she didn’t feel totally safe: She slept with a golf club by her bed and didn’t want her specific location published, in case the Chinese police tried to track her down. Her husband’s trial had recently been postponed without explanation, which gave her faint hope that the charges would be dropped and he would be freed. But Cherie also knew that outcome was most likely preordained, and the delay might just mean more time in limbo.

In her hardest moments, Cherie allowed herself to imagine how things might have been different. Before she became a mother and a pastor’s wife, she had earned a Ph. D. in genetics and held a lucrative job at a pharmaceutical company. She could picture a world in which she had never become a Christian, never married a pastor and just lived a comfortable life.

Still, in some ways her ordeal had made her feel closer to her faith, and her husband, than ever before. Between batches of dumplings, she shared a post on X calling for the pastors’ freedom, and sent a text message to the other pastors’ relatives to confirm a strategy call later that night. Whenever she had time, she typed notes into her phone, both for herself and to write in letters for her husband, even though the jail rarely let mail in or out.

“Dear Yingjia, I miss you,” she began.

***

Relatives of the detainees logged onto the video call from all over the world: a wife who had fled to California, a husband in South Korea, elderly parents inside China. Sitting at her dining table, which was still cluttered with mixing bowls and her son’s toys, Cherie greeted the other church members’ loved ones, 12 in all, on her phone screen.

“Thanks for all your work today,” she said to the father of a pastor who had spent the day writing letters of protest to government officials.

“You haven’t been feeling well lately, right?” she said to another pastor’s husband. “Do you think you have Covid?”

They hadn’t been close before the arrests. Zion Church’s leaders had been scattered across China for years, since the government barred them from gathering in Beijing. The pastors led smaller, low-profile groups instead, coming together on Sundays for sermons streamed on Zoom, many of them given by Cherie’s husband, the church’s second-in-command.

Thousands of people tuned in. The church leaders knew that the police were likely among them, but they believed it was their duty to spread the gospel proudly and fearlessly. Besides, the authorities generally hadn’t imprisoned church leaders as long as they did not directly challenge the government. Yingjia and others had been hauled in for questioning and even held for a few days, but they were always released afterward.

Growing up in the countryside of northern China, Cherie had been introduced to Christianity by her mother, who hid with fellow worshipers in pig stalls to secretly listen to a local pastor. Her mother discouraged Cherie from joining a church herself, worrying that it was dangerous. But Cherie found her own way to faith when her work at the pharmaceutical company left her feeling empty. Bubbly, sociable and fluent in English after her Ph. D. studies, she left her job and started teaching the language to fellow churchgoers.

Still, worry was never far from her mind, especially after she and Yingjia adopted their son, John, in 2021. Her health was also deteriorating — maybe, she thought, because of the stress of frequent police raids on church meetings. Last summer, rumors began spreading that a bigger crackdown might be coming.

It came on Oct. 10, when they were at home in Beijing. Cherie received a call from a lawyer who said Zion’s lead pastor had been arrested, along with around two dozen other church members.

Scrambling, they removed their SIM cards from their phones and drove with their son to a friend’s house. But the police pounded on their friend’s door in the middle of the night and took Yingjia away. They accused him of illegal use of the internet in connection with his online sermons.

Cherie returned home to find her door broken open, her apartment stripped of electronics, books and her diaries. In the following days, she vomited repeatedly. Why hadn’t Yingjia wanted to make a plan? What was she supposed to do now?

At first, she resolved to stay in China. The police wouldn’t let her see her husband, but she could see his lawyers, who were allowed to visit him. She told John that his father was on a long business trip. But John overheard her talking to the lawyers and started having nightmares about her being seized, too.

She arrived in Thailand in January. It was a shock in many ways: the humidity, the noisy streets. She found an English-speaking congregation, and at first she marveled that she could worship without fear of persecution. But she also missed the sense of urgency that had come with Zion’s furtive services in China. The new pastor’s sermons, on comfortable domestic topics like parenting and education, sometimes felt distant from her own concerns.

She hesitated to tell people she met about her situation, not wanting pity or unsolicited advice. The sight of couples and families pained her. A few other Zion members had also fled to Thailand, but Cherie often wanted to be alone. She purposely chose a house way too big for just herself and John so she had a space to withdraw.

Every night, she and John prayed together in their bedroom facing a yard with mango and papaya trees. He always prayed to go back to Beijing.

Now she was at a rented dining table, collecting morsels about her husband’s case in the only way she could: through calls with the families of other detainees. Recently, as the trial loomed, the meetings had become more frequent. Cherie now knew the other relatives’ morning and evening routines, their parents’ names, their deepest fears.

The woman who had fled to California sounded tired as she joined the conversation — it was 5 a. m. there. Her voice shaky, she said the prosecutors were threatening her husband with a decadelong sentence if he didn’t plead guilty.

“Could that be a trap?” one father interjected.

“I think we need to ask the lawyers again what’s going on,” Cherie said. She often found herself in the role of mediator and comforter, her old teaching instincts kicking in. “If anyone else’s lawyers can go, too, they should try to find out if they’re increasing the pressure.”

“Sometimes they just exaggerate,” another caller said. “They might only plan to sentence you to three years, but they say 11.”

The conversation turned to when the court might reschedule the trial, when John, who had been playing on a tablet in the next room, started shouting.

“Mom! What’s wrong with this?” When she didn’t answer, he called again. “Mom, what’s wrong with this?”

She knew that John didn’t like it when she was glued to her phone. Rarely fussy in Beijing, he had become irritable since his father’s arrest. He got into fights at school and called Cherie ugly. She, in turn, sometimes yelled at or spanked him, and always regretted doing so afterward.

Cherie set her phone on the table and walked over. “It’s out of battery,” she said.

“Mom, come with me,” he said, tugging her toward the stairs.

“You go ahead,” she said, trying to dislodge him gently. But he wouldn’t relent, so she followed him.

She returned to the dining room a few minutes later, looking weary. She unmuted herself and put on a cheery voice.

“What’s going on now?” she said.

***

When Cherie and Yingjia first met through Zion, she thought he was too short, too serious and chewed too loudly. Like her, he had done a Ph. D. — his was in theoretical physics — but unlike her, he fulfilled the stereotype of the awkward scientist. But Cherie’s mother kept pressuring her to find a husband, and there weren’t many bachelors at Zion. Cherie decided to think of her marriage as a sacrifice to Christ.

Cherie struggled with her new identity as a pastor’s wife. She felt pressure to be good, but she disliked some people at church, lost her temper with Yingjia and still argued with her parents.

It was Yingjia who told her not to worry, that she should be herself and that God would take care of them. His unflappability drove her crazy at first. But over time, it became part of what she loved about him.

Now he wasn’t around, and she felt herself trying to satisfy others’ expectations again. She was always comforting the families of other jailed members; when she got tired, she took it out on John. Yingjia seemed to know that would happen. In one of his few letters that had reached her by mail, he urged her to stop putting on a happy face. “The fact that you always share the good news but not the bad actually makes me a bit sad, because I don’t get to be by your side during the difficult times,” he wrote in a letter dated May 2.

She especially felt his absence on June 18. That was the day the court was scheduled to decide whether to move forward with the case against Zion or drop it. Cherie, feeling optimistic, considered booking a flight back home so she could greet Yingjia when he was released. But her friends urged her to wait.

The morning of the decision, the lawyer called. Some church members had been released on bail, but Yingjia had not. In fact, the court had added charges, describing the offerings Zion had collected as fraud.

Cherie broke down. Friends swarmed her house to comfort her, but she felt only irritation. Why weren’t they offering her more support? Actually, why wouldn’t they go away — how could they know how she was feeling? What if, Cherie wondered, she went back to China, Yingjia gave up pastoring, they found new jobs and just prayed secretly?

***

So much of her life now was waiting — for news from the lawyers, for a letter from her husband, for some clarity on what the rest of her life would look like. But there was also so much to deal with every day. That was why, early on the Monday after she made dumplings, Cherie nudged a sleepy John out of bed, for her first day of work.

Cherie had hesitated to take a full-time job when she felt she already wasn’t spending enough time with him. But she needed money and a visa. And the job was teaching at a Christian school, so John could attend for free.

Cherie navigated slowly through morning traffic in the used Toyota Camry she had recently bought. It was a 40-minute drive, and she was still a nervous driver, steering down streets lined with tropical flowers and banana trees.

“What song do you want to listen to today?” she asked John.

“I don’t want to listen to songs,” he mumbled, his eyes still closed.

“Let’s listen to the songs I like then,” she said, putting on a Chinese worship song. “Buckle your seatbelt.”

“I don’t have the energy,” he said.

Lately, Cherie had been returning to one song in particular: “Never Ending Grace.” She had awakened with it playing in her head the morning after her husband wasn’t released on bail. It seemed like a sign, a reminder that everything she was going through had a higher purpose.

Every trial faced where I nearly stumbled

Every day that arrived unnoticed

Every peaceful moment taken for granted

What seemed ordinary was actually grace

So she was trying to give herself more grace, too. She had cut back on her meetings with the other families, so she could take John to soccer practice. She went to Muay Thai classes to build up strength (though, she noted in a letter to Yingjia, her abs were still in hiding). She invited her sister to visit from China to help take care of John.

And she prayed, constantly. There was an irony to her situation: Now, when the burden of being a pastor’s wife was heavier than ever, she was finally doing what Yingjia had always advised her to do, just giving up control and trusting in God.

Cherie sang quietly as she drove. She decided to put the lyrics in her next letter to Yingjia.

***

Cherie made it through her first day of work, but she couldn’t rest yet. After a dinner of steamed buns prepared by her sister, Cherie called a family meeting, a tradition from Beijing that had fallen off in the chaos of leaving China. She gathered her sister, her sister’s two children and John around the table to light a candle, sing a hymn and read the Bible.

At least, that was the plan. As Cherie played a hymn on YouTube, John wriggled out of his seat and blew out the candle. While she read aloud from Psalm 29, he stood on his chair, propping one foot on the table in a Superman pose.

“You think Jehovah is so awesome. That’s why you’re standing, right?” Cherie said. “Could you please sit down?”

When he didn’t move, her voice turned firmer: “You’ll break the table. Sit in the chair.”

She asked him to say a prayer. Still giggling, he complied.

“Thank you Jesus thank you Dad come home quickly thank you Mom,” he blurted in one breath. “Amen!”

The next morning, Cherie got up early to write to Yingjia. There was always so much to share. About how John had made a friend and stopped praying to return to Beijing. About how she had lost her temper with the boy, again, and he had bitten his arm until the skin broke. About how he was visibly happier with his aunt and cousins around.

But then John woke up and called for her.

And then it was time to go.

“Sorry, I’m about to be late. I have to go to work now. John wanted me to keep him company just now, so I couldn’t finish writing,” she wrote. “Love you always.”

I've been covering the Chinese government’s crackdown on Zion Church since the arrests last October. Since then, a lot of attention has focused on the pastors who were arrested. But I was also interested in the people left behind — the family members who hadn’t chosen the same level of risk, but found themselves caught up in the consequences anyway. Cherie Geng left behind a prosperous, comfortable life to become a Christian and marry a pastor, and now has to deal with the fallout alone.

Vivian Wang is a correspondent based in New York, where she writes about how China's global rise and ambitions are shaping the lives of people both inside and outside its borders.

How to Claim Your Cut of Apple’s $250 Million Siri Settlement

Wired September 22, 2026

In May, Apple agreed to pay out $250 million as part of a class action lawsuit over claims the company overhyped its Apple Intelligence tools, specifically the long-delayed Siri AI overhaul.

Although the revamped Siri AI voice assistant is now available for owners of newer iPhones via iOS 27, you may still be eligible to claim cash back for past purchases. This settlement covers customers in the US who made their purchases from June 10, 2024 to March 29, 2025, and bought certain iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 models from Apple. If you qualify, you might receive up to $95 for each phone.

This settlement revolves around Apple’s promotion of Siri features to sell iPhones. “I expected to receive a Siri Apple Intelligence feature and did not receive it,” reads part of the statement you have to sign when filling out the claim form. As part of the settlement, Apple denies any wrongdoing.

“We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” read part of Apple’s statement from May about the settlement.

To file a claim, visit the dedicated website: smartphoneaisettlement. com. Click the blue button in the top-right corner of the page labeled File A Claim. First, you’ll be asked whether you have a Claim ID and PIN to enter. It’s not required for you to already have this info on hand. On the final page, you’ll need either your iPhone’s serial number or Apple Account ID on hand to file the claim.

Not sure where your serial number is located? Open the Settings app, tap General, then choose About. Your serial number will be a string of letters and numbers near the top of the screen.

You can choose to receive the settlement money through PayPal, Venmo, an electronic bank transfer, or a paper check. If you have multiple devices and want to make claims for all of them, then you’ll need to fill out the form again for every eligible device. iPhone owners have until December 21 to make their claims.
